lessons.plain: Most companies already keep a master list of employees and their groups in an internal directory, such as Microsoft Active Directory. This objective covers two ways to bring that setup into Google Cloud. The first is copying the list of users and groups from your directory into Google's identity service on a schedule, so accounts appear and disappear automatically. The second is letting people sign in to Google Cloud through the company's own login system, so there is one place to check a password and one place to turn someone off. Both reduce how many separate accounts people have to manage.
lessons.guessPrompt: If an employee leaves the company and their account is disabled in the office directory, should they still be able to sign in to Google Cloud the next day? What would have to be true for that to stop happening automatically?
lessons.teach:
Cloud Identity is Google's identity service. It stores the user accounts and groups that can be granted access to Google Cloud. A directory is a central database of people and groups, usually run by the company, such as Microsoft Active Directory. Google Cloud Directory Sync, called GCDS, is a tool that reads your directory and writes matching users and groups into Cloud Identity on a schedule. It is one-way: the directory is the source of truth, so edits made in Cloud Identity to synced objects are overwritten at the next run.

GCDS works from sync rules, which say which parts of the directory to read, such as particular organizational units, and exclusion rules, which skip accounts such as service or test accounts. A simulation or dry-run mode shows what would change without changing anything, which is the safe way to check a new configuration first. Passwords are not normally copied; if password sync is enabled, the directory still checks the password itself.

Third-party single sign-on, or SSO, means a separate identity provider, called an IdP, such as Okta or Azure AD, handles the login. The user signs in once to the IdP, which vouches for them to Google. Google Cloud trusts that answer, so disabling the user at the IdP cuts off access without editing each project.

Worked example: an accounts team disables Priya in the directory at 17:00. GCDS runs at 18:00, sees that her account is no longer in the synced organizational unit, and suspends it in Cloud Identity. Her existing browser sessions may last until they expire, which is why session policy matters too.

Common mistake: adding a synced user to a group inside Cloud Identity and expecting it to stay there. The next sync reverts the change because the directory is the source of truth.

Consequence: if a sync fails silently, leavers keep working access. Sync runs must be monitored, not assumed.

questions.prompt: Bramble Clinics adds a sync rule to read its 'Contractors-2024' organizational unit (a folder of users in the company directory) and an exclusion rule that skips accounts whose names start with 'test-'. Before turning on live changes, the admin runs the tool in simulation mode, which reports what would change without changing anything. The report lists 212 changes, including 9 suspensions of active staff who were placed in the wrong unit by mistake. Step 1: the admin reads the report. Step 2: the admin finds the nine staff are wrongly placed in the directory. Step 3 is missing. What should the admin do next?
choices: Switch to live sync at the next scheduled run, since a simulation cannot change anything
Turn off password sync so that the suspensions are not applied
Correct the sync rule or the directory unit membership, then rerun the simulation until the reported changes match what was intended
Move the nine staff into a Cloud Identity group so the sync skips them
questions.why: The simulation is the safe check, so the fix belongs in the source configuration or the directory and the dry run must be repeated until its output matches intent before going live.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes Google Cloud Directory Sync (GCDS), the tool that copies users and groups from a company directory into Cloud Identity?
choices: It copies the password of every user into Cloud Identity on every run, so passwords are always identical
It is one-way, with the directory as the source of truth, so changes made in Cloud Identity to synced objects are overwritten on the next run
It is two-way, so edits made in Cloud Identity to synced users are carried back into the directory
It runs only when an administrator starts it by hand, so there is no schedule to monitor
questions.why: The teaching text states GCDS is one-way and that the directory is the source of truth, so Cloud Identity edits to synced objects are overwritten at the next run.

questions.prompt: A company uses a third-party identity provider (IdP, the separate service that handles login and vouches for users to Google) for single sign-on. A contractor's job ends, and the admin wants Google Cloud access to stop without editing each project. What is the correct action?
choices: Remove the contractor from every project's IAM policy one by one
Delete the contractor's browser cookies on each staff laptop
Disable the user at the identity provider, since Google Cloud trusts the IdP's answer
Wait for the next GCDS run, which will remove the contractor from the IdP
questions.why: In third-party SSO, Google Cloud trusts the IdP's sign-in answer, so disabling the user at the IdP cuts off access centrally.

questions.prompt: A sync rule reads the 'Finance' organizational unit in a directory. An exclusion rule matches accounts whose names start with 'svc-'. An account named 'svc-reporting' sits inside Finance. What happens to it during the sync?
choices: It is copied into Cloud Identity as a suspended account that cannot be changed
It is skipped and not written into Cloud Identity, because the exclusion rule matches it
It is copied into Cloud Identity but its password is cleared
It is copied into Cloud Identity and given every Finance group membership
questions.why: Exclusion rules skip matching accounts, so an account named svc-reporting is not written into Cloud Identity even though it sits in the synced unit.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we need both Directory Sync and single sign-on when both involve the company directory. Explain to them in your own words what each one does, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on a scheduled sync.
lessons.modelAnswer: Directory Sync copies users and groups from our directory into Cloud Identity on a schedule, so the accounts and group memberships exist in Google's system. Single sign-on is different: it decides where the password check and login happen, so a person signs in through our identity provider and Google trusts that answer. You can use one without the other, though they are often combined. The main tradeoff of a scheduled sync is delay. If someone is disabled in the directory at 17:00 and the sync runs at 18:00, there is a gap, and if the sync fails the gap grows silently. Sessions that were already open can also outlive the change, so we need to check session length and monitor sync results, not just configure the job once.
rubricPoints: Directory Sync copies users and groups from the directory into Cloud Identity on a schedule, one way
Single sign-on moves the login check to an identity provider that Google trusts
A scheduled sync has a lag, and a failed sync can go unnoticed
Open sessions may keep access after the account change, so session policy and monitoring matter

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly product configuration facts and vocabulary, which reading the official setup concepts covers better than any current OpsForge mission.

lessons.plain: Every company's cloud identity system needs one account that can fix anything, including the settings that control who can sign in and what they can do. On Google Cloud this is called a super administrator account. It is tied to the organization's identity directory rather than to any single project. Because it can override almost every other control, it is the most dangerous account in the setup. Managing it well means keeping very few of them, protecting them with the strongest sign-in checks, never using them for daily work, and watching every time they are used. Think of it as the master key kept in a safe, not the key on your keyring.
lessons.guessPrompt: If one account can reset every user's password and change every security setting, what is the safest number of such accounts a company should have, and why?
lessons.teach:
Cloud Identity is the directory service that holds the users and groups for an organization. A super administrator is the highest built-in admin role in that directory. A super admin can reset any user's password, turn two-step verification on or off, and grant other admins their roles. Because it sits above the other controls, every other control ultimately depends on it. This is why it matters: the super admin is the recovery path. If it is lost or taken over, no lower-level admin can fully undo the damage, because those lower admins received their powers from it.

Worked example. A company has one super admin, used for everyday tasks. Step 1: an attacker tricks its owner into revealing the password. Step 2: with no second factor required, the attacker signs in, resets the passwords of the other admins, and gives their own account the organization-level IAM administrator role. Step 3: they create a long-lived service account key and copy data out, while the logs show only what looks like a normal admin sign-in.

Common mistake: treating the super admin as a convenience login. A safer setup keeps two or three super admins, each used only in emergencies, each protected by two-step verification using a hardware security key, with recovery contacts kept current. Day-to-day work goes to delegated admin roles that carry only the powers each person needs.

Consequence: every super admin sign-in and privilege change should trigger an alert, because one unexpected use can change policy across every project in the organization. The super admin account is safe only when it is rarely used, tightly guarded, and watched.

questions.prompt: Northwind Retail, a regional chain with 400 staff, has three super administrator accounts in Cloud Identity. One of them is used every morning by the finance manager to reset staff passwords. The company plans a clean-up in four steps. Step 1: move the finance manager's routine password resets to a delegated admin role that covers only password resets for the finance group. Step 2: enroll the two emergency super admin accounts in two-step verification using hardware security keys, stored in separate safes. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: review the recovery contact details on all three super admin accounts each quarter. Which action belongs in the missing Step 3?
choices: Create a long-lived service account key so the finance manager's scripts keep running without interruption
Turn off two-step verification on the emergency accounts so that lockouts cannot delay recovery
Configure alerts for every super admin sign-in and every change to admin privileges
Lower the finance manager's account to a standard user and leave the super admin role in place for the emergency accounts
questions.why: The missing step is the alerting step, because the teaching text says every super admin sign-in and privilege change should trigger an alert, and the other choices either weaken protection or do not match the clean-up plan.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a super administrator in Cloud Identity?
choices: A service account that applications use to call Google Cloud APIs with a stored key
A role limited to viewing billing reports for a single project
The highest built-in admin role in the directory, able to reset any user's password and grant other admins their roles
The group that contains every end user who signs in to the organization's applications
questions.why: The teaching text defines the super administrator as the highest built-in admin role in the Cloud Identity directory, with powers to reset passwords, change two-step verification, and grant admin roles.

questions.prompt: A small firm wants its operations engineer to reset passwords for staff members, but the engineer should not be able to change two-step verification settings or grant admin roles to anyone. Which setup fits the least-privilege idea from the teaching text?
choices: Give the engineer the shared super administrator password so the team lead does not need to be involved
Make the engineer a super administrator so there is one admin with full access to avoid confusion
Assign the engineer a delegated admin role that carries only the password reset power
Create a long-lived service account key and let the engineer run password resets through a script
questions.why: A delegated admin role that carries only the powers the person needs matches the teaching text's guidance, while the other options give far more power than the requirement calls for.

questions.prompt: A company keeps one super administrator account for everyday work, and that account has no second factor. An attacker obtains its password. Which outcome best matches the risk described in the teaching text?
choices: Nothing beyond the one account, because lower-level admins keep their powers even if the super admin is compromised
The attacker can reset other admins' passwords and grant their own account admin roles, and lower admins cannot fully undo this because they got their powers from the super admin
The attacker can only read the organization's billing report, since admin roles are separate from the directory
Only the single user whose password was stolen is affected, because other admins have separate recovery paths
questions.why: The teaching text explains that lower admins receive their powers from the super admin, so a takeover lets an attacker reset other admins and grant roles in ways lower admins cannot fully reverse.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would set up and manage the super administrator accounts for a new company's cloud organization, and name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would keep two or three super admin accounts, separate from anyone's normal login, and store their recovery details securely offline. Each would use two-step verification with a hardware security key, and nobody would use them for routine work. Routine admin tasks would go to delegated roles, so each person has only the powers their job needs. I would turn on alerts for any super admin sign-in or privilege change, and I would test the recovery process once a year. The tradeoff is friction. Emergency access takes longer because the accounts are kept locked away, and if the security keys and backup codes are lost together, recovery becomes hard. So I would keep at least two keys in separate physical locations and document exactly who can authorize using them.
rubricPoints: Keep a small number of super admin accounts, separate from daily-use logins
Protect them with strong two-step verification, ideally hardware security keys
Use delegated admin roles for routine work so least privilege still applies
Monitor and alert on super admin sign-ins and privilege changes
Name a real tradeoff, such as slower emergency access or recovery risk if keys are lost

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly console settings, account policy, and product facts, which a reading lesson covers better than any current mission or planned engine.

lessons.plain: User lifecycle management means handling a person's account from the day they join, through any change of role, to the day they leave. Automating it means a trusted source, such as the HR system or an approved request, drives the account changes so people do not have to remember each step. Done well, a new hire gets exactly the access their role needs on day one, and a leaver loses sign-in and access quickly and completely. The hard part is rarely creating accounts; it is removing access that nobody remembered to take away.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose an employee moves from one team to another, and their old project access is never removed. Why does this happen when access is granted to individual users, and what would change if access were granted to groups instead?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A lifecycle is the sequence of states an identity passes through: joiner (account created), mover (role or team changes), and leaver (no longer needs access). Cloud Identity is Google's directory service for user accounts and groups; a user account there is the identity people sign in with. Provisioning means creating and configuring accounts and their access. Deprovisioning means removing or suspending them. Suspending a user blocks sign-in while keeping the account record, whereas deleting it removes the account itself.

Why automation works. People change roles without telling the security team, so manual steps get missed. If a source of truth (an HR record or an approved request) feeds the directory, and access is granted to groups rather than individual users, then one change in the source propagates to every place the group grants access. Adding someone to a group gives them the group's roles; removing them takes those roles away everywhere at once.

Worked example. A contractor's HR record gets an end date of Friday 17:00. Automation runs that evening: first it suspends the Cloud Identity account, which blocks new sign-ins; second it removes the account from the groups that carry project roles; third it flags any keys or tokens the person created, because those live outside the directory and survive a suspension, so they go to a person for review. On Monday, an audit shows no active grants tied to that contractor.

Common mistake. Granting roles directly to individual users. When that person leaves, someone must find every direct grant across every project, and any grant they miss keeps working.

Consequence. A leaver whose account still signs in, or whose group membership was never removed, can read and change resources long after the working relationship ended. This is a typical finding in an access review.

Access follows the group, and the group follows the source of truth.

questions.prompt: A university research lab runs this flow for a PhD student moving from the genomics team to the imaging team. The registrar's record changes on Monday at 09:00. Step one: automation removes the student from the genomics group, which removes that team's dataset roles across every project. Step two is blank and must be filled in. The imaging team's dataset roles are attached to a group called imaging-readers. Which single action completes the flow?
choices: Grant the imaging-readers roles directly to the student so the change is immediate
Leave the student in the genomics group until their old files are archived
Add the student to the imaging-readers group, so the group's roles apply to them
Suspend the student's account, which removes all of their team roles at once
questions.why: Access follows the group, so adding the student to imaging-readers gives them the imaging roles, while direct grants and leaving old memberships are the mistakes the teaching warns about.

questions.prompt: In directory administration, what is the difference between suspending a user account and deleting it?
choices: Suspending and deleting both keep the record, but deleting also removes group memberships
Suspending moves the account to a new directory, while deleting archives its files
Suspending blocks sign-in but keeps the account record, while deleting removes the account itself
Suspending removes the account record permanently, while deleting only blocks sign-in
questions.why: Suspension blocks sign-in while the account record remains, and deletion removes the account itself, as stated in the definitions.

questions.prompt: A consultant's account is suspended at the end of their contract. Two weeks earlier, the consultant created a service account key for a data export script. What is the main risk after the suspension?
choices: The key is automatically deleted when the group memberships are removed
The key is copied to the consultant's replacement, who can now use it
The key stops working as soon as the account is suspended
The key remains usable because keys and tokens live outside the directory and survive suspension
questions.why: Keys and tokens created by a person sit outside the directory and survive a suspension, so they must be reviewed separately.

questions.prompt: An engineer changes teams. Their old team's project was given to them as a direct grant on the user, not through a group. What problem does this create when they move on?
choices: Someone must find that direct grant in every project, and any grant they miss keeps working
The direct grant expires automatically after thirty days
Their account is suspended until the direct grant is manually approved
The new team cannot see the project because the grant is tied to the old group
questions.why: Direct grants on individual users are spread across projects and are easy to miss, so a leftover one keeps granting access after the person has moved or left.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how automating user lifecycle management reduces access risk, and name one limit or tradeoff of automating it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Automation ties account creation, changes and removal to a trusted source, usually the HR record or an approved request, so access changes happen whenever a person's status changes rather than whenever someone remembers a ticket. Granting access through groups means a change in the source propagates to every resource the group covers, which is what makes removal reliable. The limit is that automation only acts on what it knows about. If an HR record is late, or a person holds keys or tokens created outside the directory, the automation will not revoke them, so we still need periodic access reviews and a step that handles credentials the person owns. There is also a speed-versus-safety tradeoff: removal that is too aggressive can lock out someone who is only changing roles, so mover logic needs to be tested as carefully as leaver logic.
rubricPoints: Automation links account changes to a trusted source such as an HR record or approved request.
Granting access through groups makes removal propagate to every resource the group covers.
Automation only covers what it knows about, so late records or externally created credentials can be missed.
Aggressive removal can wrongly lock out movers, so mover and leaver logic both need testing and review.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission exercises cloud identity lifecycle, and the core skill here is explaining the propagation and its limits back to a teammate.

lessons.plain: Administering user accounts and groups programmatically means creating, changing, and removing people and team collections in an identity directory by writing a script or calling an API instead of clicking through a console. A user account is one person's login identity. A group is a named collection of accounts, so you can grant access to the group once rather than to each person in it. Doing this in code makes changes repeatable, reviewable, and easy to audit, and it prevents the drift that happens when many people edit things by hand. The skill is knowing which system holds the identity, which interface to call, and what permission the automation itself needs.
lessons.guessPrompt: A new engineer joins a team of forty people, and the team's access to a project should change with them. Would you rather add the engineer to one existing group, or grant the engineer each individual permission on the project one by one? Why?
lessons.teach:
A directory is the system that stores identities: users (individual accounts), groups (named sets of users), and sometimes organizational units (containers that hold accounts for policy purposes). On Google Cloud, these identities usually live in Cloud Identity or Google Workspace, which share the same directory behind the admin console. Administering them programmatically means calling that directory's API to create, read, update, suspend, or delete users and to add or remove group members. Common interfaces include the Admin SDK Directory API and the Cloud Identity Groups API.

Why this works: an API call has a defined shape, so the same request can be run again, stored in version control, reviewed by a second person, and recorded in logs. A sequence of console clicks leaves no reliable record of intent. The automation runs under its own identity, usually a service account, which should hold only the directory privileges its job requires. Domain-wide delegation, where an administrator lets a service account act on behalf of users in the domain, is powerful and must be scoped tightly.

Worked example: a script must add an analyst to the group data-readers@example.com. Step 1: the script authenticates as its service account. Step 2: it reads the group to confirm it exists. Step 3: it sends a membership request with the analyst's email and the role MEMBER. Step 4: it reads the membership back to confirm the change. Step 5: the audit log records the change under the automation's identity. Because the project grants access to the group rather than to the person, the analyst inherits that access with no separate permission edit.

Common mistake: giving the automation the super administrator role so nothing fails. That lets it change every account in the organization, including its own privileges. Assign a narrowly scoped admin role instead, and never use a super administrator account for scripts.

Consequence: a script that loops over a bad list can suspend many users at once, cutting off a whole team. Dry-run modes and small batches limit that blast radius.

questions.prompt: A company called Lumen Sprocket Ltd, on the domain sprocket.example.org, is offboarding 40 contractors. A script suspends their accounts. Step 1: the script authenticates as its service account, which holds only a user-management admin role and no super administrator role. Step 2: it runs in dry-run mode and writes the 40 addresses it would suspend to a file. Step 3: a reviewer checks that file against the offboarding ticket. Step 4: the script suspends accounts in batches of 10. Step 5: [missing step]. Step 6: the audit log is checked for 40 suspension entries under the script's identity. Which choice fills the gap at Step 5?
choices: The script grants the super administrator role to itself so that later batches do not fail.
The script skips verification and checks only the audit log after all 40 accounts are done.
The script deletes each suspended account so the addresses cannot be reused.
After each batch, the script reads back each account's status to confirm the suspension took effect before starting the next batch.
questions.why: The teaching text says changes should be confirmed by reading them back, and checking after each small batch limits how much damage a bad run can do before it is caught.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes administering user accounts and groups programmatically?
choices: Changing users and group membership by clicking through the admin console and saving screenshots as proof.
Storing user passwords in a shared spreadsheet that a script reads at each login.
Giving every employee a personal service account so each person can run jobs.
Calling the directory's API to create, read, update, suspend, or delete users and to add or remove group members.
questions.why: The teaching text defines this as calling the directory's API to manage users and group members, which gives repeatable, reviewable, logged changes.

questions.prompt: A cleanup script reads a list of 2,000 email addresses. A bug makes it treat every row as a suspend request. Which measure best limits the damage?
choices: Store the list in version control so the job runs faster.
Run it in dry-run mode first and in small batches so a bad list affects only a few accounts.
Run the script with more memory so it handles the list in one pass.
Give the script a longer timeout so it has more time to finish.
questions.why: The teaching text names dry-run modes and small batches as the way to limit the blast radius of a script that loops over a bad list.

questions.prompt: A service account is granted domain-wide delegation. What does that allow it to do?
choices: Act on behalf of users in the domain, so the grant must be tightly scoped.
Read every file in the company's storage without any further permission.
Become a permanent super administrator of the organization.
Operate without any role at all, because the delegation replaces roles.
questions.why: The teaching text explains that domain-wide delegation lets a service account act on behalf of domain users, which is powerful and must be scoped tightly.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why you would grant project access through groups and have a script manage membership, rather than granting each person roles directly. Name one limit or tradeoff of doing it programmatically.
lessons.modelAnswer: Granting roles to groups means access is defined once per team, so onboarding and offboarding become a membership change instead of a series of permission edits on every resource. Automating the membership changes makes them repeatable, reviewable, and logged under the automation's identity, which helps with audits. The tradeoff is that the automation becomes a high-value target: whoever controls its credentials or its delegated privileges can change access across the directory. So the script's identity needs a narrowly scoped admin role, its key or delegation must be protected and audited, and bulk operations should be tested in a dry run first. A bad input file can otherwise remove many people at once.
rubricPoints: Groups hold the access, so membership changes replace many individual permission edits.
Scripted changes are repeatable, reviewable, and logged with the automation's identity.
The automation's own privilege is a risk and must be narrowly scoped and protected.
Bulk operations can cause wide damage, so dry runs and small batches are needed.

suggested.rationale: Directory API facts and console steps are reference material, and no listed mission or planned engine has the learner administer users and groups.

lessons.plain: Workforce Identity Federation lets people in your company sign in to Google Cloud using the login system they already have, such as a corporate single sign-on service, instead of each person needing a separate cloud account. Think of a building where the front desk accepts the badge your employer issued and then hands out a visitor pass that expires. Google Cloud trusts the outside system to vouch for people, then decides what each vouched person may do using its own permission rules. Mastering this means knowing which part proves who someone is and which part decides what they can touch.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a company already has one login system for all its staff, should each employee also need a separate cloud account to reach cloud resources, and what would you check before letting anyone in?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A workforce identity provider is the outside system that really checks passwords and second-factor prompts, such as a corporate single sign-on service. A workforce identity pool is a container in Google Cloud that holds the trust settings for one or more of those providers. An attribute mapping copies fields from the provider's signed sign-in statement, such as a department or group name, into attributes Google Cloud can read. An attribute condition is a filter that decides which provider users are accepted at all. An accepted person is represented as a principal, and access is granted by binding IAM roles to principals or to principal sets, which are groups of principals selected by an attribute.

Why it works. Google Cloud does not check the password itself. It verifies that the provider's signature is valid and that the condition passes, then issues a short-lived access token. Authorization still happens in IAM, so changing a role binding changes what a person can do.

Worked example. A payments company runs an OpenID Connect provider, a sign-in system that issues signed identity statements. Step 1: create a pool and a provider that trusts that issuer. Step 2: map the department field to an attribute called department. Step 3: set the condition so only users whose department is payments are accepted. Step 4: bind a read-only storage role to the principal set for department payments on one project. A payments engineer signs in, receives a token, and can read the bucket. A marketing user is refused at step 3 and never reaches IAM.

Common mistake. Teams map attributes but skip the condition, or bind a broad role to the whole pool. Then every account the provider can authenticate, including old contractor accounts, gets access.

Consequence. Access depends on the provider. Disabling a person there stops new tokens, and tokens already issued expire quickly because they are short-lived.

questions.prompt: A hospital network trusts its own sign-in provider through a workforce identity pool. The team has already completed three steps for a new auditor group. Step 1: create a pool and a provider that trusts the hospital's sign-in provider. Step 2: map the group field from the provider's signed statement to an attribute called team. Step 3: set the attribute condition so only users whose team equals audit are accepted. The auditors need read access to audit logs in the single project records-audit-prod, and nobody else. Which step completes the setup?
choices: Bind the log viewer role to the whole workforce identity pool so every accepted user can read logs.
Turn off the multi-factor prompt in the hospital's sign-in provider so auditors can sign in faster.
Bind the log viewer role on records-audit-prod to the principal set where the team attribute equals audit.
Create a service account key for each auditor and store it in the project for them to use.
questions.why: The condition in step 3 already limits who is accepted, and binding the role to that principal set on one project gives read access only to the auditors and only where it is needed.

questions.prompt: Which term names the container in Google Cloud that holds the trust settings for one or more outside sign-in providers?
choices: Principal
Workforce identity pool
Workforce identity provider
Attribute mapping
questions.why: A pool is the container that holds trust settings for one or more providers, while the provider is the outside system that actually checks passwords and second-factor prompts.

questions.prompt: A retail company's sign-in provider can authenticate former contractors as well as employees, and the pool currently accepts every account it can authenticate. Only employees in the store-ops group should read a reporting dataset. What change fixes this most directly?
choices: Shorten the token lifetime so contractors' tokens expire faster.
Give the reporting role to the whole pool and ask contractors to stop signing in.
Rotate the sign-in provider's signing key every month.
Add an attribute condition that accepts only store-ops group members, then bind the dataset role to that principal set.
questions.why: The condition decides which provider users are accepted at all, and a role bound to the store-ops principal set limits access to that group, while the other options do not restrict who is accepted.

questions.prompt: An engineer was disabled in the company's sign-in provider two minutes ago but can still read a storage bucket. Which explanation fits how the setup works?
choices: IAM role bindings are removed automatically when a provider disables a user, so the bucket should be blocked immediately.
The principal set is cached permanently in the pool, so the engineer keeps membership until the cache is cleared by hand.
A token issued before the disable is still within its short lifetime, so it keeps working until it expires.
Google Cloud checks the password again on every request, so the old password still works for a short time.
questions.why: Google Cloud does not check passwords itself, and disabling a user only stops new tokens, so a token issued earlier continues to work until its short lifetime ends.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only used a shared company login how Workforce Identity Federation lets staff reach Google Cloud without personal Google accounts, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on an outside provider.
lessons.modelAnswer: Staff keep signing in to the company's existing identity provider. Google Cloud is set up with a workforce pool and a provider that trusts that system. The provider's signed statement is checked, an attribute condition decides who is accepted, and the person gets a short-lived token. Permissions still come from IAM role bindings on the principal or principal set, so the cloud side does not store a password for each person. The tradeoff is dependence: if the provider is down or its group membership is wrong, access changes with it, and a loose condition can admit more people than intended. So I always review the condition and keep the roles narrow.
rubricPoints: Describes the outside identity provider as the place where people authenticate, with a pool and provider as the trust link
Separates authentication (who the person is) from authorization (IAM roles granted)
Explains the role of attribute mapping and attribute conditions in deciding who is accepted
Names a real limit, such as dependence on the provider or the risk of a loose condition

suggested.rationale: Explaining the trust chain back to a teammate is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine teaches federation directly.

lessons.plain: A service account is an identity for software rather than a person. An app, a virtual machine, or a pipeline signs in as it to call cloud services. Cloud projects often come with default service accounts that are created automatically, and in the past these often carried very broad permissions that nobody chose on purpose. Securing them means finding which ones exist, removing powers they do not need, giving real workloads their own dedicated accounts, and watching which identity does what. The goal is that if one piece of software is compromised, the damage stays small.
lessons.guessPrompt: A new virtual machine starts running and was never given a specific account of its own. Without anyone choosing it, what do you think that machine can do inside the project, and why would that be a risk?
lessons.teach: A service account is an identity used by software. Google Cloud's access system, IAM (Identity and Access Management), decides what any identity may do by checking the roles granted to it. A role is a named bundle of permissions, such as permission to read objects from one storage bucket. A default service account is one the platform creates for you automatically, typically for compute machines and for Google's own services acting on your behalf. Its name follows a predictable pattern, so it is easy to overlook. Why this matters: a workload running as an account inherits that account's roles. If a default account was granted a broad role such as Editor when the project was created, every machine running as it can change almost anything in the project. An attacker who takes control of one web server then gets the same reach. Protection works in layers. First, inventory the accounts and the resources that use them. Second, revoke broad roles from default accounts and replace them with narrow roles on the specific resources needed. Third, give each real workload its own user-managed account holding only the roles its job requires. Fourth, use an organization policy to stop automatic broad grants to new default accounts. Finally, review audit logs to see which identity made which call. Worked example: a nightly batch job reads files from one bucket but runs as the project default account, which has Editor. Step 1, create a dedicated account for the job. Step 2, grant it only the read role on that one bucket. Step 3, switch the job to the new account and confirm it still works. Step 4, remove Editor from the default account if nothing else depends on it. Common mistake: assuming a default account is harmless because nobody logs in as it. Machines may still run as it, so disabling it without checking usage can break workloads. Consequence: a compromised machine running as an over-privileged account can delete data or create resources across the whole project, not just the one thing it needed.

questions.prompt: A video transcoding service at a media company runs as the project's default compute account, which was given the Editor role when the project was set up. The team fixes it in steps. Step 1: list every workload that runs as that default account, which finds this one service. Step 2: create a user-managed service account named transcode-sa and grant it read access on the source bucket and write access on the output bucket only. Step 3 is missing. Step 4: remove Editor from the default account. What belongs in the missing Step 3?
choices: Delete the default account so nothing can run as it again
Turn on billing alerts for the project before changing anything
Point the transcoding service at transcode-sa and confirm its jobs still complete
Give transcode-sa the Owner role so the switch cannot fail
questions.why: The service must actually run as the new account and be checked to work before Editor is removed, because removing the broad role first could break a workload that still depends on it.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a default service account in Google Cloud?
choices: A key file you download once and store in source control so code can authenticate
An identity the platform creates automatically, often for compute machines, whose roles may be broader than the workload needs
A human user account that the platform creates for the project owner to sign in with
A group that bundles several user-managed accounts so they can be granted roles together
questions.why: A default service account is an identity created automatically for machines and platform services, and it may carry broad roles granted at project creation.

questions.prompt: A team disables the default compute account in a project because nobody signs in as it. Afterward a scheduled backup virtual machine fails to write its files. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The backup virtual machine was running as that account, so disabling it cut off an identity the machine depended on
Disabling accounts deletes all audit logs for the project, so the backup job has no record to resume from
Editor was automatically granted to the backup virtual machine when the account was disabled
Service accounts can only be disabled during a billing change, so the disable step did not finish properly
questions.why: Machines can run as a service account without any human logging in as it, so disabling an account in use breaks the workloads that rely on it.

questions.prompt: A payroll reporting service must write one new file into a single storage bucket named payroll-out and nothing else. Which setup follows least privilege?
choices: Grant the service's identity the Owner role on the whole project so later changes are easier
Grant the default account Owner on the project so it can manage its own permissions
Create a dedicated service account and grant it only the object creator role on the payroll-out bucket
Leave the service on the default account, which already has Editor on the project
questions.why: A dedicated account with one narrow role on the one bucket it needs gives only the access the job requires, while the other choices give far more reach than the task needs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a default service account is a security risk, what you would do about it, and one limit or tradeoff of your fix.
lessons.modelAnswer: A default service account is created automatically and can end up with broad roles such as Editor, which lets it change most resources in the project. Any machine or service that runs as it inherits those powers, so one compromised workload could reach far beyond its job. My fix is to find what runs as it, give each real workload its own user-managed account with a narrow role on the specific resource it uses, and then remove the broad grant from the default account. A tradeoff is that this takes effort: you must map dependencies first, because removing access too early can break a running service. An organization policy can stop automatic broad grants on new projects, but it only helps going forward, so existing projects still need a review.
rubricPoints: Default service accounts are created automatically and may hold broad roles nobody intended.
A workload inherits every permission of the account it runs as, so over-privilege spreads risk.
The fix is a dedicated account per workload with narrow roles on specific resources, and removing broad default grants.
Changes must be preceded by finding dependencies, and an organization policy only prevents future automatic grants.

suggested.rationale: A planned authorization policy evaluator would let learners test whether a given role grant on a service account allows or blocks a specific action, which is the core reasoning this objective needs.

lessons.plain: Some software needs to call a cloud service on its own, with no person typing a password. A backup script on a server, a web app that reads files from storage, or a deployment pipeline that updates a running system are all examples. These programs need their own identity, a kind of account for a machine. In Google Cloud that identity is called a service account. Deciding when a task needs one, instead of borrowing a person's login, is the skill this lesson covers.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly script running on a virtual machine must copy files from a storage bucket. Should it sign in as the engineer who wrote the script, or use a separate identity made for that machine? Why?
lessons.teach:
A service account is an identity that belongs to a program or machine rather than to a person. It can be granted permissions the same way a user can, and a program running as that identity can call cloud APIs, such as reading a storage bucket or starting a job. A permission is granted through an IAM role, which is a named bundle of allowed actions attached to a specific resource, project, or folder. IAM, identity and access management, is the system that decides who can do what. A human signs in with a user account from the company directory; a workload acts through a service account.

Use a service account when the caller is non-human: an application on a server, a container, a scheduled job, a CI/CD pipeline, or a function that runs with nobody present. Do not use one to let a person do their own work. People keep their own identity, and their access is granted through groups.

Why this works: the program's permissions are separate from any person, so when the engineer leaves, the job keeps running, and audit logs show which workload performed each action. Attach the account to the workload so the program receives short-lived credentials automatically, rather than shipping a long-lived key file.

Worked example: a reporting job runs on a virtual machine and writes to a bucket named reports. Step one: create a service account called reporting-job. Step two: grant it a role that allows writing objects, scoped to the reports bucket only. Step three: run the virtual machine with that account attached. Step four: the job's writes succeed, and attempts to read other buckets are refused.

Common mistake: granting a broad project-level owner role to the account because the job failed once. The consequence is that if the job is ever compromised, the attacker inherits those broad rights across the whole project.

A service account is the right identity for software, and its permissions should be as narrow as the job needs.

questions.prompt: A service account is an identity that belongs to a program rather than a person. An IAM role is a named bundle of allowed actions attached to a specific resource. Harbor Foods runs a nightly invoice exporter as a Cloud Run service in project ledger-prod. It reads PDF files from the bucket invoice-archive and must write CSV summaries to the bucket export-drop. The engineer has completed three steps: created a service account named invoice-exporter, granted it read-only object access on invoice-archive only, and deployed the service with invoice-exporter attached. The exporter now fails when it writes to export-drop. Which step is still missing for least privilege?
choices: Grant invoice-exporter the Owner role on the whole ledger-prod project so that no write will ever be blocked again
Grant invoice-exporter a write-capable role attached to the export-drop bucket only
Create a long-lived JSON key for invoice-exporter and paste it into the container image so the service can authenticate
Add the finance engineers' group to the export-drop bucket so the service can borrow their access
questions.why: The exporter still needs permission to create objects, and the least-privilege fix is a role that allows writing, scoped to the one bucket it writes to, matching how read access was already scoped.

questions.prompt: Which situation most clearly calls for a service account rather than a person's own user account?
choices: A scheduled script that copies log files from one storage bucket to another every hour with nobody present
A manager who needs to view a dashboard that her team already shares through a group
A contractor whose access should end automatically on a fixed date
A new analyst who needs to sign in to the reporting console each morning to check figures
questions.why: An unattended scheduled program is a non-human caller, which is exactly when a service account is the right identity, while the other three involve people who should keep their own identities.

questions.prompt: A CI/CD pipeline (an automated system that builds and deploys software) must deploy to the staging project in an organisation with several projects. Which permission setup follows least privilege?
choices: Grant the pipeline's service account the Owner role on the whole organisation so that deploys never fail for missing rights
Store a long-lived key file for the pipeline's account in the shared repository so it can authenticate from any machine
Give the pipeline's service account a deploy-capable IAM role on the staging project only
Let the pipeline run using whichever developer's personal account is currently signed in on their laptop
questions.why: Scoping a deploy-capable role to the single staging project gives the pipeline only what it needs, whereas the other options grant excessive rights, borrow a person's identity, or expose a long-lived credential.

questions.prompt: An engineer says: the reporting job broke last week, so I'll give its service account the Editor role on every folder in the organisation. What is the main risk of this change?
choices: Audit logs will stop recording the account's name, so actions cannot be traced to the job
The account will be unable to authenticate until its password is reset by an administrator
If the job is ever compromised, an attacker inherits broad rights across many projects, not just the resource the job needs
Nothing changes in practice, because roles only take effect after the job is restarted
questions.why: Broad roles attached to a service account carry across the whole scope they are granted on, so a compromised workload would gain far more access than its task requires, which is the core failure this objective guards against.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you decide whether a new task needs a service account or a normal user login, and name one limit or tradeoff of using service accounts.
lessons.modelAnswer: I ask who or what is making the call. If a person is signing in to do their own work, they get a user identity from the company directory, and their access comes through groups. If the caller is software that runs without anyone present, such as a scheduled job, a pipeline, or an app on a server, it needs a service account. I then grant only the roles that task needs, on the narrowest resource possible, and attach the account to the workload so it does not depend on a downloaded key file. The tradeoff is that service accounts need active governance. Someone has to own each one, review what it can do, and avoid or rotate its keys, because a leaked key works from anywhere until it is revoked. A service account also cannot give accountability for a human action in the audit logs, so I keep human actions on human identities.
rubricPoints: Service accounts are identities for non-human callers such as applications, jobs, and pipelines.
Human users keep their own identity and receive access through groups rather than through a service account.
Permissions should be granted narrowly, on the specific resource the workload needs.
Keys are a risk: a leaked key works until revoked, so attaching the account to the workload is preferred.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style situation about which identity fits a given workload adds the most here.

lessons.plain: A service account is an identity for a program rather than a person. When an application, a virtual machine or a scheduled job needs to call a cloud service, it signs in as a service account, and that account is given only the permissions it needs. Creating one gives you a new identity, disabling one stops it from signing in while keeping it around so you can switch it back on, and authorizing one means deciding which actions it may take on which resources. Think of it as giving a program its own badge with a short list of doors it can open, instead of lending it your own keys.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly report job on a cloud platform needs to read files from one storage location. Should it run under your own personal login, or under its own separate identity with access only to that location? Why?
lessons.teach:
A service account is a Google Cloud identity meant for software, not a human. It has an email-style address, and you can grant it roles, which are named bundles of permissions such as the right to read stored objects or start a virtual machine. IAM, identity and access management, is the system that stores these grants. A grant is a binding that combines three things: a principal (the identity being allowed), a role (the bundle of permissions), and a resource (a project, a folder, or one single storage bucket). Every request is checked against the bindings on the resource and on the places above it in the hierarchy.

Creating a service account gives you a fresh identity with no permissions at all. Disabling it means it can no longer be used to authenticate, but its grants and configuration remain, so you can re-enable it. Disabling is a containment step, used when you suspect misuse or before deleting, and you should first check which running workloads still depend on the account, because they will start failing at once.

Authorizing means granting the smallest role on the smallest resource that still lets the job work. This works because a stolen credential can only do what its bindings allow.

Worked example: a nightly report job must read files in one bucket called reports-raw. Step 1: create a service account named report-reader. Step 2: grant it a read-only object role on the reports-raw bucket only. Step 3: run the job as that account. Step 4: the job lists and reads objects there, and any attempt to write is refused, because a read-only role does not include write.

Common mistake: granting a broad basic role such as Owner or Editor at project level to silence a permission error. The consequence in a running system is that if that job's credentials leak, an attacker controls the whole project, and disabling the account later may break unrelated services that shared it.

A service account should hold only the access its one workload needs.

questions.prompt: A small dental clinic runs a nightly job that uploads backup files to a storage bucket named dental-backups-2024. The team follows these steps. Step 1: create a service account named backup-uploader. Step 2: grant backup-uploader a role that allows creating new objects in the dental-backups-2024 bucket only. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: the job runs and uploads the day's files, while an attempt to delete last year's backups is refused. Which step correctly fills the gap at Step 3?
choices: Delete backup-uploader and create a new account with the same grants under a different name.
Grant backup-uploader the Owner role on the whole project so that no future upload can fail with a permission error.
Disable backup-uploader so that it cannot be misused while the job is idle.
Configure the nightly job to authenticate as backup-uploader instead of the project's default identity.
questions.why: Creating the account and granting it a narrow role only protects anything if the job actually authenticates as that account, so the job must be configured to use it.

questions.prompt: A research group creates a new service account for a data-cleaning script. Immediately after creation, and before anyone grants it a role, what can the account do?
choices: It can do nothing, because a new service account starts with no permissions until a binding grants it some.
It can sign in to the console with a password set at creation time.
It can read every storage bucket in the project by default.
It automatically inherits the Editor role from whoever created it.
questions.why: A service account begins with no permissions, and access only exists once a binding gives it a role on a resource.

questions.prompt: A payments team suspects that a service account used by a reporting service has been misused. They disable the account immediately. Within minutes, an unrelated scheduled export and a second dashboard both start failing. What step was skipped, and what is the correct lesson?
choices: They should have granted the account the Owner role so that disabling it would not break the export.
Nothing was skipped; disabling an account never affects other workloads, so the failures must come from elsewhere.
They should have checked which running workloads still depended on the account before disabling it, since disabling stops every use of it at once.
They should have deleted the account first, because deletion is the only containment step that is reversible.
questions.why: Disabling stops authentication for every workload using the account, so dependencies should be identified first, and disabling (unlike deleting) keeps grants so the account can be re-enabled.

questions.prompt: A logistics company needs a script to read sensor files stored in one bucket named sensor-archive, and the script must never be able to modify or delete them. Which grant best meets this requirement?
choices: Grant a dedicated service account a read-only object role on the whole project, so future buckets are covered too.
Grant the script's account the Editor role on the project that contains the bucket.
Grant a dedicated service account a read-only object role on the sensor-archive bucket only.
Grant the script's account the Owner role on the bucket, then remove the delete permission from its personal account.
questions.why: The smallest role on the smallest resource that still lets the job work is a read-only role on that single bucket, held by a dedicated account.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when a workload should get its own service account rather than using a person's login, and name one limit or tradeoff of disabling a service account compared with deleting it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Give a workload its own service account whenever it runs without a person at the keyboard, such as a scheduled job, a web service or a build pipeline. A personal login is tied to one human, so it tends to get shared around, outlives that person's role, and carries all of their permissions. A dedicated account can be granted only what that workload needs, its activity shows up separately in the logs, and it can be disabled without touching anyone's own access. The tradeoff with disabling is that it is a blunt switch: any running process that depends on the account will start failing immediately, so you have to find its dependents first. Deleting is cleaner for retiring an account, but it is harder to undo, so disable first, watch for breakage, and delete later once you are sure nothing needs it.
rubricPoints: Names a workload with no human at the keyboard as the reason to use a service account.
Explains that a dedicated account gets only the permissions that workload needs and can be traced separately in logs.
States that disabling stops authentication immediately and can break dependent workloads.
Says deletion is harder to undo, so disable first and delete later once dependencies are confirmed.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a scenario about which identity fits and what the smallest grant is adds the most here, since no listed mission drills Google Cloud service accounts directly.

lessons.plain: A service account is an identity that software, not a person, uses to call cloud services. A service account key is a downloadable secret, usually stored in a file, that proves a program is that identity. Anyone who holds the file can act as that program from anywhere, and by default the key keeps working until someone deletes it. This objective is about keeping those files from leaking, finding out who has used them, and removing the risky ones.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team's build server needs to call a cloud API. Someone proposes downloading a long-lived key file and storing a copy in the project's code repository. Name two things that could go wrong, and suggest one safer alternative.
lessons.teach:
A service account is an identity for software rather than a person. A service account key is a downloadable credential, usually a JSON key file, that contains a private key. Whoever holds the file can sign in as that service account. Unlike a short-lived token, a key does not expire on its own by default, so it stays valid until someone deletes it.

Why this is risky: the key is a bearer secret. The cloud service checks that the request carries the key, not where the request came from. A copy in a code repository, a chat message, a laptop backup, or a container image is as powerful as the original.

Securing means limiting how keys are created and stored. An organization policy constraint can block creation of new service account keys across the resource hierarchy, so teams must use other ways to authenticate. Auditing means reading Cloud Audit Logs, which record key creation and deletion as administrative activity and record API calls made by the service account, so you can see what it did. Mitigating means deleting keys that are unused or exposed and rotating the ones you must keep.

Worked example: a build job's key is committed to a repository. Step 1: the file is pushed. Step 2: a scanner or outsider finds it. Step 3: they call an API as the service account. Step 4: the audit log shows calls from an unfamiliar address. Step 5: you list the account's keys, delete the leaked one, review the logged actions, and move the job to a credential that expires.

Common mistake: deleting the whole service account to stop the leak. That breaks every workload that depends on it and can destroy evidence you need. Remove only the exposed key after checking the logs.

Consequence: until the key is deleted, anyone holding it has the same permissions as the service account, so an over-privileged account turns one leaked file into a project-wide compromise.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's invoice-sync service account has a key whose ID ends in 3f2a, and a public code snippet has just exposed it. The response runs as follows. Step 1: the security lead confirms the key ID from the exposure report. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: the team deletes key 3f2a. Step 4: the sync job is moved to a credential that expires. Which step belongs in the gap?
choices: Rename the service account so the exposed key no longer matches its name
Review Cloud Audit Logs for calls made with key 3f2a since the exposure, to see what the key was used for
Turn off the organization policy that blocks key creation so the job can get a new key
Delete the invoice-sync service account and recreate it with the same roles
questions.why: Reviewing the audit logs for the exposed key before deleting it shows what an outsider may have done with it, while deleting the whole account or renaming it would break workloads or leave the key valid.

questions.prompt: A payroll service account has a key that was created with no expiry date and was copied to a shared drive. Which property of this key makes the copy dangerous?
choices: Whoever holds the file can sign in as the account, and the key does not expire by default
The cloud service checks the device that presents the key before accepting it
The key only works when presented from the IP address where it was originally created
Only the account owner can read the contents of the file once it is downloaded
questions.why: A service account key is a bearer secret: the service checks that the key is presented, not who or where the presenter is, and the key stays valid until deleted.

questions.prompt: A reporting service account has three keys. One was created two years ago and has not been used in over a year. The file for a second key was found in a container image pushed to a public registry. The third key is used by a nightly job. What should be done with the keys?
choices: Delete only the exposed key now, and leave the unused key until the next annual review
Leave all three keys in place, because deleting a key could break the nightly job
Delete the whole service account so no key can be misused
Delete the unused and exposed keys after checking logs, and rotate the key the nightly job needs
questions.why: Mitigating means deleting unused or exposed keys after checking the logs and rotating the keys you must keep, without deleting the whole account.

questions.prompt: An organization policy blocks creation of new service account keys across the whole resource hierarchy. A developer creates a new project under the same organization and tries to make a key there. What happens?
choices: The creation succeeds, because new projects start with a clean policy
The creation succeeds, because the developer's own account is not a service account
The creation succeeds, but the key is set to expire after one hour
The creation is still blocked, because the constraint applies across the hierarchy beneath where it was set
questions.why: An organization policy constraint applies across the resource hierarchy, so a new project under the organization is covered and key creation remains blocked there.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would stop service account keys from becoming a security risk in our project, and name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would first block creation of new service account keys with an organization policy, so nobody can make a new long-lived file by default. Then I would audit the existing keys: list each service account's keys, check Cloud Audit Logs for recent use, and delete any key that is unused or whose owner cannot be identified. For workloads that still need access, I would move them to credentials that expire, such as short-lived tokens or workload identity federation. The main tradeoff is that some older systems may not support the newer method, so blocking keys can break them until they are migrated. A temporary exception process with an end date helps, but it has to be tracked or it becomes permanent.
rubricPoints: Explains that a service account key is a long-lived bearer secret that works until deleted.
Names blocking key creation with an organization policy as a preventive control.
Describes using Cloud Audit Logs to see key creation and the account's API activity.
States a tradeoff, such as legacy systems breaking until they move to short-lived credentials.

suggested.rationale: That mission makes the learner fix a deploy's authentication without exposing the secret, which is the core handling skill behind this objective.

lessons.plain: Some access is granted for a few minutes or hours and then stops working on its own. These are short-lived credentials: a temporary pass, like a day visitor badge instead of a permanent key card. A program or person asks for the pass, uses it for a task, and when it expires the system refuses it without anyone having to remember to cancel it. Security engineers prefer them because a copied pass is only useful for a short window, while a permanent key copied from a laptop keeps working until someone notices and removes it. Learning this means knowing where such passes come from and how to make software request them safely instead of storing a permanent secret.
lessons.guessPrompt: A script runs on a server every night and needs to read files from a cloud storage bucket. Option A: store a permanent password for a robot account in the script's config file. Option B: have the script ask the cloud for a pass that expires after an hour each time it runs. If an attacker copies that config file, which option leaves them less to work with, and why?
lessons.teach:
A credential is anything that proves who or what is making a request. A long-lived credential, such as a password or a downloaded key file, stays valid until someone deletes or rotates it. A short-lived credential is an access token: a random string issued by the cloud's identity system that carries a fixed expiry time. Google Cloud access tokens usually last about an hour by default. Once that time passes, the token is rejected, even if nobody revoked it.

Why it works: the window of damage is bounded by the lifetime. If a token leaks, an attacker can use it only until expiry, not forever. When the client needs more access, it asks for a new token, and the identity system grants one only if the caller still proves its identity and is still permitted to do the task.

Managing them has three parts. First, decide which identity gets tokens: a service account (a non-human identity used by software) or a person signing in. Authorization checks then decide what that token may do. Second, obtain tokens through the official client flow rather than storing them, so the program requests a fresh token at start-up or when the old one nears expiry. Third, keep lifetimes as short as the task allows.

Worked example: a nightly export job starts and presents its service account identity to the token service. The service issues a token valid for one hour. The job reads the bucket with that token. At the next run, which begins more than an hour later, the job asks again and receives a new token, because the old one has expired.

Common mistake: caching a token in a file or baking it into an image and reusing it for weeks. It works until expiry, then every call fails with an authentication error. A saved copy is still a secret that needs protecting.

Consequence: a long-running service that fetches its token once at start will start failing about an hour later, often overnight, with no code change. The fix is to let the client library refresh the token automatically.

Short-lived credentials limit how long a stolen token helps. They do not replace careful access control, because a valid token still carries every permission its identity holds.

questions.prompt: A clinic chain runs an appointment-sync service every 20 minutes under its own service account. At 08:00 the service presents its service account identity to the token service and receives a token valid for 60 minutes, until 09:00. It uses that token at 08:20 and 08:40, and both calls succeed. At 09:05 the next run begins, and the service must make a call that the token service will accept. The missing step is what the service does before making that 09:05 call. Which action fills the gap?
choices: Edit the stored token file to push the expiry time forward by one hour
Request a token with a 24-hour lifetime so that future runs never need to ask again
Keep using the 08:00 token, since it was already accepted twice and nothing has revoked it
Present its service account identity again and request a fresh token, because the 08:00 token expired at 09:00
questions.why: The token expired at 09:00 regardless of revocation, so the service must obtain a new one by proving its identity again, and the token service grants it only if the identity is still permitted.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines a short-lived credential as the course uses the term?
choices: A key file downloaded once and stored on a server until someone deletes it
A password that the user must change every few weeks to stay secure
A permission list attached to a bucket that limits which identities may read its objects
A random token issued by the identity system with a fixed expiry time, rejected after that time even if never revoked
questions.why: A short-lived credential is an access token with a built-in expiry time that the system enforces automatically, which is what the third option states in plain terms.

questions.prompt: A payroll exporter for a logistics firm fetched its token once during deployment on Monday morning. By Tuesday afternoon every call fails with an authentication error, though the code has not changed. What is the most likely cause and the right fix?
choices: The bucket was deleted overnight, so the fix is to recreate it and redeploy
The service account lost its key file, so the fix is to generate a new long-lived key and paste it into the config
The token expired about an hour after it was fetched, so the fix is to let the client library request fresh tokens automatically
The firewall blocked the export port, so the fix is to open all outbound ports on the network
questions.why: Tokens expire after roughly an hour, so a program that fetches once will fail later with no code change, and the course's fix is automatic refresh through the client library.

questions.prompt: An engineer stores a valid access token in a config file, and an attacker copies it within its one-hour lifetime. The engineer argues that the short lifetime makes the token harmless. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: The token is harmless only if the attacker lacks the bucket name, because tokens are bound to resource names
The token is fully safe because the attacker must also know the service account password to use it
The short lifetime limits the window but not the reach, since the token still carries every permission its identity holds during that hour
The token is harmless because it expires within the hour and cannot be used after that
questions.why: Short lifetimes bound how long a stolen token works, but during that time it grants all of the identity's permissions, so least-privilege access control is still required.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we keep a permanent service account key out of deployment scripts, what a short-lived token does instead, and one limit of the short-lived approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: A permanent key file is a secret that stays valid until someone rotates or deletes it, so if it leaks through a repository, a log, or a copied config file, an attacker has indefinite access. A short-lived token instead has a fixed expiry, usually about an hour, and the job requests a new one whenever it needs it, provided its identity is still allowed. That bounds the damage from a leak to the token lifetime. The limit is that the token is still a bearer credential: anyone holding it can use it until it expires, and it carries all the permissions of its identity. So we also keep those permissions narrow and make sure the job refreshes tokens properly rather than caching one and breaking later.
rubricPoints: A permanent key stays valid until rotated, so a leak has no natural end date
A short-lived token expires on its own, bounding how long a leak helps an attacker
Software should request fresh tokens through the client flow rather than store them
A valid token still carries its identity's permissions, so least privilege still matters

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style scenario about which credential type fits a job will teach the choice better than a catalogue-style read, and no listed mission covers token lifetimes directly.

lessons.plain: Workload Identity Federation is a way for software running outside Google Cloud, such as a build job on another provider or a pipeline on a code-hosting service, to prove who it is using the identity it already has, and then act inside Google Cloud without anyone handing it a stored key file. Think of it as a trusted translator at a border: the outside system shows its own badge, the translator checks that the badge comes from an issuer you chose to trust, and then issues a temporary pass that Google Cloud accepts. The main benefit is that nothing long-lived has to be copied around, stored in a config file, or rotated by hand. It is about machines and workloads, not about people logging in.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your CI job runs on a different cloud provider and needs to upload files to a Google Cloud storage bucket. What is the safest way to give it access, and why might the usual approach of downloading a long-lived key file be risky?
lessons.teach:
Workload Identity Federation is the mechanism that lets an external workload exchange a token from its own identity provider for a short-lived Google Cloud credential. An identity provider (IdP) is the system that vouches for identities, for example a cloud provider's workload identity service, a CI platform's token issuer, or a Kubernetes cluster's OpenID Connect issuer. A workload identity pool is a container you create in Google Cloud to hold the external identities you trust. A provider inside the pool describes one specific IdP: which issuer to trust, how to check its tokens, and an attribute mapping that turns claims in the external token, such as a repository name or account ID, into attributes you can write rules against. An attribute condition is an extra filter that must be true before the exchange is allowed.

Why it works: the external token is checked against the trusted issuer, the mapped attributes identify the workload, and the Security Token Service issues a short-lived federated token. Access is then granted in one of two ways. You can grant roles directly to a principal set, meaning a group of federated identities that match an attribute, such as every run from one repository. Or the federated identity can be allowed to impersonate a service account, which then carries the roles.

Worked example: a CI job from repository acme/fleet-api presents its token. The provider maps the repository claim to an attribute, and its condition requires the owner to be acme. The condition passes, the token is exchanged, and the job impersonates a deploy service account that has write access to one bucket. The resulting token expires within an hour, and no key file exists anywhere.
