Common mistake: leaving the attribute condition empty or too broad, so that any repository from the trusted issuer can get in. The consequence in a running system is that an unrelated project or a forked repository could write to production resources. The condition is the real trust boundary, so it must be as narrow as the workload it serves.

questions.prompt: Lumen Freight runs a nightly export from a self-hosted build agent. The agent's tokens come from a Kubernetes cluster's OpenID Connect issuer. The team creates a workload identity pool named freight-ops and a provider inside it that trusts that issuer. The provider maps the token claim for the namespace into an attribute called namespace. The export job should be able to impersonate a service account named export-reader, which has read access to one reporting bucket. Trace the flow. Step 1: the provider checks the agent's token against the trusted issuer. Step 2: the namespace claim is mapped to the namespace attribute. Step 3: [missing step, to be completed by you]. Step 4: the Security Token Service issues a short-lived federated token. Step 5: the job impersonates export-reader and reads the bucket.
choices: Confirm the attribute condition is true for the mapped namespace value, such as requiring the namespace to be the export namespace, before the token exchange is allowed.
Create a service account key file for export-reader and copy it onto the build agent so the job can authenticate.
Skip the condition, because the issuer is already trusted by the provider and the issuer's tokens are therefore safe from any namespace.
Grant the cluster administrator role to the federated principal set so the exchange has enough rights to succeed.
questions.why: The attribute condition is the filter that must pass before the exchange is allowed, so step 3 is checking that the mapped namespace value satisfies it.

questions.prompt: In Google Cloud, which object is the container you create to hold the external identities you choose to trust?
choices: A provider, which describes one specific identity provider and its token checks.
A workload identity pool, which holds the external identities you trust.
An attribute condition, which is an extra filter applied during the token exchange.
A service account, which carries roles that a federated identity can impersonate.
questions.why: A workload identity pool is the container that holds trusted external identities, while the provider sits inside it and describes one specific issuer.

questions.prompt: A team at Harbor Analytics sets up a provider that trusts a CI platform's token issuer. Its attribute condition only checks that the token is well formed, with no check on which organisation or repository the token came from. A fork of an unrelated public project presents a valid token from the same issuer. What is the most accurate description of the risk?
choices: The provider will reject the fork because the issuer signature is unknown to Google Cloud.
The fork can complete the exchange and reach whatever the federated identity is allowed to do, because the condition does not narrow who may enter.
The fork gains owner rights on the whole project, because a missing condition defaults to the highest role.
The token will expire too quickly for the fork to use it, so the risk is small.
questions.why: An empty or overly broad attribute condition is the real trust boundary, so a valid token from the trusted issuer can get in and use the granted access.

questions.prompt: A reporting job from one repository needs to read a single dataset in a Google Cloud project. Which setup follows least privilege most closely?
choices: Grant the Owner role on the whole project to the principal set that matches the repository, so the job never hits a permission error.
Create a long-lived service account key and store it in the repository's secrets so the job can authenticate without the exchange.
Give the job's federated identity permission to impersonate a read-only service account, and make the attribute condition match only that repository.
Grant the Editor role to every federated identity from the issuer, then rely on the dataset's name to keep the job focused.
questions.why: Impersonating a narrow read-only service account, combined with a condition that matches only the one repository, limits both who can enter and what they can do.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we use Workload Identity Federation instead of downloading a service account key for an external CI job, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: A downloaded service account key is a long-lived secret. It can be copied, committed by accident, or leaked from a CI log, and it stays valid until someone rotates or deletes it. With Workload Identity Federation, the CI job presents the token its own platform already issues. Google Cloud checks that token against an issuer we explicitly trust, applies an attribute condition, and gives back a short-lived credential that expires on its own. Nothing secret is stored in the repository or the CI settings. The tradeoff is setup complexity: we have to configure the pool, the provider, the attribute mapping, and the condition correctly, and a loose condition can let the wrong workloads in. Also, the external platform must be trusted, so if its token issuer is compromised, our trust is compromised too.
rubricPoints: Explains that the external workload exchanges its own identity token for a short-lived credential, so no long-lived key is created or stored
Names the trust chain: a pool and provider that trust a specific issuer, plus attribute mapping and conditions
States a limit or tradeoff such as setup complexity, dependence on the external issuer, or risk from a broad condition
Notes that access is granted through roles on a principal set or through service account impersonation

suggested.rationale: That mission makes the learner fix how a deploy authenticates without leaking a secret, which is the same problem this federation approach solves.

lessons.plain: A service account is an identity meant for a program or machine rather than a person. Impersonation means one identity temporarily acting as that service account: it asks for a short-lived pass that lets it do what the service account is allowed to do, without ever holding the service account's long-term secret. It works like a manager letting a trusted assistant sign documents in the manager's name for one task, for a short time, with a log entry showing who actually did it. The assistant borrows authority rather than being handed a permanent copy of the manager's signature.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a build job needs to act as a deployment service account, would you give the job a long-lived key file for that account, or let the job borrow the account's authority for a short time? What is your reason?
lessons.teach:
A principal is any identity that Google Cloud can grant access to, such as a user, a group, or a service account. A service account is a principal used by software rather than a person. Impersonation is when one principal asks Google Cloud for short-lived credentials that act as a service account. The caller never needs the service account's long-term key. The right that makes this possible is the Service Account Token Creator role, which lets the holder mint those short-lived credentials for a named service account. This is different from the Service Account User role, which only allows attaching a service account to a running resource.

Why it works: credentials expire within about an hour, so a leaked token is less useful than a leaked key, and every impersonated call is recorded with both the caller and the target account.

Worked example. A CI runner called ci-deployer must deploy as release-sa. Step 1: identify the caller, ci-deployer. Step 2: identify the target, release-sa. Step 3: grant ci-deployer Token Creator on release-sa only. Step 4: at run time, ci-deployer requests a token for release-sa; the platform checks the binding and issues a token that expires soon. Step 5: the deployment calls are logged under release-sa with the delegation recorded.

Common mistake: granting Token Creator at the project level. That lets the caller impersonate every service account in the project, including powerful ones it never needed.

Consequence: if the runner is compromised, its blast radius is the set of accounts it can impersonate. A narrow binding limits that damage to one account; a project-wide grant turns one stolen job into control of the whole project.

questions.prompt: Harbor Retail runs a nightly job called nightly-etl that must publish sales files as the service account reports-sa, which lives in a different project. Step 1: identify the caller, nightly-etl. Step 2: identify the target, reports-sa. Step 3: this step is missing and is the one you must supply. Step 4: at run time nightly-etl asks for a token for reports-sa, and the platform issues a short-lived token. Step 5: the publish calls are logged under reports-sa with nightly-etl recorded as the delegate. Which choice correctly fills the missing step 3?
choices: Give nightly-etl the Service Account User role on the whole project so it can run jobs as any account there.
Create a JSON key for reports-sa and store it in the job's configuration so it can authenticate without a token request.
Grant nightly-etl the Token Creator role on reports-sa only, leaving other accounts untouched.
Grant nightly-etl the Token Creator role at the Harbor Retail organisation level so future accounts are covered automatically.
questions.why: Step 3 must give the caller the minting right on the one named target account, which is what makes the later token request succeed and keeps the blast radius narrow.

questions.prompt: Which role lets a principal request short-lived credentials that act as a named service account?
choices: Project Viewer
Organisation Policy Administrator
Service Account Token Creator
Service Account User
questions.why: Token Creator is the role that allows minting short-lived credentials for a named service account, whereas Service Account User only allows attaching the account to a running resource.

questions.prompt: A developer holds only the Service Account User role on a service account named billing-reader. What can they do with that role alone?
choices: Grant billing-reader Token Creator on other accounts, which the role automatically allows.
Attach billing-reader to a running resource, but this role alone does not let them request tokens that act as it.
Mint short-lived tokens that act as billing-reader, because any user role on a service account allows impersonation.
Download the long-term key for billing-reader, since that is the purpose of the role.
questions.why: Service Account User only permits attaching the service account to a running resource; minting impersonation tokens requires Token Creator, and impersonation never needs a long-term key.

questions.prompt: A reporting job's service account is granted Token Creator at the project level. That project holds twelve service accounts, one of which has payroll access. The job is compromised. What is the extent of the damage?
choices: Only the reporting job's own service account, since it is the one that ran.
Only the payroll account, since it holds the sensitive data.
Every service account in that project it can impersonate, including the payroll account.
Nothing beyond the job's runtime, because tokens expire within about an hour.
questions.why: A project-level Token Creator grant lets the caller impersonate every service account in the project, so a compromised job can reach the payroll account as well as the rest.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what service account impersonation is, how it differs from giving a program a service account key file, and one limit or risk of granting impersonation rights too broadly.
lessons.modelAnswer: Impersonation lets a principal, such as a CI runner, request short-lived credentials that act as a service account, without ever holding that account's key. The caller needs the Token Creator right on that specific service account. A key file is long-lived and can be copied, so it stays dangerous after it leaks; impersonated tokens expire within about an hour, and the logs show both the caller and the account acted as. The main limit is scope. If the Token Creator right is granted on the whole project, the caller can impersonate every account in it, including high-privilege ones. The fix is to grant it per service account and to review those bindings regularly, since a compromised caller can only reach what it is allowed to impersonate.
rubricPoints: Defines impersonation as obtaining short-lived credentials for a service account rather than holding its key
Contrasts impersonation with a long-lived key file that can be copied and misused
Names the Token Creator right and says it should be granted on the specific service account
Identifies the risk of a project-wide grant and its blast radius

suggested.rationale: Explaining the caller-to-target relationship and its scope back to a teammate is the core skill here, and no listed OpsForge mission covers cloud IAM.

lessons.plain: A password and session policy is the set of rules an organization sets for how people's login passwords must look, and for how long a signed-in session stays trusted before the system asks the person to prove who they are again. Think of it like the rules for a secure building: how strong the access code must be, and how long you can stay inside before you have to badge in again. Good policies balance security with usability, because rules that are too annoying push people toward weak workarounds.
lessons.guessPrompt: An employee signs in on a shared office computer, walks away, and leaves the session open all day. Which single setting would most reduce the risk that a stranger uses that open session, and what tradeoff comes with it?
lessons.teach:
A password policy is the set of rules that decide what a valid password must look like, such as a minimum length, whether it may match a recently used one, and whether it must change on a schedule. A session is the period after a successful sign-in during which the system keeps trusting that same person without asking again. A session policy sets how long that trust lasts. It can include a maximum session length, after which the user must authenticate again, and sometimes an idle timeout that ends the session after a period of no activity.

Why it works: a password only proves identity at the moment it is typed. Rules make guessing harder at sign-in, and session limits shrink the window in which a stolen or left-open login can be used. The two controls cover different moments, one at sign-in and the other during use.

Worked example: an organization sets a minimum password length of 12 characters, blocks reuse of the last five passwords, and requires re-authentication every 8 hours. Step 1: Maria signs in at 08:30 with a 12-character password, which passes the length rule. Step 2: she works until 16:30, when the 8-hour limit is reached. Step 3: the system asks her to authenticate again instead of silently continuing. Step 4: if her laptop was stolen at 17:00, the thief finds the session has already ended.

Common mistake: treating a password rule as the whole policy, or leaving session limits very long or absent for sensitive administrator accounts, so one unlocked laptop stays signed in for days.

Consequence: session length is the maximum damage window after a login is misused, so it should be shorter for accounts that can change production systems.

questions.prompt: Ravi works at a logistics firm, Harbor Freight Ltd. (a different organisation from the teaching example). Its policy for production database administrators sets an idle timeout of 20 minutes and a maximum session length of 4 hours. Step 1: Ravi signs in at 07:00 as a database administrator. Step 2: he steps away from his desk and makes no activity, so the idle timeout ends his session at 07:20. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: his unlocked laptop, left at 07:30, cannot make any database changes without a new sign-in.
choices: Ravi must authenticate again before the system grants any further access to the database.
The system blocks Ravi from reusing his last three passwords, which ends his session at the same time.
The system resets Ravi's password to a new random value so that no one else can use the old one.
The session continues for the full 4 hours, because an idle timeout only pauses the clock and does not end the session.
questions.why: An idle timeout ends the session after a period of no activity, so the trust granted at 07:00 is gone and a fresh authentication is required before further access.

questions.prompt: Which statement best defines a session policy as opposed to a password policy?
choices: It sets the minimum length of a password and whether old passwords may be reused.
It sets how long the trust after a successful sign-in lasts, including any maximum length and idle timeout.
It decides which people are allowed to sign in to the system at all.
It stores a hashed copy of each password so that the system can check it later.
questions.why: A session policy governs the period after sign-in during which the system keeps trusting the user, including maximum session length and idle timeout, while a password policy governs what a valid password looks like.

questions.prompt: A company runs a payments platform. Its finance administrator accounts can change production payment settings, and its read-only analyst accounts only view reports. Currently both have a maximum session length of 10 hours. Which change best reduces the damage window in line with the guidance that accounts able to change production systems need shorter sessions?
choices: Raise the analyst limit to 24 hours so that all accounts behave the same way.
Keep both at 10 hours, because the analysts also need long sessions to finish reports.
Shorten the finance administrator maximum session to 1 hour and keep a limit on the analysts as well.
Remove the maximum session length from the analysts only and keep the administrators at 10 hours.
questions.why: Session length is the maximum damage window after a login is misused, so the administrator accounts that can change production settings should get the shortest session, while the read-only accounts still keep a limit.

questions.prompt: A team sets a minimum password length of 16 characters and blocks reuse of the last six passwords for all accounts. However, it sets no maximum session length for its production administrator accounts. An administrator signs in on Monday morning and leaves an unlocked laptop open until Thursday, and the session is still active. What is the gap in the team's policy?
choices: The password rules only act at sign-in, and the missing session limit means trust for the administrator never ends.
The reuse rule should have been applied to session tokens rather than passwords.
The minimum password length is too long, so administrators are forced to write passwords down.
Blocking password reuse makes the sessions expire sooner than intended.
questions.why: Password rules make guessing harder at sign-in but do not limit how long a signed-in session stays trusted, so without a maximum session length or idle timeout the administrator's open session remained usable for days.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a password and session management policy controls, and name one limit or tradeoff of making session lengths very short.
lessons.modelAnswer: A password and session policy sets two things. First, the rules a password must meet, such as minimum length and not reusing recent passwords. Second, how long a sign-in stays trusted before the user must prove identity again, plus any idle timeout. The password rules make guessing harder at sign-in, and the session limits cap how long a stolen or unattended login remains usable. The main tradeoff of very short sessions is friction. People re-authenticate constantly, get annoyed, and may start writing passwords down or sharing accounts, which weakens security. The sensible approach is to match session length to risk: shorter for administrators with production access, longer for low-risk read-only work, and pair it with stronger sign-in methods so that frequent prompts are less of a burden.
rubricPoints: Describes password rules as controlling what a valid password looks like, such as minimum length or reuse limits
Describes session policy as controlling how long a sign-in stays trusted and when re-authentication is required
Explains that session limits shrink the window in which a stolen or unattended login can be misused
Names a tradeoff of very short sessions, such as user friction leading to workarounds

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises identity password and session settings, so reading the policy concepts is the best available route.

lessons.plain: Two standards let one system trust another system's answer about who someone is, or let an app act on someone's behalf without ever seeing their password. SAML is an older XML-based format where a company's login system vouches for a user to a cloud service by sending a signed message. OAuth is a permission-delegation standard: a user approves an app for a specific job, and the app receives a short-lived token limited to that job. Setting them up means deciding which system is trusted, what it is allowed to say, and what each app is allowed to touch.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company already has a staff login directory and wants its staff to sign in to Google Cloud with it, without creating separate Google passwords. Before any teaching, which system do you think should vouch for the staff member, and what would you use if a third-party reporting tool needs to read a staff member's calendar without ever learning their password?
lessons.teach:
SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) is a standard for single sign-on, abbreviated SSO, meaning a user signs in once at a trusted place and other services accept that sign-in. The system that holds user accounts and checks passwords is the identity provider, or IdP. The service being accessed is the service provider, or SP. When a user starts sign-in at the SP, the SP redirects them to the IdP. The IdP authenticates the user and returns a signed XML message called an assertion that names the user. The SP checks that signature against a certificate it was given during setup, so it trusts only the IdP it was configured with.

OAuth 2.0 solves a different problem: delegated authorization. An app registered as an OAuth client asks the user for consent to named scopes, which are specific permissions such as read-only calendar access. An authorization server issues an access token, a short-lived credential the app presents to an API. The app never receives the user's password.

Why it works: each standard puts trust in one place. SAML moves trust in identity to the IdP. OAuth moves trust in permission to the user's recorded consent.

Worked example: a staff member opens the cloud console. Step 1: the SP sees no session and redirects to the company IdP. Step 2: the user signs in there, and the IdP returns a signed assertion naming the user's email. Step 3: the SP verifies the signature, matches the email to an existing cloud identity, and starts a session. Separately, a reporting tool asks for read-only calendar scope, the user consents, and the tool gets a token that covers only that scope.

Common mistake: matching the wrong user identifier in the assertion, so the email does not map to an existing account and sign-in fails for some staff. Another is granting an OAuth client broad scopes because it is easier to configure, which hands it more access than its job needs.

Consequence in a running system: if the signing certificate expires, every SAML sign-in fails at once, locking out staff even though nothing else has broken.

questions.prompt: A warehouse planning tool wants to read a user's inventory counts through an inventory API. The user's company uses an authorization server that issues OAuth access tokens. Step 1: the tool sends the user to the authorization server and asks for the scope inventory.read, which is permission to view counts but not change them. Step 2: the user reviews the request and approves it. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: the tool calls the inventory API with the token in the request, and the API returns counts for that user.
choices: The tool asks the user to type their password into the tool so it can log in on their behalf
The tool requests the broadest scope available so that later features do not need a new consent
The authorization server issues a short-lived access token to the tool, covering only the approved scope
The inventory API issues a SAML assertion naming the user, which the tool then stores
questions.why: After consent, the authorization server issues a short-lived access token limited to the approved scope, which the tool then presents to the API, while the password never reaches the tool and SAML is not part of OAuth.

questions.prompt: In a SAML sign-in, which party is the identity provider (IdP), the system that holds user accounts, checks passwords, and returns a signed assertion naming the user?
choices: The OAuth client that asks the user for consent to scopes
The service being accessed, which checks the user's password directly
The system that holds user accounts and checks passwords, which signs the assertion
The browser, which stores the signed assertion for later use
questions.why: The text defines the identity provider as the system that holds accounts, authenticates the user, and returns a signed assertion, while the service provider only verifies that assertion.

questions.prompt: A cloud service has been configured for SAML single sign-on with a partner's identity provider. The partner rotates its signing certificate, but the service still holds the old one. What is the most likely result?
choices: The service automatically downloads the new certificate and continues without interruption
Only users with administrator roles are locked out, since they use a different path
Sign-in works because the service accepts any valid XML message
Every SAML sign-in fails, because the new signature cannot be checked against the certificate the service was given
questions.why: The service provider checks the assertion signature against the certificate it was given during setup, so a rotated certificate that is not updated causes every SAML sign-in to fail at once.

questions.prompt: A third-party expense app needs to read a user's approved expense totals from the company's finance API, and the user should not share their password with the app. Which approach fits the requirement best?
choices: Register the app as an OAuth client that requests only the read-only expense totals scope, and have the user consent
Give the app a full-access scope so it never needs to ask again
Send the user through SAML sign-in and let the app keep the assertion as its permission
Ask the user for their password and store it so the app can log in each month
questions.why: OAuth is the delegated authorization standard here: the app gets a short-lived token limited to the named read-only scope after the user consents, and it never receives the password.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a new teammate the difference between SAML and OAuth, and name one limit or tradeoff of using each for a team's sign-in and app access setup.
lessons.modelAnswer: SAML is for proving who a person is. Our company login system signs a message saying a given person is signed in, and the cloud console trusts that signature because it was set up with the company's certificate. OAuth is for letting an app do a limited job. The person approves a reporting tool for read-only access, and the tool gets a short-lived token for only that scope, never their password. The limit of SAML is that the cloud side depends entirely on the identity provider and its certificate. If the certificate expires, or the user identifier in the message does not match an account, sign-in breaks for everyone or for specific people. The limit of OAuth is that the consent is only as narrow as the scopes the app asks for, so reviewing which apps are registered and what scopes they hold is part of the job. Neither one decides what a person may do on a resource; that is still controlled by IAM roles.
rubricPoints: SAML handles single sign-on by having a trusted identity provider sign an assertion about the user for the service provider to check
OAuth handles delegated access by issuing a scoped, short-lived token after the user consents, without sharing the password
A limit of SAML is dependence on the IdP and its signing certificate, plus user identifier matching
A limit of OAuth is that access is only as narrow as the requested scopes, so apps need periodic review
Neither standard replaces IAM role decisions on resources

suggested.rationale: Choosing between SAML and OAuth and explaining the tradeoffs back to a teammate is the core skill, and no listed OpsForge mission covers federated sign-in or OAuth consent.

lessons.plain: Two-step verification means a sign-in needs two different kinds of proof: something you know, like a password, and something you have, like your phone or a physical security key. Even if someone steals a password, they still cannot get in without the second item. In a company, the administrator decides who must use it, how the change rolls out so people are not locked out on day one, and which second-step methods are allowed. Think of it like a building that needs both a key card and a door code. This lesson covers switching it on and making it mandatory for accounts in your organization, in general terms.
lessons.guessPrompt: A staff member's password was leaked in a data breach. Without any other changes, what extra thing would stop an attacker from signing in with it, and what would you need to decide before requiring it for everyone on the same day?
lessons.teach:
Two-step verification (2SV), also called two-factor or multi-factor authentication, is a sign-in rule that asks for a second, independent proof after the password. The proofs fall into categories: something you know (the password), something you have (a phone that receives a prompt, a one-time code generator, or a hardware security key), and something you are (a fingerprint). A second factor only helps if an attacker who has the password does not also have the second item.

Enforcement is set by an administrator in the identity provider's admin settings, usually scoped to a group or organizational unit. Enforcement is normally rolled out in two stages. First comes enrollment, where users register at least one second-step method without being blocked. Then comes enforcement, where sign-in requires it. Admins can also limit which methods are allowed. Security keys resist phishing best because they check the website's address, while SMS codes are the weakest option and can be intercepted or redirected.

Worked example: Priya signs in with her password from a new laptop. Step 1, the system checks the password, which is correct. Step 2, because 2SV is enforced for her group, it sends a prompt to her phone. Step 3, she approves the prompt and the session starts. An attacker holding only the password stops at step 2.

Common mistake: turning on enforcement for everyone on day one before anyone has enrolled. Users with no registered method get stuck at the second step and open tickets, and if the only super administrator is among them, nobody can change the setting. Keep a recovery path and at least two administrator accounts that use strong methods.

In a running system, a locked-out administrator cannot fix other accounts, so enforcement changes must be planned with an enrollment window and recovery codes stored safely.

questions.prompt: A school IT administrator, Mrs. Okafor, plans two-step verification for the teachers group of 60 staff. Step 1: she opens an enrollment window, and teachers register at least one second-step method without being blocked. Step 2: she checks that every teacher has a method registered and that two administrator accounts use hardware security keys and have their recovery codes stored safely. Step 3 is missing from the plan. Which action should come next so that the rollout is staged correctly?
choices: Remove the administrators' second factor so that they cannot be locked out.
Turn on enforcement for every group in the school at once to save time.
Turn on enforcement for the teachers group only, now that enrollment is confirmed.
Disable the enrollment window so that no teacher can change their registered method.
questions.why: Enforcement comes after enrollment and is scoped to the group that was prepared, so enabling it for the teachers group only, once enrollment is confirmed, follows the staged approach.

questions.prompt: In two-step verification, which of these is an example of something you have?
choices: A password you memorized
A security question about your first pet
A hardware security key plugged into your computer
A fingerprint read by a sensor
questions.why: A hardware security key is a physical item you possess, which is the something-you-have category; the password and security question are things you know, and a fingerprint is something you are.

questions.prompt: An administrator for a small accounting firm wants to limit which second-step methods the finance group may use, choosing the option that best resists phishing. Which should the administrator allow?
choices: A second password emailed to the user
A hardware security key, which checks the website address before it responds
A longer password of 20 characters
Codes sent by text message to a phone number
questions.why: Security keys resist phishing best because they check the website's address, while text codes can be intercepted or redirected and a second password is still something you know.

questions.prompt: A company turns on enforcement of two-step verification for all 300 users on the first day, before anyone has enrolled a method. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: Users without a registered method get stuck at the second step, and if the only super administrator is among them, nobody can reverse the setting.
Sign-in works with the password alone for every user.
Nothing changes, because enrollment completes automatically once enforcement is on.
Only administrators are affected, and password resets stop working for them.
questions.why: Enforcing before enrollment blocks users who have no registered method, and a locked-out super administrator cannot fix the setting for anyone else, which is the failure described in the common mistake.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would roll out mandatory two-step verification for a 200-person company without locking anyone out, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with a pilot group, such as the IT team, and turn on enforcement for them only after they enroll at least two methods, ideally a phishing-resistant security key plus a phone prompt. Then I would open an enrollment period for everyone else with clear instructions and a deadline. Only after most people have registered methods would I switch enforcement on group by group, starting with lower-risk groups and finishing with administrators. Before any of that, I would confirm there are at least two super administrator accounts with strong methods and that recovery codes are stored securely. The tradeoff is time: a staged rollout takes weeks, and during the gap some accounts are protected only by a password. Users without a phone or key also need a provisioning path, which adds support work.
rubricPoints: Two-step verification requires a second, independent factor beyond the password, so a stolen password alone is not enough.
Enforcement should be staged: enrollment first, then enforcement by group, so users are not locked out.
Recovery paths matter, including at least two strong-method administrator accounts and stored recovery codes.
A tradeoff exists: the staged rollout takes time and leaves a gap, and users without devices need an alternative path.

suggested.rationale: Admin console settings, enrollment options and allowed-method choices are catalogue-style facts, and no listed mission or planned engine covers two-step verification.

lessons.plain: Privileged access means the powerful permissions that let someone change who can do what, or change the most sensitive parts of a system. Separation of duties means splitting those powers so that no single person can complete a risky action alone. On Google Cloud, IAM (Identity and Access Management) controls this by deciding which people and groups get which roles on which resources. The core habit is to keep admin powers narrow, spread them across different groups, and never let one identity hold both halves of a sensitive pair of jobs. Think of a bank vault that needs two keys held by two different people.
lessons.guessPrompt: If one engineer can both change who has access to a production project and delete that project's audit logs, what could go wrong, and how would you split those powers between people?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A principal is the identity that receives access: a user account, a Google group, a service account, or a domain. A permission is one specific action, such as reading a storage object or setting an IAM policy. A role is a named bundle of permissions. A binding attaches a role to a principal on a resource. Resources sit in a hierarchy of organization, folder, project and individual resource, and a binding made higher up is inherited by everything below it. Separation of duties is the rule that one identity should not hold two powers whose combination lets it cause harm alone, such as both approving and executing a change, or both administering access and auditing it.

Why it works: access is only possible if a principal holds the permission, so control comes mostly from the roles you decline to grant. The basic roles Owner, Editor and Viewer bundle very large numbers of permissions and are too broad for routine work. Predefined roles are narrower, and custom roles let you pick exact permissions when no predefined role fits. A privileged role is any role that can change access itself, such as the role that edits IAM policies. These should go to a small, named group.

Worked example: project payments-prod. The group platform-deployers receives a role that manages Compute Engine instances. The group security-auditors receives a logging viewer role. No one belongs to both. Dana, a member of security-auditors, tries to edit the project's IAM policy. The check gathers Dana's group memberships, gathers every binding on the project and above it, finds no permission to set IAM policy, and returns denied.

Common mistake: granting Owner to a whole team so that nobody gets blocked. Owner can change IAM and disable logging, so one stolen password becomes a full takeover. In a running system, a single compromised account holding a privileged role on production can grant itself more access without a second person noticing, unless audit logs are kept where the account that acts cannot alter them.

Separation of duties is enforced by splitting groups and roles, not by trusting people to behave.

questions.prompt: Company Lumen Freight has a folder called ops-eu that holds a project called routes-staging. The group route-reviewers holds a role that reads audit logs on routes-staging. The group policy-admins holds a role that sets IAM policy, and that role is bound on the folder ops-eu. Sam belongs only to route-reviewers and tries to change the IAM policy on routes-staging. Step 1: list Sam's group memberships, which gives route-reviewers. Step 2: gather every binding on routes-staging and above it, which includes the log-reading binding on the project and the policy-admin binding on the folder, inherited downward. Step 3: ____. Step 4: return the result. Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Delete the folder binding so that routes-staging no longer inherits anything from ops-eu.
Check whether any binding that reaches Sam through group membership includes the permission to set IAM policy; none does, because policy-admins is a group Sam does not belong to.
Note that Sam is also in policy-admins, so the folder binding applies to Sam.
Check whether Sam holds the Owner basic role on the organisation, since that overrides every binding below it.
questions.why: Inheritance only helps a principal who is actually a member of the group named in the binding, so Sam's memberships decide which bindings count, and none of them grants setting IAM policy.

questions.prompt: Harbor Logistics has a project called fleet-telemetry. An engineer named Ruth can create service accounts, which are identities for software rather than people, and she can also approve exporting their keys. Which arrangement follows separation of duties?
choices: Ruth receives the Owner basic role so she can also audit her own approvals.
Creating service accounts goes to one group and approving key exports goes to a different group, with no one in both.
Ruth keeps both powers but sits in a group that is reviewed each quarter.
Ruth keeps both powers, since she is trusted and works closely with the team.
questions.why: Separation of duties means no single identity holds two powers whose combination lets it cause harm alone, so the two powers must sit in different groups with no overlap.

questions.prompt: An ops lead gives the Owner basic role to a 12-person night-shift group so that nobody is ever blocked. Which consequence matters most for a running production system?
choices: Any single stolen account in that group can change access and turn off logging, so one compromise can become a full takeover.
Nothing meaningfully changes, because Owner is a narrow predefined role that cannot change IAM.
The group loses access automatically once it has more than ten members, which limits the damage.
Owner only allows reading billing data, so the main risk is unexpected cost overruns on the account.
questions.why: Owner bundles very large numbers of permissions, including the ability to change IAM and disable logging, so one compromised member of an overly broad group can take over the project.

questions.prompt: A binding is granted to a group on the folder retail-apac. The project pos-tests sits inside that folder. Which statement about this binding is correct?
choices: The binding applies to pos-tests only if the same binding is repeated on pos-tests itself.
The binding applies to pos-tests only when the group members are service accounts.
The group receives the role only on resources created after the binding date.
The group receives the role on pos-tests and its resources, because a binding made higher in the hierarchy is inherited by everything below it.
questions.why: Bindings made higher in the resource hierarchy are inherited by all resources below, so the group gets the role on pos-tests without any separate binding there.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate proposes making everyone on the platform team Owner on the production project so nobody is blocked during incidents. Explain to them, in your own words, how you would separate privileged roles instead, and name one real tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not make the whole team Owner, because Owner includes the power to change IAM and to turn off logging, so any one compromised account could take over the project and hide it. Instead I would split the work into groups: one group that deploys and manages workloads with a narrow predefined role, one group that can change IAM policies with a small, named membership, and an auditing group that can read logs but cannot change access or delete them. No person sits in both the access-changing group and the audit group. The tradeoff is friction. During an incident, an engineer who needs a permission they do not hold has to be added to a group, which takes time and some approval, so the team must plan for that and keep a documented break-glass path with its own logging.
rubricPoints: Owner and other broad basic roles bundle too many permissions, including the power to change access and logs.
Privileged roles should go to a small named group, and sensitive powers should be split across different groups.
No single identity should hold both the ability to change access and the ability to audit or remove the evidence.
Narrower access brings a real cost, such as slower incident response, which needs a planned exception path.

suggested.rationale: An authorization policy evaluator would let the learner test which principals and role combinations allow or deny privileged actions, which is the reasoning this objective requires.

lessons.plain: Every cloud account lets many people and programs do things, and the provider must decide, for each request, whether it is allowed. Managing permissions means writing down who may do what, on which thing, and nothing more. Think of a building with keycards: the card reader makes the check, and the list behind it is the policy. In Google Cloud the main tool is IAM, which attaches a list of who gets which role to a resource such as a project or a storage bucket. Some older services use ACLs, which are simpler per-item lists. The goal is least privilege: give each identity only the access its job needs, then check that it still does.
lessons.guessPrompt: A contractor needs to read one storage bucket inside a company's cloud project. Would you grant them a role on the whole project or on just that bucket, and why?
lessons.teach:
An IAM (Identity and Access Management) policy is a document attached to a resource such as an organization, folder, project or bucket. It holds bindings. A binding pairs a role with one or more members. A member is an identity: a user account, a group, a service account, or a whole domain. A role is a named bundle of permissions, and a permission is one specific action written as service.resource.verb, such as storage.objects.get. An ACL (access control list) is an older, simpler list attached to a single item. Some services still use them, but many setups turn them off in favor of IAM. Least privilege means granting the smallest set of permissions that still lets the job get done.

Why it works: when a request arrives, the system gathers the policies on the target resource and on every ancestor above it, because access flows downward through the hierarchy. It then asks whether any binding grants the needed permission. Deny policies are checked as well, and a matching deny overrides any allow. Nothing is permitted unless something explicitly grants it.

Worked example: a group called analysts needs to read files in the bucket reports-q3, which sits in the project acme-data. Step 1: name the need, which is reading objects. Step 2: pick the narrowest role that contains storage.objects.get, the object viewer role. Step 3: bind that role to the analysts group on the bucket only. Step 4: test a read, which is allowed, and a write, which is denied because the viewer role has no write permissions.

Common mistake: granting a broad basic role such as Owner or Editor on the whole project so that a task just works. Those roles inherit down to every resource in the project, including resources created later.

Consequence: one broad grant at a high level can quietly expose every bucket, dataset and instance beneath it, and removing it later can break services that depended on it. Scope grants as narrowly as the requirement allows.

questions.prompt: Pinecrest Labs runs a project called pine-ml with a bucket named ckpt-drop that holds model checkpoints. A service account named trainer-sa must upload new checkpoint files into ckpt-drop, but it must never read or delete files there. Worked steps: Step 1, name the need: creating new objects. Step 2, choose the narrowest role containing storage.objects.create, which is the Storage Object Creator role. Step 3, [missing]. Step 4, test: an upload succeeds, and a read is denied because the creator role has no read permission. What belongs in Step 3?
choices: Bind the Storage Object Creator role to trainer-sa on the ckpt-drop bucket only, not on the project.
Add a deny policy on the pine-ml project that blocks trainer-sa from reading objects.
Create an ACL entry on ckpt-drop for trainer-sa instead of using an IAM binding, because ACLs always override IAM.
Grant the Storage Admin role to trainer-sa on the pine-ml project so it can also manage any bucket created later.
questions.why: Binding the narrow role to the service account on the single bucket keeps the grant as small as the requirement, while the other choices either widen the grant through inheritance or misuse ACLs and deny policies.

questions.prompt: In an IAM policy attached to a folder, one binding grants the role roles/viewer to the group field-auditors. Which part of that binding is the member?
choices: The folder itself
field-auditors
roles/viewer
storage.objects.list
questions.why: A member is the identity being granted access, and here that is the group field-auditors, while the role is the named bundle of permissions and the folder is the resource holding the policy.

questions.prompt: The Editor basic role is granted to a team on the project fin-ledger-prod. Three months later an engineer creates a new bucket inside that project. Does the team's Editor grant reach the new bucket?
choices: Only if the new bucket is in the same region as the project.
Yes, because access flows downward through the hierarchy to resources beneath the project, including ones created later.
No, because a grant only covers resources that existed when the grant was made.
No, unless a separate binding is added to the new bucket itself.
questions.why: Policies on a project are inherited by every resource below it, so the Editor grant applies to the new bucket automatically, which is why broad grants at high levels are risky.

questions.prompt: A project policy binds the role storage.objects.get-containing viewer role to the group quarry-analysts, so the allow looks correct. A deny policy is then attached to the parent folder and blocks storage.objects.get for quarry-analysts. A member of that group requests a read of an object in the project. What happens?
choices: The read succeeds, because allow bindings on the closer resource take priority over deny policies higher up.
The read fails only if the member also has no other role, because the deny needs a matching allow to take effect.
The read is denied, because a matching deny overrides any allow and the deny applies to the project through the folder.
The read succeeds for the first hour, then the deny starts applying.
questions.why: The system checks deny policies as well as allows, and a matching deny overrides any allow, so the read is blocked even though the project binding would otherwise permit it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Google Cloud decides whether a request is allowed when permissions are set on both a project and one bucket inside it. Name one limit or tradeoff of relying on inheritance.
lessons.modelAnswer: When a request comes in, the system collects every IAM policy that applies to the target resource: the policy on the bucket itself and the policies on its parents, the folder and the project, and sometimes the organization. Access is inherited downward, so a role granted on the project applies to the bucket too. Then it checks whether any binding grants the permission the request needs. Any matching deny policy overrides allows. The main tradeoff is that inheritance is convenient but hard to see: a broad grant at the project level silently covers resources created later, so you can end up with access nobody intended. You can only narrow access at a lower level, never remove what a parent already grants there, so the safe habit is to grant at the narrowest level the job requires and audit the higher levels regularly.
rubricPoints: Access is evaluated from the target resource plus all inherited ancestor policies.
Any matching deny overrides allows, and nothing is allowed by default.
Inheritance flows downward, so broad grants cover future resources too.
A child resource cannot remove access that a parent already grants, so grant narrowly at the start.

suggested.rationale: The authorization policy evaluator would let the learner trace allow and deny bindings across a resource hierarchy, which is the core reasoning this objective needs.

lessons.plain: When you give someone access to a cloud resource, you normally say who may do what on which thing. This objective covers two tools that make that access narrower. An IAM condition adds a test, such as a date limit or a required resource name, so the access works only while the test passes. An IAM deny policy is a block that refuses certain actions even when another grant allows them. Together they let you give access that is no bigger than the job needs, and they stop one careless broad grant from doing damage.
lessons.guessPrompt: A contractor needs to read only the reports folder for two weeks. Without further reading, how would you make that access stop on its own after two weeks, and what could block a delete even if some other grant allowed it?
lessons.teach: An IAM condition is an extra rule attached to a permission grant. The grant counts only when the rule is true at the moment someone makes a request. Typical rules check the time, an expiry date, the name of the resource, or a tag on the resource. An IAM deny policy is a separate kind of rule. It lists permissions that are blocked, it can be attached at the organization, folder or project level, and it overrides any allow, wherever that allow came from. A deny policy can also name exception principals, which are specific identities or groups that are still allowed through. The reason this works is the order of checks. For each request, the system collects the allow grants that apply, tests their conditions against the request, and then checks deny policies. A matching deny stops the request even when an allow matched. Worked example: a contractor is granted a read role on a project with the condition that the resource name starts with reports and the date is before 30 June. On 10 June, a read of reports/q3.csv finds an allow whose condition is true, and no deny matches, so it succeeds. A read of payroll/salaries.csv finds the same allow, but its name condition is false, so no allow applies and the request is refused. Next, the organization adds a deny on deleting objects, with an exception for the storage admins group. The contractor tries to delete reports/q3.csv. A role allows it, but the deny matches and the contractor is not an exception, so the delete is refused. Common mistake: believing a condition can be attached to a role granted somewhere else, or that a conditional grant is checked only when it is created. Conditions are tested on every request. Consequence: a deny placed high in the hierarchy applies to everything beneath it, so a deny added to a production project can stop a running service until it is removed. Deny policies therefore need testing and exceptions before rollout. Conditions are also not supported for every permission, so check support before relying on one.

questions.prompt: A regional insurance firm grants an outside auditor a viewer role on its project 'claims-archive', with a condition that the resource name starts with ledger-2023. The auditor reads ledger-2023-q1.csv, and this trace follows. Step 1: the system collects the allow grants that apply to the request and finds the one viewer grant. Step 2: it tests that grant's condition against the request. The name starts with ledger-2023, so the condition is true. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: no deny matches, so the read succeeds. Which statement fills step 3?
choices: It re-tests the condition only when the auditor's grant was first created, then skips the test on later reads.
It checks whether the auditor also holds a separate role at the organization level before allowing the read.
It checks the deny policies at each level of the hierarchy, and a matching deny would stop the read even though an allow matched.
It gives the auditor a permanent copy of the grant so later reads need no checks at all.
questions.why: Deny policies are checked after the allow conditions are tested, and any matching deny blocks the request regardless of allows.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes an IAM deny policy?
choices: It can only be attached to a single resource and cannot apply to folders or the organization.
It lists blocked permissions, overrides any matching allow, and can name exception principals that are still allowed through.
It is a condition that is attached to a role and only tests the time of the request.
It is checked before any allow grant is collected, so allows never reach the condition test.
questions.why: A deny policy blocks listed permissions across the hierarchy it is attached to, overrides allows, and may exempt named identities or groups.

questions.prompt: At Brightwater Foods, a developer group holds an editor role on project 'web-staging' with a condition that the resource tag env equals staging. The organization adds a deny policy that blocks stopping compute instances, with an exception for the sre-oncall group. A developer tries to stop an instance on web-staging tagged env=staging. What happens?
choices: The stop succeeds, because the tag condition on the developer's allow is true.
The stop is refused, because the deny matches and the developer is not an exception, even though the allow condition is true.
The stop succeeds, because the deny only applies to instances created after it was added.
The stop is refused only if the deny is attached to the web-staging project itself.
questions.why: Conditions decide whether an allow applies, but a matching deny still blocks the request unless the requester is a named exception.

questions.prompt: A payments company adds a deny policy at the level of its production project to block deleting objects in storage. A cleanup service that removes temporary files in that project starts failing right away, though it was working before. The team had not tested the deny first. Why did the service break?
choices: The deny was attached to a project, and it applies to everything beneath that project, so the service's delete requests match it and are refused until the deny is removed or an exception is added.
Deny policies expire after 24 hours, so the service failed when the rule activated.
Conditions on the service's allow were cached when it was created, so the deny cannot change them.
The deny only affects human users, so the service should have been unaffected but its allow was removed automatically.
questions.why: A deny high in the hierarchy applies to all resources beneath it, so it can stop running services and must be tested with exceptions before rollout.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between an IAM condition on an allow grant and an IAM deny policy, using one concrete example. Then name one limit or tradeoff of using deny policies.
lessons.modelAnswer: A condition is attached to an allow grant. It says the grant only applies when a test is true, for example when the resource name starts with reports and the date is before a set day. If the test is false, the grant simply does not apply and the request is refused by default. A deny policy works the other way. It blocks a permission and wins over any allow, even one granted by a role somewhere else. For example, we could deny object deletion across the organization, with an exception for the storage admins group. The tradeoff is that a deny is broad and sits high in the hierarchy, so a mistake can stop a production service that was working fine. You need to test it, keep the exception list tight, and remember that not every permission supports conditions or denies.
rubricPoints: A condition on an allow grant is tested at request time and only grants access when true.
A deny policy overrides any matching allow and can be scoped at organization, folder or project level.
Exception principals let a named group through a deny, and should be kept narrow.
A broad deny can break running services, so it needs testing and a rollout plan, and not every permission supports conditions.

suggested.rationale: A planned authorization policy evaluator would let the learner test allow conditions and deny precedence against sample requests before any real change.

lessons.plain: Least privilege means giving someone only the access they need for their job, and no more. In Google Cloud, access is handed out at several levels that nest inside each other: the whole organization at the top, then folders (groups of projects), then projects (containers that hold resources such as storage buckets or virtual machines), then individual resources. A grant made high up does not stay high up; it flows down to everything beneath it. So the skill is choosing the lowest level that still lets the work get done. Think of a building: a key to the whole building opens every room, while a key to one room opens only that room.
lessons.guessPrompt: A contractor needs to read the logs of one project out of forty in your company. Where would you grant the reading permission: on the whole organization, on the folder that holds that project, or on that one project? Give a reason for your choice.
lessons.teach:
An allow policy is the set of bindings attached to a resource in Google Cloud. Each binding connects a principal (a user, a group, or a service account, which is an identity used by software) to a role. A role is a named bundle of permissions, such as permission to read logs or to create virtual machines. The resource hierarchy has four levels: organization, folder, project, and resource. A binding made at one level applies to that level and to every level beneath it. This downward flow is called inheritance. Allow policies only add access. Narrowing access that a higher level granted needs a separate kind of rule, a deny policy, which is covered in another lesson.

Why least privilege works here: every level you grant at adds reach. A role granted on a folder reaches every project in that folder, including projects created later. So you bind the narrowest role, to the narrowest group, at the lowest level that still lets the job happen. Prefer predefined roles scoped to one service over the basic roles Owner, Editor and Viewer, which carry very broad permissions across almost every service in a project.

Worked example: a log reviewer needs to read logs in project payments-dev, which sits in folder Payments under the organization. Step 1: the reviewer's group receives a logs-read predefined role on payments-dev only. Step 2: the binding is attached to that project, so it reaches that project's logs and nothing else. Step 3: the sibling project payments-prod is unaffected, because a binding on one project does not flow sideways. Step 4: if the reviewer later needs a second project, add a second project-level binding rather than widening the folder.

Common mistake: granting Editor on the folder so that one deployment works. That single binding now lets the account change resources in every project in the folder, including production.

In a running system this matters because a stolen credential is only as dangerous as the bindings above it. A narrow project binding limits a compromise to one project, while a folder-level Editor grant lets the same compromise reach all of them.

questions.prompt: Northwind Clinics has an organization with a folder named Imaging. Inside Imaging are two projects, clinic-scans-test and clinic-scans-prod. A vendor group called imaging-vendors needs to upload scan files to a storage service in clinic-scans-test only. The team follows these steps. Step 1: the group receives a predefined role that allows writing objects to storage, not a basic role. Step 2: the binding is attached to project clinic-scans-test. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: months later a second test project needs the same upload access, so the team adds a second project-level binding rather than widening the folder.
choices: Confirm that no binding for this group already exists on the Imaging folder or the organization, because a binding at a higher level would already flow down into clinic-scans-test and into its sibling project.
Grant the same storage role on the Imaging folder so that any future project in the folder inherits upload access automatically.
Add the imaging-vendors group to the basic Owner role on the organization so that uploads never fail.
Delete the predefined storage role so the binding becomes smaller and cannot grow over time.
questions.why: A binding at any level applies to every level beneath it, so the team must check that no higher binding already reaches the project and widens the group's reach beyond the one test project.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is an allow policy in Google Cloud?
choices: A list of projects that a person is forbidden to open, which overrides any role they hold.
A password rule that forces every service account to rotate its key every thirty days.
A report that lists every permission a user has used during the past quarter.
The set of bindings attached to a resource, where each binding connects a principal to a role.
questions.why: An allow policy is the collection of bindings on a resource, and each binding links a principal such as a user, group, or service account to a role.

questions.prompt: Vantage Retail has a folder called Stores with two projects, pos-east and pos-west. The Stores folder currently has an Editor binding for a group called store-ops. A new developer needs to read logs in pos-east and nothing else. Which change follows least privilege?
choices: Grant the developer Editor on the pos-east project so they can also fix configuration problems.
Move pos-east out of the Stores folder so that no folder bindings reach it at all.
Grant a predefined logs-read role to the developer on the pos-east project only, leaving the folder binding unchanged for others.
Keep the Editor binding on the Stores folder and tell the developer to only read logs in pos-east.
questions.why: A predefined role granted at the narrowest level, the pos-east project, gives read access there and nothing wider, while avoiding broader grants at the folder.

questions.prompt: An admin at Lumen Labs removes a role binding for a user from project research-sandbox. The user can still change resources in that project. The organization has a binding for a group the user belongs to, with an Editor role on the organization. What explains this?
choices: Bindings flow downward through inheritance, so the organization-level Editor binding still reaches research-sandbox and grants the access.
Bindings only apply at the level where they are created, so the project binding should have had no effect in the first place.
The removed binding was on a service account, so it cannot affect human users in the project.
The user has a cached session, and the change will take effect the next time the project is opened.
questions.why: Inheritance means a binding at the organization level applies to every project beneath it, so removing a project-level binding does not remove access granted higher up.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we grant access at the project level instead of the folder level, and name one limit or tradeoff of granting it that narrowly.
lessons.modelAnswer: We grant at the project level because bindings flow downward, so a folder grant reaches every project in it, including ones that exist only in the future and ones that hold production data. A project-level binding keeps the blast radius of a mistake or a stolen credential to one project. The tradeoff is administrative work: each new project needs its own bindings, and if the same group needs the same access in ten projects, we have to manage ten bindings or script them. Teams often handle this by using a group for the people and keeping the role list short and consistent. We accept the extra bindings because the cost is paperwork, while a broad grant's cost is an incident across the whole folder.
rubricPoints: Bindings apply to the level they are set on and everything beneath it (inheritance).
Grant the narrowest role at the lowest level that still lets the job happen.
Allow bindings only add access; narrowing needs deny policies, which are covered separately.
Name a tradeoff, such as more bindings to manage versus a smaller blast radius.

suggested.rationale: An authorization policy evaluator would let the learner trace which bindings at each hierarchy level actually reach a given resource, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: Context-based access means letting someone in only when the situation around a request looks right, not just when their role is right. Think of a building whose badge reader also checks that you are on the office network and carrying a company-issued laptop. In Google Cloud, Access Context Manager is the service where an organization defines those situational rules, called access levels, and attaches them to protected resources. A person's permissions stay the same. The access levels add a second gate that checks where and how the request comes from.
lessons.guessPrompt: A developer has the role that lets them read a sensitive storage bucket, but they are working from a coffee shop on a personal laptop. Should the read succeed just because the role allows it? What would you want checked besides the role?
lessons.teach: An access level is a named set of conditions about a request's context, such as the IP address or network range it comes from, the region, whether the device is enrolled and managed by the company, and sometimes the identity or time of day. Access Context Manager stores these access levels for an organization. Access levels never grant anything on their own. Other services check them, most often a service perimeter, which is a boundary around a group of projects that blocks calls to protected services unless the request satisfies a listed access level. Identity and Access Management (IAM) answers the question of which roles an identity holds. The context layer answers the question of where the request comes from and on what device. A request succeeds only when both answers are yes. Worked example: a perimeter accepts an access level called office-managed, defined as a source IP inside the office range and a managed device. Step 1: an engineer on the office network with a managed laptop calls the storage API using a role that includes read permission. Step 2: IAM confirms the read permission. Step 3: the perimeter checks the request against office-managed, and it matches. Step 4: the call succeeds. The same engineer on a home network fails at step 3, even though IAM would have allowed the read. Common mistake: assuming an access level replaces IAM or that a broad role is safe because a level exists. Levels only narrow what IAM already permits. Consequence in a running system: an overly strict level can break a CI pipeline whose runner IP has changed, so teams usually trial a new perimeter in a mode that logs would-be denials before enforcing it. Access levels are a gate on top of permissions, never a substitute for them.

questions.prompt: Harbor Dental keeps claims data in a BigQuery dataset inside a service perimeter. The access level front-desk-kiosk is defined as a source IP inside 192.0.2.64/26. A billing clerk at a kiosk with source IP 192.0.2.70, using a role that includes query permission, sends a query. Step 1: the request reaches BigQuery with the clerk's credentials and that source IP. Step 2: IAM confirms the query permission. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the query runs and returns rows. Which statement correctly fills Step 3?
choices: The perimeter skips the source IP check because the clerk already holds a role with query permission.
The perimeter asks the clerk's manager to approve the kiosk before the query is allowed to run.
The access level grants the query permission, so IAM is no longer needed for this request.
The perimeter checks 192.0.2.70 against front-desk-kiosk, finds it inside the range, and lets the request continue.
questions.why: The perimeter evaluates the request's context against the named access level, and a match is what lets the call proceed alongside the IAM yes.

questions.prompt: In Access Context Manager, what is an access level?
choices: A role that bundles read and write permissions for a group of projects.
A key that encrypts data before it leaves a project boundary.
A named set of conditions about a request's context, such as source network or device state, that other services can check.
A list of user accounts that are allowed to create service accounts.
questions.why: The teaching text defines an access level as a named set of context conditions, stored by Access Context Manager and checked by other services such as perimeters.

questions.prompt: Tidewater Logistics has a perimeter that protects its Cloud Storage projects. The perimeter lists the access level warehouse-net, defined as a source IP in 10.20.0.0/16 plus a managed device. A CI service account holds a role with object read permission, and its runner calls the storage API from 172.16.4.9 on a device that is not in the warehouse range. What happens to the call?
choices: The call succeeds, because the service account's read role is checked first and the access level is then ignored.
The call is denied by IAM, because a role cannot be used from an IP outside the access level's range.
The call succeeds, because access levels only apply to human users and never to service accounts.
The call is denied by the perimeter, because the request does not satisfy warehouse-net, even though IAM would allow the read.
questions.why: IAM and the context check are both required, and a failed context check blocks the call at the perimeter even when the role itself is sufficient.

questions.prompt: A team's CI pipeline breaks right after its perimeter is enforced with a tightened access level. An engineer proposes giving the CI account a broad owner role so the pipeline runs again. Which response is most accurate?
choices: The owner role is correct, because a broad role overrides any access level that blocks a request.
The owner role is harmless, because roles and access levels are checked separately and only the role matters.
The owner role is the right fix, because the perimeter only blocks requests when the account has too few permissions.
The broad role does not address a context block, since access levels only narrow what IAM permits; the runner location or device condition needs review, and the broad role adds risk.
questions.why: Access levels are a gate on top of IAM and never a substitute for it, so widening IAM cannot clear a context failure and only increases exposure.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, why an access level by itself cannot let someone into a protected project, and name one tradeoff of enforcing a strict access level on a production service.
lessons.modelAnswer: An access level is only a set of conditions about the request, such as source network, device health, or region. It does not carry any permissions. Access to a protected project needs two things to be true at the same time. First, IAM must grant the identity a role that includes the permission for that action. Second, the boundary that protects the resource, such as a service perimeter, must find that the request satisfies an access level. If the role is missing, the access level does not help. If the access level is not met, the role does not help either. The main tradeoff of enforcing a strict level is operational breakage. Legitimate traffic from a changed IP range, an unmanaged device, or an automated runner can be blocked suddenly, so a new rule should first run in a logging-only mode and be reviewed before it is enforced.
rubricPoints: An access level holds conditions about the request, not permissions.
Access is granted only when IAM permission and the access level are both satisfied.
Access levels narrow access that IAM already allows; they do not widen it.
A strict level can block legitimate workloads, so it should be trialled before enforcement.

suggested.rationale: The policy-eval engine would let the learner test combined role and context conditions against sample requests, which is the reasoning this objective requires.

lessons.plain: Access tends to pile up over time. Someone gets a role for one project, then a second one for a short job, and nobody removes the first. Policy Intelligence is the set of Google Cloud analysis tools that read the record of what identities actually did and what permissions they actually hold, then help you spot grants that are wider than needed. Think of a building manager who checks the badge logs, sees that a contractor has not entered the server room in a year, and suggests taking that key back. These tools also answer questions like who can reach a given resource and why a request was refused, so you can change access based on evidence rather than guessing.
lessons.guessPrompt: A developer was granted a broad editor role six months ago for a one-week migration, and the access logs show they have only ever read from one storage bucket since. What would you check before deciding whether to remove the role, and why is looking at the role name alone not enough?
lessons.teach: Identity and access management, or IAM, is the system that decides which principal may perform which action on which resource. A principal is a user, a group, or a service account, meaning an identity used by software. A permission is one allowed action, such as reading objects from a storage bucket. A role is a named bundle of permissions. Least privilege means granting only what a principal really needs. Policy Intelligence is a family of analysis tools built on top of IAM. IAM Recommender looks at how a principal has actually used its permissions over a lookback window, then suggests removing unused permissions or swapping a broad role for a narrower one. Policy Analyzer answers who has access to a resource. Policy Troubleshooter explains why one specific request was allowed or denied. Policy Simulator previews what a change would do before you make it. Worked example: a developer holds a broad editor role on a project. The logs show only reads from one bucket during the lookback window. Step one: note the usage evidence. Step two: the Recommender proposes a read-only role scoped to that bucket. Step three: the Simulator previews the change against recent requests. Step four: apply the narrower grant and watch for new denials. Common mistake: accepting a recommendation without checking the window. A quarterly audit job that did not run during the lookback period looks unused, and removing its access breaks the next cycle. Consequence: a recommendation is evidence about past use, not proof of future need, so confirm the owner and the schedule before removing anything. Policy Intelligence narrows access safely only when the evidence covers the full pattern of work.
