Step 4: a request to an unknown site matches no allow rule, so the default deny blocks it and the attempt is logged.

Common mistake. Assuming a proxy alone blocks everything. If the workload still has another route to the internet, that direct path bypasses the proxy completely. The proxy only controls traffic that is actually sent through it.

Consequence. A running system that depends on a blocked hostname fails in a way that looks like a network outage: downloads time out or return errors until the allow rule is updated. Change the policy deliberately, check the logs first, and avoid opening everything to make the errors stop.

questions.prompt: Harbor Dental runs lab VMs in a private subnet. Secure Web Proxy (SWP), a managed forward proxy that outbound web requests are sent through so policy can be applied before they leave, is in place. The VMs must fetch time-zone data from one hostname, tzdata.harbordental-lab.example, and nothing else on the web. Here is the sequence. Step 1: the VMs' outbound web traffic is directed to the proxy. Step 2: the proxy receives a request for tzdata.harbordental-lab.example. Step 3: MISSING. Step 4: a request from a VM to a social media site matches no allow rule, so the default deny blocks it and the attempt is logged. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: The VM uses its default internet route so the request leaves without going through the proxy.
The proxy matches the hostname against an allow rule and forwards the request to the destination.
The proxy returns an error to the VM and asks it to retry the request later.
The proxy decrypts the HTTPS content with a trusted certificate to read the file path before it decides.
questions.why: An allow rule matching the requested hostname is what permits the request, and the proxy then forwards it, which is the only option consistent with the proxy making the decision from the hostname.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines a forward proxy as the teaching text uses the term?
choices: A gateway placed in front of servers that receives inbound requests from the internet and spreads them across backends.
A private tunnel that links two office networks so they can share files without using the public internet.
A gateway on the client side that makes outbound web requests on behalf of internal machines so policy can be applied.
A DNS service that translates hostnames into addresses for every workload in a project.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a forward proxy as sitting on the client side and making requests on behalf of internal machines, which is the second option.

questions.prompt: A team configures its workloads to send web traffic through SWP and blocks nothing else in its policy. Yet a build job still reaches a site that is not on the allow list. The workloads also keep a route to the internet through a NAT gateway. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The proxy has decrypted the HTTPS traffic and cleared it for the build job.
SWP cannot match on hostnames, so every request is allowed by default.
The allow list is stored in the wrong region, so the proxy ignores it.
The build job's direct route to the internet bypasses the proxy entirely.
questions.why: The proxy only controls traffic actually sent through it, so a second route to the internet lets requests skip the policy, which the teaching text names as the common mistake.

questions.prompt: A company wants its workloads to reach only api.partner-logistics.io over HTTPS through SWP, without installing a trusted certificate for TLS interception. On what does SWP usually base its decision for each HTTPS request?
choices: The full encrypted body of each request, read after the connection is established.
The date and time the company last updated its firewall rules.
The requested hostname, which is visible when the HTTPS connection is set up.
The workload's CPU load and memory use at the moment the request is made.
questions.why: Without TLS interception the proxy decides by the hostname visible at connection setup rather than by reading encrypted content, which is the first option's reverse, so the hostname-visible answer is the one given here.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Secure Web Proxy does for a private workload that must fetch data from outside Google Cloud, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Secure Web Proxy is a managed forward proxy for outbound web traffic. Instead of letting a private workload connect straight to the internet, we point its web requests at the proxy, which checks the destination hostname against our policy and allows or denies each request, logging both outcomes. So if the job needs one vendor repository, we allow that hostname and default-deny the rest. The main limit is that it only governs traffic actually sent through it. If a workload has another route out, that path bypasses the proxy. Also, for HTTPS it mostly decides on hostname, so inspecting encrypted content needs TLS interception and a trusted certificate authority, which adds operational work and trust decisions. Blocked destinations also look like timeouts, so we rely on the logs to diagnose them.
rubricPoints: Describes Secure Web Proxy as a managed forward proxy controlling outbound web traffic from private workloads
Explains that policy matches destinations, such as hostnames or URL lists, and default-denies unlisted ones
Names a limit: only traffic routed through the proxy is governed, so direct routes bypass it
Notes that deep inspection of HTTPS content needs TLS interception and a trusted certificate authority

suggested.rationale: An exam-style situation asking which boundary mechanism enforces a given outbound rule adds the most, since no listed mission covers proxies or egress control.

lessons.plain: Think of DNS as the internet phone book: you give it a name and it returns a number. Cloud DNS is Google Cloud's managed phone book service. Its security settings answer three questions. Who may look up names that exist only inside your private network? How can a visitor's computer prove that an answer really came from the domain's owner and was not swapped along the way? Do you keep a record of lookups so you can investigate unusual behaviour later? Getting these settings right keeps internal names from leaking out, stops forged answers from sending users to the wrong place, and leaves a trail to follow.
lessons.guessPrompt: If your company has a internal server called db.corp.internal, should a stranger on the public internet be able to look up its address, and what could go wrong if they could?
lessons.teach:
A DNS zone is a container of records for one part of the name space, such as example.com or corp.internal. A record maps a name to a value, such as an address. Cloud DNS is the managed service that hosts zones and answers queries for them. Its security settings control three things: who can resolve names, whether answers can be proven genuine, and whether lookups are recorded.

A private zone answers queries only from the virtual networks you attach to it. Outside those networks the name simply does not resolve. This keeps internal host names out of public view without running your own name servers.

DNSSEC, the DNS Security Extensions, adds digital signatures to a public zone. Each record set carries a signature made with a key the zone owner controls. A validating resolver, which is the lookup service on the user's side, checks that signature chain up to the top of the DNS tree. A forged or altered answer fails the check. Signing alone is not enough. The fingerprint of the zone's signing key, called a DS record, must also be published at the parent zone through the domain registrar, so the chain of trust can be followed.

Worked example: a company signs example.com and enables DNSSEC in Cloud DNS. The company copies the DS record to its registrar. A user's resolver asks for www.example.com and receives the answer with its signature. The resolver follows the DS link from the parent and verifies the signature. The answer is accepted. If an attacker injects a fake address, the signature will not match and the resolver refuses it.

Common mistake: turning on signing but skipping the DS record step. The zone is now signed, but the parent has no link to the key. Validating resolvers treat the answers as bogus and return failures, so users cannot reach the site even though the records are correct.

Query logging records lookups for investigation. In a running system a missing DS record is an outage, so DNSSEC changes need the same care as any production change.

questions.prompt: Blue Harbor Bank wants the internal name billing.bh-lab.internal to be answered only for two of its virtual networks, lab-a and lab-b, and never on the public internet. The engineer follows these steps. Step 1: create a private zone for bh-lab.internal. Step 2: add an address record so billing.bh-lab.internal points to 10.40.2.15. Step 3: ______. Step 4: a virtual machine in lab-b asks for billing.bh-lab.internal and receives 10.40.2.15. Which action completes step 3?
choices: Enable DNSSEC on the private zone so that resolvers can verify the answer
Turn on query logging so that lookups from lab-b are permitted
Attach both lab-a and lab-b to the private zone as networks that may query it
Publish a DS record for bh-lab.internal at the domain registrar
questions.why: A private zone answers only queries from the virtual networks attached to it, so attaching lab-a and lab-b is the step that lets lab-b receive the answer, while the other options either concern signing or logging and do not control who can resolve the name.

questions.prompt: The zone ops.harbor-lab.internal is a private zone attached only to the virtual network vpc-prod. A laptop on a VPN that is not attached to vpc-prod asks for ops.harbor-lab.internal. What happens?
choices: The laptop receives the address, but the lookup is refused until logging is enabled
The laptop receives the correct address because internal names are always public
The name does not resolve for that laptop because the private zone answers only attached networks
The laptop receives an unsigned answer that it can still use
questions.why: A private zone answers queries only from the networks attached to it, so a lookup from an unattached network gets no answer for the name.

questions.prompt: Gulf Freight has three virtual networks, freight-east, freight-west and freight-core, that must all resolve the internal host names for its warehouse systems. The company must keep those names out of public view and avoid running its own name servers. Which setting meets this requirement?
choices: Query logging turned on for the public zone
A private zone attached to freight-east only
A public zone with DNSSEC signing enabled
A private zone attached to freight-east, freight-west and freight-core
questions.why: A private zone hides names from the public and answers the three named networks once all three are attached, with no self-run name servers needed.

questions.prompt: A fintech company signed its public zone pay.northlight-fin.example with DNSSEC and copied the DS record to its registrar last week. Customers now report that the site fails to load, and the records themselves are correct. The DS record was later removed from the registrar during a cleanup and was not restored. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The private zone was attached to the wrong virtual network
Validating resolvers can no longer follow a verified link from the parent to the signing key, so they reject the signed answers
The address records are too long for the resolver to accept
Query logging was disabled, so the failures cannot be traced
questions.why: Without the DS record at the parent, the chain of trust cannot be followed, so validating resolvers treat the correct but signed answers as bogus.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would keep an internal service name private while protecting a public domain against forged answers. Name one limit or tradeoff of each control you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: Cloud DNS has a few security controls, and each covers a different risk. A private zone serves internal names only to the VPC networks I attach it to, so internal hostnames never appear on the public internet. DNSSEC signs a public zone so resolvers can check that an answer was not forged. The catch is that the signature chain only works once the DS record is published at the registrar. A mismatch makes validating resolvers reject good answers, which causes an outage. Query logging gives us an audit trail of lookups, but it produces a lot of data and records client activity, so we keep retention and access tight. My point to the team: these controls protect names and answers, not the traffic itself, so they complement firewalls rather than replace them.
rubricPoints: A private zone limits name resolution to chosen VPC networks, keeping internal names off the public internet.
DNSSEC signs records so resolvers can detect forged or altered answers.
DNSSEC needs the DS record published at the parent or registrar, or validation fails.
Query logging provides an audit trail but adds data volume and privacy considerations.
DNS controls protect names and answers, not the traffic, so they complement other controls.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between a private zone, DNSSEC, and logging for a stated requirement is an exam-style reasoning task, and no listed mission or planned engine covers DNS settings directly.

lessons.plain: Modern systems expose their features as APIs, which are doorways that other programs use to ask for data or make changes. Once an API is switched on, many people and tools can call it, so two questions matter: who is using it, and is that use allowed? Continually monitoring an API means watching who calls it, how often, and whether anything unusual happens, much like a building manager reviewing door access records. Restricting an API means narrowing who can reach it, which services may be turned on at all, and what each caller is permitted to do. This objective covers both halves, because an API that nobody watches tends to drift beyond what was intended.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team's API key was pasted into a public code repository. Which single change would most limit what a stranger holding that key can do, and why?
lessons.teach:
An API, short for application programming interface, is a defined set of requests one program can make to another, such as asking a storage service to read a file. Each cloud service exposes its own APIs, and a project must turn a service on before its APIs answer. Restricting an API means limiting which services can be enabled, which callers can use them, and from where. Monitoring means recording calls and reviewing or alerting on them over time. Three mechanisms do most of this work. An organization policy is a rule set above individual projects that can, for example, allow only an approved list of services to be enabled. An API key is a long random string that identifies a calling application; it can be restricted to named APIs and to particular callers or network addresses. Audit logs are records the platform writes for administrative actions and, where switched on, data access, so you can see who called what and when.

Worked example. A team wants a mapping service in a test project. Step one: the organization policy allows only three approved services, and mapping is not among them. Step two: a developer tries to enable mapping and the request is refused. Step three: the refused attempt appears in the audit log, and an alert on denied requests notifies the security team. Step four: if the team truly needs mapping, they request it, and the approved list is updated deliberately rather than by accident.

Common mistake: creating an API key and leaving it unrestricted, so a leaked key can call every enabled API. Restricting the key to one API and to the expected callers limits the damage from a leak.

In a running system, an unrestricted key that leaks can be used from anywhere, quietly consuming quota and reading data, and nobody notices unless someone reviews the logs.

questions.prompt: A clinic group wants its patient-intake mobile app to use a speech-to-text service in a new project. The organization policy already allows that service. The team creates one API key for the app and restricts the key so it can call only the speech-to-text API. What step is still missing before the key is protected against a leak?
choices: Remove the organization policy so the key can reach every service the project might need.
Set the key to never expire so the app never has to be updated.
Email the key to the app team so they keep a backup copy in case the app breaks.
Restrict the key to the app's expected callers or network addresses, so a copy used from somewhere else is refused.
questions.why: Limiting the key to expected callers and addresses is what stops a leaked copy from being used elsewhere, while the API restriction alone only narrows which API it can call.

questions.prompt: In the teaching framing, what is the main job of an organization policy?
choices: To record every data read so that a security team can review it later.
To generate a long random string that identifies a calling application.
To encrypt traffic between a caller and the service it reaches.
To set a rule above individual projects, such as allowing only an approved list of services to be enabled.
questions.why: The teaching text describes an organization policy as a rule set above projects that can limit which services are enabled; the other options describe audit logs, API keys, or encryption, which are different things.

questions.prompt: A research lab has one API key with no restrictions, shared by three internal tools. The key is copied into a public code repository by mistake. What outcome is most likely, based on the teaching text?
choices: Only calls to the single API named in the key's description can succeed.
Anyone holding the key can call every enabled API from anywhere, and the misuse may go unnoticed unless someone reviews the logs.
Calls are refused unless they come from the lab's approved office address.
Google Cloud automatically deletes the key as soon as it is exposed, so no harm occurs.
questions.why: An unrestricted key can be used from any location against any enabled API, and without log review its misuse can stay hidden, which is the failure the teaching text warns about.

questions.prompt: A retail company has a development project where the approved list allows only storage and messaging services. A developer tries to turn on a payments service in that project. Which expectation is correct?
choices: The request succeeds, because developers can always enable services in their own project.
The request is refused, the refused attempt appears in the audit log, and any real need is handled by deliberately updating the approved list.
The request succeeds but is hidden from the audit log to avoid clutter.
The request is refused, and the organization policy is then deleted so the team is not blocked again.
questions.why: The approved list blocks services not on it, denied requests are recorded for review, and the teaching text says changes should be made deliberately rather than by accident.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would keep an API from being misused after it has been turned on, and name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would work in two layers. First, I would restrict what can be turned on at all, using an organization policy that allows only an approved list of services, so a new API cannot appear in a project without review. Second, for each API that is in use, I would restrict its credentials: an API key limited to that one API and to the expected callers, or an identity with only the permissions it needs. Then I would keep watching. Audit logs record who called what, and alerts on denied requests or unusual call volume tell someone when something is wrong. The main limit is that monitoring only helps if someone reads the alerts. Approved lists also add friction, because a team with a legitimate need must wait for a change. I would accept that delay, since it is a deliberate decision rather than an accident.
rubricPoints: Separates restricting which services can be enabled from restricting how each enabled API is called
Names a concrete mechanism such as an organization policy, an API key restriction, or audit logs
Explains that monitoring needs alerts and review to be useful
States a real limit or tradeoff, such as review overhead or unread alerts

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style scenario about which control enforces a given API restriction builds the mechanism-selection skill this unit tests better than reading alone, and no listed mission covers API restriction directly.

lessons.plain: A virtual private cloud, or VPC, is your own private, software-defined network inside a cloud provider. Think of it as a building's internal floor plan: rooms are subnets, doors are firewall rules, and agreements decide which buildings can talk to each other. Security here means deciding who can reach what, and by default most incoming traffic is refused. This objective covers the settings on the network itself, how two separate networks can be joined, how one organization's network can be shared across several projects, and the firewall rules that decide which connections pass.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two companies each run a private network that uses the same address range, 10.0.0.0/16. If you connect their networks with a direct link, can a machine in one reliably reach a machine with the same address in the other?
lessons.teach:
A VPC network is a virtual network that spans regions and holds subnets, which are address ranges where your resources sit. Its security properties include the rules for traffic entering and leaving it and the boundaries you draw around it. A firewall rule is evaluated by the network and allows or denies connections based on direction (ingress means traffic coming in, egress means going out), source or destination range, protocol and port, and a priority number where lower numbers are checked first. These rules are stateful, meaning a reply to an allowed connection is permitted automatically. Every VPC also has implied rules at the lowest priority: deny all ingress and allow all egress. A rule can target workloads by network tag, a label attached to the machine, which is more precise than a broad address range.

VPC peering connects two VPC networks, often in different projects, so they exchange internal addresses privately. Peering is not transitive: if A peers with B and B peers with C, A cannot reach C through B. Subnet ranges must not overlap, and each side must configure its own peering. Firewall rules still apply on both sides.

Shared VPC lets a host project own one network and share its subnets with service projects. Central network and security teams keep control of the boundary while application teams deploy into subnets they have been granted.

Worked example: an API machine tagged api-tier should accept port 443 only from a load balancer range, 35.191.0.0/16. Step 1: create an ingress rule that targets the api-tier tag. Step 2: allow tcp 443 from that source range. Step 3: give it priority 1000, which is checked before the implied deny at 65535. Traffic on 443 from the load balancer passes, and traffic from anywhere else is dropped.

Common mistake: adding an allow rule from 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22 to fix a connection problem. That opens the machine to the whole internet. In a running system, a private service becomes publicly reachable and may only be noticed when scanners find it.

The network boundary is set by firewall rules, peering stops at its direct neighbour, and Shared VPC shares a network without giving up central control.

questions.prompt: A logging team runs a metrics collector on a machine tagged metrics-sink in project obs-prod, inside the VPC obs-net. The collector should accept tcp 9100 only from the range 10.60.0.0/20, where its scrapers run. Step 1: create an ingress rule that targets the metrics-sink tag. Step 3: give the rule priority 900, so it is checked before the implied deny at 65535. The missing Step 2 is what the rule must allow, so the collector accepts only the intended connections. Which choice completes Step 2?
choices: Set the direction to egress so the collector's replies are permitted
Add an allow rule from 0.0.0.0/0 on tcp 9100 so scrapers outside the range can connect
Allow tcp 9100 from source range 10.60.0.0/20
Create a VPC peering to project obs-prod so the scrapers can reach the collector
questions.why: Step 2 sets the protocol, port and source range, and allowing tcp 9100 from 10.60.0.0/20 is what limits the rule to the scrapers, since replies are already covered by the stateful behaviour of the rule.

questions.prompt: Network A in project alpha peers with network B, and network B peers with network C in project gamma. Can resources in network A reach network C through B, and what should the team do if they must connect?
choices: Yes, because B passes traffic along once both peerings exist, so no further setup is needed
No, because peering only works between two networks in the same project, so A and C must be merged
Yes, but only if B has a firewall rule that allows traffic from A to C
No, peering is not transitive, so A needs its own direct peering with C, with non-overlapping ranges and matching configuration on both sides
questions.why: Peering connects only two networks directly and does not carry traffic through a middle network, so A needs its own peering to C with each side configured.

questions.prompt: A team wants to peer two VPC networks. The first has subnets 172.16.0.0/22 and the second has a subnet 172.16.2.0/24. Which statement best describes whether the peering can work?
choices: The peering works because the second subnet is smaller and fits inside the first range
The peering cannot be set up as planned because the subnet ranges overlap, so one range must be changed
The peering works but only for ingress traffic, because overlapping ranges are routed one way
The peering works once each network adds a firewall rule allowing the other side's range
questions.why: Peering requires non-overlapping subnet ranges, and 172.16.2.0/24 sits inside 172.16.0.0/22, so one of the ranges must be renumbered before the peering can carry traffic.

questions.prompt: On one VPC network, rule X has priority 500 and allows tcp 8080 from 198.51.100.0/24. Rule Y has priority 300 and denies tcp 8080 from the same range. A machine on that network receives a connection on tcp 8080 from an address in 198.51.100.0/24. What happens, and why?
choices: The connection is allowed, because the stateful behaviour of rule X overrides rule Y
The connection is denied by rule Y, because rule Y has the lower priority number and is checked first
The connection is allowed, because allow rules always beat deny rules regardless of priority
The connection is dropped only after the implied deny at 65535 is checked, so the outcome depends on that rule
questions.why: Firewall rules are evaluated in priority order where lower numbers are checked first, so the deny at priority 300 is reached before the allow at 500 and the connection is denied.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how VPC peering differs from Shared VPC, and name one limit of peering that you would check before proposing it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Peering joins two separate VPC networks so they can exchange internal addresses privately. Each network stays owned and administered by its own team, and each side has to set up its own peering. Shared VPC works differently: one host project owns the network and shares selected subnets with service projects, so one team keeps central control of the boundary. The main limit of peering is that it is not transitive. If A peers with B and B peers with C, A cannot reach C through B, so you would need a direct peering or a different design. Before proposing peering, I would also confirm that the subnet ranges do not overlap, because overlapping ranges cannot be routed. I would then check the firewall rules on both sides, since peering does not open any ports by itself.
rubricPoints: Peering joins two separately owned networks and needs configuration on each side
Shared VPC has one host project owning the network and sharing subnets with service projects
Peering is not transitive, so reachability does not pass through an intermediate network
Subnet ranges must not overlap, and firewall rules still apply

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly configuration facts and network-boundary concepts best learned by reading the teaching text and then explaining it.

lessons.plain: An N-tier application splits its work into layers: a web tier that talks to users, an application tier that holds the business logic, and a data tier that stores records. Network isolation means each layer can be reached only by the layers that genuinely need it, so a break-in at one layer does not hand over the whole system. Data encapsulation means wrapping traffic in protective layers, such as encrypted connections between tiers, so each hop carries only what it should and only the intended listener can read it. Together they keep the database out of reach of anyone who only compromised the front door.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web server in your application is compromised by an attacker. Should that web server be able to open a connection directly to the database? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A tier is one layer of an application. A network boundary is a line that traffic must cross through a control, such as a firewall rule or a subnet edge. A firewall rule is an instruction that permits or denies traffic by matching its source, destination, protocol and port. Isolation is the practice of letting only the traffic each tier truly needs cross each boundary. Encapsulation means packaging data inside outer wrappers: each network layer adds headers, and between tiers a TLS session can encrypt the application payload so intermediate hops cannot read it.

Why it works. Attackers move sideways. If every machine can reach every other machine on every port, one stolen credential or one vulnerable web process exposes the database. Restricting each tier to a single inbound path shrinks what a compromise can touch. In Google Cloud, VPC firewall rules can target machines by service account, a stable identity, instead of by IP address that changes. Traffic that matches no allow rule is dropped by the implied default deny for ingress.

Worked example. Three tiers: web (service account web-sa), app (app-sa), data (db-sa). Step 1: the data tier has no external IP address and no route to the internet. Step 2: an allow rule lets web-sa reach app-sa on TCP 8080. Step 3: an allow rule lets app-sa reach db-sa on TCP 5432. Step 4: a web-sa machine tries to open TCP 5432 to db-sa. No allow rule matches, so the implied deny drops it. Step 5: the app tier reaches the database normally.

Common mistake. Engineers often create separate subnets, assume segmentation is finished, and leave a broad rule allowing all internal traffic. Subnets alone do not block anything; the rules do. Also remember egress: default outbound traffic is usually allowed, so a compromised database could still call out unless outbound rules are restricted.

Consequence. In a running system, a flat network turns one compromised web machine into access to customer records. With tiered rules, the same compromise stops at the app tier, and denied attempts appear in firewall logs for investigation.

questions.prompt: A media company runs three tiers: ingest, transcode and archive. Each tier's machines run under a service account (a stable identity attached to a machine, which does not change when the machine's IP address changes). Ingest machines use ingest-sa, transcode machines use transcode-sa, and archive machines use archive-sa. Step 1: the archive tier has no external IP address and no route to the internet. Step 2: an allow rule lets ingest-sa reach transcode-sa on TCP 9000. Step 3 is missing from this write-up. Step 4: the transcode tier writes finished files to the archive tier successfully, while a direct connection from ingest-sa to archive-sa on TCP 2049 is dropped. Which step 3 completes the design?
choices: Allow ingest-sa to reach archive-sa on TCP 2049 directly so archive receives data sooner.
Allow transcode-sa to reach archive-sa on TCP 2049, the only inbound path the archive tier needs.
Give the archive tier an external IP address so the transcode machines can reach it over the public internet without any firewall rule at all.
Create a separate subnet for the archive tier, since subnets are what block traffic between tiers.
questions.why: An allow rule matching source transcode-sa and destination archive-sa on TCP 2049 is the single path the archive tier needs, and the implied deny drops everything else, including the direct ingest connection in step 4.

questions.prompt: In Google Cloud VPC firewall rules, which four things does a rule match traffic on?
choices: Region, zone, machine type and disk size
Source IP, username, password and timestamp
Source, destination, protocol and port
Subnet name, route table, NAT gateway and load balancer
questions.why: The teaching text defines a firewall rule as matching traffic by source, destination, protocol and port.

questions.prompt: A retailer keeps its ledger database on machines running under ledger-sa, and its cart service runs under cart-sa. The ledger should accept database connections only from the cart service on TCP 3306. Which rule does this?
choices: Put the ledger machines in their own subnet and rely on the subnet to stop web traffic.
An allow rule from the whole 10.20.0.0/16 range to all ports on the ledger machines.
Give ledger machines a private IP and a rule blocking ports 22 and 80, leaving other ports open to the subnet.
An allow rule with source cart-sa, targeting ledger-sa, on TCP 3306 only.
questions.why: Matching by service account and allowing only TCP 3306 restricts the ledger to exactly the traffic it needs, while subnets alone block nothing.

questions.prompt: A ledger machine is compromised and starts sending data to an external server on TCP 443. The team has written only ingress rules. What is the gap?
choices: Adding a new subnet for the ledger tier would stop the outbound call, since subnets block traffic by themselves.
Default outbound traffic is usually allowed, so the team must add restricting egress rules, because ingress rules alone do not stop outbound calls.
Outbound traffic is always protected by TLS, so an encrypted call to an external server is harmless.
The implied deny for ingress also blocks outbound traffic, so the call cannot leave the machine.
questions.why: Egress (outbound traffic) is usually allowed by default, so restricting it requires its own rules, which the team has not written.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would isolate a three-tier web application so that the database accepts connections only from the application tier. Name one limit or tradeoff of your design.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would put the web, application and database machines in their own groups and give each group an identity, such as a service account. The database group gets no external IP and no inbound rule except one that allows the application group on the database port. The application group accepts only the web group on its service port. Everything else is denied by default. The tradeoff is operational: every new service or port needs a deliberate rule, so teams must document flows and review them, or deployments stall. Also, rules control which machines can connect, not what they send, so the application still needs authentication and encrypted connections between tiers. Segmentation reduces blast radius but does not replace those controls.
rubricPoints: Each tier is grouped by identity and allowed inbound only from the tier directly above it.
The database has no public address and no broad internal allow rule.
Default deny applies to anything not explicitly allowed.
Names a real tradeoff such as extra rule maintenance or slower changes.
Notes that rules limit who connects but encryption and authentication still protect the data in transit.

suggested.rationale: Tracing which tier-to-tier paths are allowed or denied by a given rule set is the core skill, and the planned virtual network path tracer would make the learner test that directly.

lessons.plain: Imagine a company keeps valuable files in a storage locker run by a cloud provider. Normal locks check who holds the key. But a stolen key, or an insider copying files to a personal account, could still move data out. VPC Service Controls draws a fence around a group of cloud projects and the managed services inside them, and only lets data cross that fence when the request comes from an approved place or meets set conditions. It guards the boundary of managed services, not the traffic between your own servers.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team stores data in a managed cloud storage service protected by correct IAM roles. An attacker steals a valid engineer's login and copies the data to a project outside your company. Would correct IAM roles alone stop that copy? What extra boundary would you want, and what would it check?
lessons.teach:
VPC Service Controls is a Google Cloud feature that builds a service perimeter. A project is the container that holds resources and billing. A service perimeter is a named set of projects together with the managed services, such as storage or analytics APIs, that sit inside the fence. Its main purpose is to reduce data exfiltration, meaning data leaving a trusted area without authorization, even when someone holds valid credentials.

Why it works: every request to a protected service is checked against the perimeter. A request is allowed when its source is inside the perimeter. Otherwise it must match an ingress rule, which admits inbound requests from outside, or an egress rule, which lets a perimeter resource reach outside. Both rules can depend on an access level, a set of conditions such as source IP range, identity, or device. IAM still decides who may do what. The perimeter adds a second check on where a request comes from and where the data is going.

Worked example: a perimeter protects project A, which holds a storage bucket. An engineer with a valid token runs a copy command from an unmanaged laptop on a home network to a bucket in project B, which is outside the perimeter. Step 1: IAM says the engineer may read. Step 2: the perimeter sees that the caller matches no allowed access level and the destination is outside the fence. Step 3: the request is denied with a perimeter violation, and the copy never completes.

Common mistake: treating the perimeter as a firewall between virtual machines. It governs access to managed services, not traffic between your own instances. Another mistake is switching a new perimeter straight to enforced mode. Dry-run mode only logs what would be blocked, so teams can find legitimate callers first.

Consequence in a running system: a CI job or analytics pipeline that worked before can start failing with access denied once a perimeter is enforced. Add the required access levels or rules before enforcing.

questions.prompt: Halvorsen Labs keeps trial results in a BigQuery dataset inside project hl-research, and that project sits inside a VPC Service Controls service perimeter. A nightly reporting job runs in a separate build project, hl-build, which is outside the perimeter, and reads the dataset using a service account. Step 1: IAM confirms the service account holds the read role on the dataset. Step 2: the perimeter sees that the caller comes from outside the fence and matches no allowed access level, so the request would be denied. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: the read completes and the nightly job finishes. Which completion correctly fills Step 3?
choices: The team switches the perimeter from dry-run to enforced mode, which lets the request through.
The perimeter denies the request, but the job finishes anyway because IAM had already granted the read role.
IAM is bypassed because the perimeter grants read access to any caller that already holds a role inside the fence.
An ingress rule naming that service account and its source project is matched, so the perimeter admits the request.
questions.why: An ingress rule that matches the caller's identity and source admits an outside request, which is the perimeter's second check passing after IAM has already allowed the read.

questions.prompt: A financial firm wants staff who hold valid credentials to be unable to copy records from its managed analytics service onto personal devices or into a bucket owned by an outside party. Which Google Cloud mechanism best enforces this boundary?
choices: Firewall rules applied to the virtual machines on each employee's laptop.
Removing every IAM role from staff accounts so that no request can be made at all.
Cloud Armor rules attached to the public load balancer in front of the analytics tool.
A VPC Service Controls service perimeter with access levels that restrict caller location and device.
questions.why: A service perimeter checks where a request comes from and where the data is going, which is the control needed to stop exfiltration even when credentials are valid.

questions.prompt: A logistics company creates a new service perimeter around its analytics project and immediately sets it to enforced. Its nightly pipeline, which ran fine yesterday, now fails with access denied. What was the safer approach?
choices: Grant the pipeline's service account the owner role so that IAM overrides the perimeter.
Turn off the pipeline's logging so the failures do not appear in reports.
Delete the perimeter and move the analytics data into a different region.
Use dry-run mode first, then add access levels or rules before enforcing.
questions.why: Dry-run mode logs what would be blocked without blocking it, which lets the team find legitimate callers and add the needed access levels or rules before enforcement.

questions.prompt: A team puts two virtual machines in the same project and tries to use a service perimeter to stop one VM from reaching the other. Which statement is correct?
choices: Once enforced, the perimeter inspects every packet between the two instances and drops any that break policy.
The perimeter blocks the traffic only when dry-run is off and the two VMs sit in different projects.
The perimeter cannot block this because perimeters only run when IAM has already denied the request.
Perimeters guard managed services, so VM-to-VM traffic needs another control such as firewall rules.
questions.why: A service perimeter governs access to managed services rather than traffic between your own instances, so a different control such as firewall rules is needed for that job.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what VPC Service Controls protects against that IAM roles do not, when you would choose it over a firewall rule, and one limit or tradeoff they should know before enforcing a perimeter.
lessons.modelAnswer: IAM roles decide which identity may perform an action, so a valid login with the right role can still read data. VPC Service Controls adds a perimeter around projects and managed services and checks where the request comes from and where the data is going. So it helps against data leaving the trusted area through stolen credentials or insider copying. I would not use it to control traffic between our own virtual machines; that is what firewall rules are for. The main tradeoff is operational. An enforced perimeter can break legitimate callers such as CI runners, pipelines, or admin laptops that are not in an approved access level. We should run dry-run mode first, review the logs, add the needed access levels or rules, and only then enforce.
rubricPoints: IAM controls who may act, while the perimeter controls where requests come from and where data goes
It targets data exfiltration from managed services, not traffic between own VMs, which firewall rules handle
Access levels and ingress or egress rules define the allowed exceptions
Enforcing without dry-run can break legitimate pipelines and callers

suggested.rationale: Telling a perimeter-protected request apart from one that IAM alone would allow is an exam-style reasoning skill, and no listed mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: When machines in different private networks need to talk, or when a machine with no public address needs to reach Google's own services, you need a deliberate private link. This objective covers three tools. VPC peering joins two separate networks so their internal addresses can reach each other. Shared VPC lets one central network be owned by a host project and used by other projects. Private Google Access lets machines that have only private addresses reach Google services. Each solves a different boundary problem, and choosing the wrong one is a common cause of outages.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two teams each run their own cloud network, and both use the private address range 10.0.0.0/16. Can you connect the two networks privately so their machines talk over internal addresses? What would you need to check first?
lessons.teach:
A VPC network is a private, software-defined network in Google Cloud, made of subnets, each holding a range of private IP addresses. Machines inside one VPC reach each other by internal address without touching the public internet. This objective asks how to let traffic cross between VPCs or projects, or reach Google services, without public addresses. VPC peering links two separate VPC networks so their internal addresses route to each other. Each side creates its own peering link, and each network keeps its own administrators. Peering is not transitive: if A peers with B and B peers with C, A cannot reach C through B. Shared VPC designates one host project that owns a VPC network. Service projects attach to it and launch resources into its subnets, so a central team controls the network while application teams control their workloads. Private Google Access is a per-subnet setting that lets VMs with only internal IP addresses reach Google APIs and services. It does not give general internet access.

Worked example: network A has subnet 10.10.0.0/20 and network C has 10.30.0.0/20, with no overlap. You create a peering from A to C and from C to A. A VM in C at 10.30.0.5 can now open a connection to 10.10.0.7 in A. Next, add network D, peered only with A. A VM in D cannot reach C, because peering does not pass through A. Had D's range overlapped A's, the peering could not route the overlapping addresses at all.

Common mistake: assuming peering or Private Google Access gives internet access, or assuming a VM with no public IP can reach Google APIs just because its subnet is private, when Private Google Access is off.

Consequence: a VM without Private Google Access that tries to download packages or call an API hangs until it times out. This usually looks like a broken application rather than a missing network setting.

questions.prompt: A data-science project called lab-analytics runs a VM named notebook-1 in a subnet with range 192.168.8.0/24. The VM has only an internal IP address and no external IP. The team wants notebook-1 to read files from Cloud Storage, a Google service reached through its API. Step 1: Confirm notebook-1 has no external IP, so it cannot use the public internet. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: Rerun the read from notebook-1; it now completes within seconds instead of hanging. What belongs in Step 2?
choices: Create a VPC peering from the lab-analytics network to the project that holds the Cloud Storage bucket.
Make the lab-analytics project a Shared VPC service project so it inherits Google API access.
Turn on Private Google Access for the 192.168.8.0/24 subnet.
Give notebook-1 an external IP address so its traffic can leave toward Google.
questions.why: Private Google Access is the per-subnet setting that lets VMs with only internal addresses reach Google APIs, so enabling it on that subnet is the missing step that makes the read succeed.

questions.prompt: A central networking team wants to own one VPC network and its subnets, while three separate application teams in their own projects launch VMs into those subnets. Which mechanism fits this requirement?
choices: A public IP address on each application VM
VPC peering between each application project and the central project
Private Google Access enabled on every subnet
Shared VPC, with the central project as the host and the application projects as service projects
questions.why: Shared VPC lets one host project own the network while service projects launch resources into its subnets, which matches the split of control described.

questions.prompt: Network P is peered with network Q, and Q is peered with network R. A VM in P tries to open a connection to a VM in R using internal addresses. What is the result?
choices: It fails, because peering does not pass traffic through an intermediate network.
It works only if Private Google Access is enabled on R's subnet.
It works, because P and R are both connected to Q.
It works only if P and R have an external IP address.
questions.why: Peering is not transitive, so P can reach Q and Q can reach R, but P cannot reach R through Q.

questions.prompt: A team peers its VPC with a partner's VPC and also turns on Private Google Access for the subnet that holds its VMs. One VM has only an internal IP address and tries to load a public news website on the open internet. What happens?
choices: It loads, because Private Google Access gives general internet access to internal VMs.
It loads only after the team adds a public IP to the partner's subnet.
It does not load, because neither peering nor Private Google Access provides general internet access.
It loads, because peering to the partner network opens an internet route.
questions.why: Peering links internal address ranges between networks and Private Google Access only reaches Google APIs and services, so neither gives the VM a path to the public internet.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why their VM with only an internal IP cannot reach a Cloud Storage bucket after their network was peered with another team's, and whether peering is the right way to link three teams' networks. Explain which mechanism fits each case, and name one limit of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: Peering did not fix the bucket problem because peering only connects two VPC networks. The VM needs Private Google Access turned on for its subnet, which lets internal-only VMs reach Google services without a public address. For three teams, peering alone is awkward because peering is not transitive: team A and team C cannot reach each other through team B unless each pair is peered directly, and overlapping address ranges block routing. If one central team should own the network and the other teams should deploy into it, Shared VPC fits better. Its limit is that it centralizes network administration in the host project, so it needs careful role assignment. Peering keeps each team's administration separate, but it scales poorly beyond a few networks.
rubricPoints: Peering links two VPC networks so internal addresses route between them, and it is not transitive.
Shared VPC has a host project that owns the network and service projects that deploy into its subnets.
Private Google Access is a per-subnet setting for reaching Google APIs without public IPs, not general internet access.
Overlapping IP ranges prevent routing between networks.
Each mechanism has a tradeoff in administration or scale.

suggested.rationale: Tracing which paths exist between networks and subnets is the hands-on skill behind choosing peering, Shared VPC, or Private Google Access, which the planned path tracer would model.

lessons.plain: Companies often need their own data centers or offices to talk to cloud networks without that traffic crossing the open internet in readable form. Google Cloud offers two ways to build that link. One is an encrypted tunnel that runs over the normal internet, scrambling the data so outsiders cannot read it. The other is a private physical link, bought directly or through a partner, that does not touch the public internet. Choosing between them depends on how much bandwidth you need, how strict your privacy rules are, and how much uptime you must guarantee.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company must connect its office network to a cloud network. Auditors say the traffic must not cross the public internet in readable form. Before reading further, what would you check first to decide between an encrypted tunnel over the internet and a private physical link?
lessons.teach:
Two mechanisms carry traffic between an on-premises network (your own data center or office) and a Google Cloud VPC network (a virtual private cloud, meaning an isolated section of cloud networking that you control). HA VPN, short for high-availability virtual private network, creates IPsec tunnels, which are encrypted connections built with the IPsec protocol suite, across the public internet. Cloud Interconnect gives you a private path instead. Dedicated Interconnect is a physical connection you order at a colocation facility where Google has presence. Partner Interconnect rents capacity through a service provider. Cloud Router exchanges routes with your side using BGP, the Border Gateway Protocol, which learns routes automatically and withdraws them when a path fails.

Why it works: VPN trust comes from cryptography, because the data is encrypted even though it shares the internet. Interconnect trust comes from the private path, but a Dedicated link does not encrypt the payload by default. You must add link-layer encryption or run HA VPN over it.

Worked example: an office needs encryption and high availability. Step 1: choose HA VPN, because encryption is required and internet transit is acceptable. Step 2: create two tunnels on two interfaces in separate zones. Step 3: have Cloud Router announce the office prefixes over BGP on each tunnel. Step 4: if one tunnel fails, BGP withdraws its routes and traffic shifts to the surviving tunnel.

Common mistake: assuming Cloud Interconnect is automatically encrypted, so an auditor requirement goes unmet. A single tunnel is also a mistake, because one failure drops the whole connection. Consequence: running systems may send plaintext over a link everyone assumed was secure.

Choose the mechanism by matching the encryption, privacy and availability requirements first, and bandwidth second.

questions.prompt: A regional bakery chain has three stores and a central office connected to a Google Cloud VPC. Its policy forbids any traffic between the stores and the cloud from crossing the public internet, so HA VPN is ruled out. The team orders a Dedicated Interconnect circuit at a colocation facility. Step 1: the private-path rule removes HA VPN, leaving Interconnect. Step 2: the team chooses Dedicated Interconnect because it is a physical private link they control. Step 3: [missing step] Step 4: Cloud Router exchanges routes with the bakery's routers using BGP, and if the circuit fails, BGP withdraws the routes. Which missing step completes the design so the encryption requirement is also met?
choices: Add link-layer encryption on the Dedicated Interconnect link, because the private path alone does not encrypt the payload.
Rent a second Dedicated circuit from a different provider so that both circuits carry the same plaintext.
Turn off BGP and use hand-written static routes so Cloud Router does not need to withdraw anything.
Replace the Dedicated link with a single HA VPN tunnel so the traffic is encrypted again.
questions.why: A Dedicated Interconnect link gives a private path but does not encrypt the payload by default, so link-layer encryption must be added to meet the encryption requirement.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the job of Cloud Router in a hybrid connection?
choices: It exchanges routes with the on-premises side using BGP and withdraws a route when its path fails.
It rents physical capacity from a service provider at a colocation facility.
It encrypts every packet with IPsec before the packet leaves the on-premises network.
It stores firewall rules that decide which VPC subnets may be reached from the internet.
questions.why: The teaching text says Cloud Router exchanges routes using BGP and withdraws them when a path fails, which is the only option that matches this role.

questions.prompt: A logistics company uses one HA VPN tunnel between its warehouse and its VPC. Its security team says the link is safe because the traffic is encrypted. What is the main weakness of this design?
choices: Encrypted tunnels require a physical circuit at a colocation facility, which the company lacks.
IPsec tunnels cannot carry BGP routes, so the warehouse prefixes are never learned.
The tunnel traffic is sent in plaintext, so the encryption claim is false.
A single tunnel means one failure drops the whole connection, so availability is not protected.
questions.why: The text names a single tunnel as a mistake because one failure drops the whole connection, while the encryption itself is provided by the IPsec tunnel.

questions.prompt: A mid-sized insurer has no equipment inside any colocation facility and wants a private path to Google Cloud without buying its own physical circuit. Which mechanism fits this situation?
choices: Dedicated Interconnect, ordered as a physical connection at a colocation facility the insurer rents.
A Cloud Router configured with static routes and no encryption, since the private path is already trusted.
Partner Interconnect, which rents capacity through a service provider instead of a physical circuit the insurer orders itself.
HA VPN running over the public internet with two tunnels on separate interfaces.
questions.why: Partner Interconnect rents capacity through a service provider, which suits an organisation without its own presence in a colocation facility, while the other options either need that presence or give up the private path.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never configured networking when you would pick HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect, and name one limit or tradeoff of the choice you would make.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would pick HA VPN when we need encryption without ordering physical hardware and can accept traffic crossing the internet, and when our bandwidth needs are moderate. It builds IPsec tunnels, so data is encrypted in transit. With two tunnels on two interfaces plus BGP through Cloud Router, a single failure reroutes traffic to the other tunnel. The tradeoff is that internet paths add variable latency and each tunnel has a capacity ceiling, so a large, latency-sensitive transfer may not fit. I would pick Cloud Interconnect when we need high bandwidth and a private, predictable path, which means ordering a dedicated or partner link. The catch is that a dedicated link is not encrypted by default, so if policy requires encryption we run HA VPN over the Interconnect or enable link-layer encryption, and we still need redundant links to meet the availability target.
rubricPoints: HA VPN encrypts traffic with IPsec tunnels over the public internet
Cloud Interconnect provides a private path that avoids the public internet
Interconnect does not encrypt Dedicated link traffic by default
Redundant tunnels or links with BGP through Cloud Router are needed for high availability

suggested.rationale: Choosing between these two mechanisms is factual product knowledge that the teaching text already covers, and no listed mission or planned engine exercises it.

lessons.plain: Some services you use, such as file storage or data APIs, are reached over the network. A server with no public address normally cannot reach them, or would send that traffic out across the public internet. Private connectivity keeps the traffic on the provider's own internal network, using internal addresses. Google Cloud offers three related ways to do this: a subnet setting that lets servers without public addresses reach Google services, a restricted route option that tightens which services are reachable, and an internal endpoint you create inside your own network that points at a chosen service. The right choice depends on what must be reached and how tightly the access must be controlled.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server has only a private address and no public address, yet it must read files from a cloud storage service. Without any special setting, what do you think happens to its traffic, and what would you change to keep it on the provider's network?
lessons.teach:
Google APIs are the service endpoints Google runs for things like storage and analytics. By default, a virtual machine with only an internal address cannot reach them unless traffic can exit through a gateway. Private Google Access, often shortened to PGA, is a setting on a subnet. When it is on, virtual machines in that subnet that have only internal addresses can reach Google APIs and services, and the traffic is delivered across Google's own network rather than the public internet. No external address or NAT gateway is needed for those calls.

Restricted Google access is a variant that uses a fixed set of Google-owned addresses reserved for services that support VPC Service Controls, a perimeter feature that limits where data can move. You point name resolution at the restricted hostname, which resolves to that fixed range, and route that range toward the default internet gateway. Traffic still stays on Google's network.

Private Service Connect, or PSC, creates an endpoint: an internal IP address inside your own network that forwards to a chosen target, either Google APIs or a service published by another project or organization. Your workloads just call that internal address.

Worked example: a VM at 10.0.1.5 with no external address calls a storage API. Step 1: its subnet has PGA enabled. Step 2: the name resolves to Google's API addresses. Step 3: the packets leave the VM toward those addresses and are carried on Google's network, so the call succeeds without an external address.

Common mistake: assuming PGA alone stops data from being copied to an unauthorised project. It does not; that control belongs to VPC Service Controls. Consequence: if PGA is missing, a batch job on a no-public-address VM times out on every API call, and enabling the subnet setting fixes it without adding a NAT gateway.

questions.prompt: Marlow Freight runs a reporting VM at 10.40.2.9 that has no external address, in a subnet where Private Google Access is already on. The team's security rules now require that calls to a storage API stay inside a VPC Service Controls perimeter, so they switch that path to restricted Google access. Their runbook has three steps. Step 1 is done: name resolution for the API hostname now points at the restricted hostname, which resolves to the fixed restricted range. Step 2 is missing from the runbook and is the step that tells the VM's traffic for that fixed range where to go. Step 3 is the test, which succeeds with the traffic kept on Google's network. Which entry correctly fills the missing step 2?
choices: Attach a temporary external IP address to the reporting VM so it can reach the restricted range
Create a NAT gateway for the subnet and send the restricted range through it
Add a route for the restricted range with the default internet gateway as the next hop
Turn off Private Google Access on the subnet so the restricted hostname is used instead
questions.why: Restricted Google access depends on routing the fixed restricted range toward the default internet gateway, which keeps the traffic on Google's own network without any external address or NAT.

questions.prompt: A team has a Compute Engine VM in a subnet with no external IP address. Which setting, applied to the subnet, lets that VM reach Google APIs and services over Google's network?
choices: Private Google Access enabled on the subnet
A VPN tunnel to the public internet
Turning off name resolution for googleapis.com
A static external IP on each VM
questions.why: Private Google Access is a subnet-level setting that lets internal-only VMs reach Google APIs over Google's network without an external address or NAT.

questions.prompt: A company's application in one Google Cloud project needs to call a service published by a partner organisation. The app must reach it through a single internal IP address in its own network. Which mechanism creates that endpoint?
choices: Restricted Google access with the restricted hostname
A default internet gateway route to the partner's public address
Private Google Access on the app's subnet
Private Service Connect endpoint
questions.why: Private Service Connect creates an internal IP address in your own network that forwards to a chosen target, including a service published by another organisation, which matches the requirement.

questions.prompt: An engineer enables Private Google Access on a subnet and then assumes that data from the VMs in it can no longer be copied to a storage bucket in an unauthorized project. Why is that assumption wrong?
choices: Private Google Access blocks only traffic that uses external addresses
Private Google Access encrypts all outbound data so copies cannot be read
Private Google Access is turned off automatically when a bucket is in another project
Private Google Access only changes the path; limiting where data can move is a VPC Service Controls job
questions.why: Private Google Access only provides a private path to Google APIs; it does not limit where data can be copied, which is the job of VPC Service Controls.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would choose Private Google Access, restricted Google access, or Private Service Connect for a private-only VM that must read from cloud storage. Name one limit of the choice you make.
lessons.modelAnswer: For a VM with only an internal address that just needs to reach Google APIs, I would start with Private Google Access on its subnet, since it is a single setting and keeps traffic on Google's network. If the organisation wants to restrict which Google services can be reached and to stop data leaving the boundary, I would use restricted Google access, which uses a fixed Google-owned range that works with VPC Service Controls. If the workload must reach a service through an internal address that other projects or on-premises hosts can also use, or a service owned by another team, I would create a Private Service Connect endpoint. A limit to mention is that PGA alone does not prevent data copying, and restricted access still needs DNS and routing set correctly for every client, including hosts outside the VPC.
rubricPoints: Private Google Access is a subnet setting that lets internal-only VMs reach Google APIs over Google's network.
Restricted Google access uses a fixed Google-owned range tied to VPC Service Controls for tighter boundary control.
Private Service Connect provides an internal endpoint IP that forwards to a chosen Google or published service.
A stated limit, such as PGA not stopping data exfiltration or DNS and routing needing correct configuration.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers cloud network boundaries, so a scenario-based reasoning exercise about choosing the right mechanism adds the most.

lessons.plain: Some computers need to reach the internet to download updates or call an outside service, but should not be reachable from the internet themselves. Cloud NAT is a Google Cloud service that lets machines with only private addresses send requests out to the internet, while the replies find their way back. Think of an office where staff can call out through one shared switchboard number, but outside callers cannot dial a desk directly. The machines stay hidden, and only their outgoing traffic shows the shared address.
lessons.guessPrompt: A virtual machine has only a private address and no public address. Without giving it a public address, how could it download a software package from a server on the internet, and why would an outside stranger still be unable to start a connection to that machine?
lessons.teach:
Network address translation, or NAT, is the rewriting of addresses on network packets as they pass through a device. Cloud NAT is Google Cloud's managed form of this. It gives virtual machines that have only an internal, private address a way to start connections to the internet using shared public addresses. A private address is one that is not routable on the public internet. A Cloud NAT gateway is the managed configuration that performs this rewriting for one region and one network. You attach it to a Cloud Router, the component that manages routing settings for the network and holds the NAT configuration.

Why it works: when a private machine sends a request out, the gateway records a mapping from the machine's internal address and source port to a shared public address and a port it chooses. The reply arrives at that public address and port, the gateway looks up the record, and it forwards the reply to the right machine. The gateway only creates records for connections that began inside, so unsolicited traffic from the internet has no record and is dropped. You get outbound access without inbound exposure.

Worked example: a VM at 10.0.0.5 calls a package mirror at 203.0.113.10 on port 443. The gateway picks public address 198.51.100.7 and source port 40001, stores the mapping, and sends the packet. The mirror replies to 198.51.100.7 port 40001. The gateway matches that to 10.0.0.5 and delivers it. A stranger sending to 198.51.100.7 port 22 has no mapping and gets nothing.

Common mistake: assuming a private VM behind NAT can be reached from the internet. It cannot, so inbound traffic needs a different path, such as a load balancer. Another mistake is ignoring port limits. Each shared public address offers a finite number of ports, so many busy connections to one destination can exhaust them, and new outbound calls then fail intermittently under load while the gateway itself looks healthy.

In a running system, a fleet of private workers that suddenly cannot fetch dependencies often points to port exhaustion or a missing route to the gateway, not to a broken application.

questions.prompt: Harbor Labs runs a reporting VM with only a private address, 172.20.3.14, in region us-central1 on the analytics-vpc network. The VM must call a vendor API at 198.51.100.80 on port 443. The team attaches a Cloud NAT gateway, the managed configuration that rewrites private addresses to shared public ones, to a Cloud Router in us-central1 on analytics-vpc. Walkthrough: (1) The VM sends its request toward the vendor. (2) The gateway picks shared public address 203.0.113.25 and port 61004, and records the mapping from 172.20.3.14 to that address and port. (3) The vendor replies to 203.0.113.25 port 61004. (4) Missing step. (5) The VM receives the reply. Which statement completes step 4?
choices: The gateway creates a new mapping for the reply and assigns it a fresh public port before forwarding.
The gateway forwards the reply to 198.51.100.80 so the vendor can confirm it was received.
The reply is delivered straight to 172.20.3.14, because private addresses are routable from the vendor's side.
The gateway looks up the stored mapping for 203.0.113.25 port 61004 and forwards the reply to 172.20.3.14.
questions.why: The gateway keeps a record of each outbound connection, so it uses the public address and port the reply arrives on to find the private VM and deliver the packet.

questions.prompt: Which property stops an unsolicited connection from the internet from reaching a private VM through Cloud NAT?
choices: The VM's operating system firewall silently rejects every packet from outside.
The Cloud Router encrypts all traffic before it leaves the region.
Each private VM is given a unique public address that is hidden from the internet.
The gateway only creates records for connections that started inside, so unsolicited inbound traffic has no record and is dropped.
questions.why: Cloud NAT tracks only connections initiated from inside, so inbound packets without a matching record have nowhere to be delivered and are dropped.

questions.prompt: A fleet of private worker VMs in a different company's project makes many simultaneous calls to a single external service. Calls begin failing intermittently under peak load, while the NAT gateway's status shows healthy. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The external service has started blocking the company's IP range.
The shared public addresses have run out of available source ports for those many connections.
The Cloud Router has been detached from the network and needs reattaching.
The workers' application code has a memory leak that only shows under load.
questions.why: Each shared public address offers a finite number of ports, so many busy connections to one destination can exhaust them, causing intermittent outbound failures even though the gateway looks healthy.

questions.prompt: A team needs customers on the internet to reach a web application running on a VM that has only a private address. Which Google Cloud mechanism fits this inbound need, and what does Cloud NAT do for it?
choices: A Cloud Router, because it forwards inbound requests to private addresses.
A load balancer in front of the VM for inbound traffic; Cloud NAT only handles the VM's outbound connections.
Cloud NAT alone, because it maps inbound requests to the VM's private address.
Cloud NAT with a larger port range, which makes inbound requests possible.
questions.why: Inbound traffic needs a separate path such as a load balancer, because Cloud NAT only supports connections started from inside and cannot make a private VM reachable from the internet.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Cloud NAT does for a group of private virtual machines, and name one limit or tradeoff they must plan for.
lessons.modelAnswer: Cloud NAT lets our private virtual machines, which have no public addresses, start outbound connections to the internet, such as fetching packages or calling a third-party API. The gateway rewrites each machine's internal address to a shared public address and remembers the mapping, so replies come back to the correct machine. Unsolicited inbound connections from the internet have no mapping and are dropped, so the machines stay unreachable from outside. The main tradeoff is port capacity. Each shared public address has a limited number of ports, so heavy traffic to one destination can exhaust them and cause intermittent outbound failures. We would watch port usage, add public addresses or adjust per-machine port allocation if needed, and use a different inbound path such as a load balancer for anything that must receive traffic.
rubricPoints: Cloud NAT gives private machines outbound-only internet access by sharing public addresses.
The gateway tracks each outgoing connection so replies return to the correct machine.
Unsolicited inbound traffic from the internet is dropped because no mapping exists.
Port capacity is finite, so heavy outbound traffic can exhaust ports and cause failures.
Inbound reachability needs a different mechanism such as a load balancer.

suggested.rationale: Tracing the path of an outbound request from a private VM through the gateway to a public destination and back would practise the translation idea, and no current mission covers it.

lessons.plain: Sensitive Data Protection is the Google Cloud service for finding personal information hidden in your data and then changing it so people who should not see the real values cannot. Imagine a shared spreadsheet where you want to keep names and card numbers out of view but still count how many customers there are. The work happens in two steps. First you scan and recognize things like email addresses or card numbers. Then you transform them: remove them, hide part of them, or swap them for stand-in values. Pseudonymization means swapping a real identifier for a consistent stand-in that only someone holding the right key can reverse.
lessons.guessPrompt: A support team exports a table with customer emails and wants to count unique customers across two tables without anyone seeing the real addresses. Which kind of transformation would you reach for first, and why?
lessons.teach:
Inspection is the step that finds sensitive data. The service uses detectors called infoTypes, which are built-in patterns such as email address, phone number or credit card number, plus custom ones you define. De-identification is the step that changes the values. Redaction removes a value entirely. Masking replaces some characters, such as showing only the last four digits. Pseudonymization replaces a real identifier with a stand-in. Deterministic encryption and keyed cryptographic hashing produce the same stand-in every time the same input appears, which keeps joins and counts working across tables. Format-preserving encryption, usually called FPE, encrypts a value but keeps its shape, so a 16-digit card number still looks like a 16-digit number and downstream systems that check format keep working. The key is held outside the data. A key can reverse the encryption; a one-way hash cannot be reversed.

Worked example: a support export has the address alice@example.com in an email column. Inspection with the EMAIL_ADDRESS infoType flags it. A deterministic transform with a key turns it into a fixed ciphertext string. The same address in a second table produces the same string, so you can still count unique customers. Someone without the key sees only the string.

Common mistake: treating an unkeyed hash as anonymization. Values such as phone numbers have a small set of possibilities, so an attacker can hash every candidate and match the result. Use a keyed transform when matching must be controlled.

Consequence in a running system: if the key is lost, pseudonymized values cannot be restored, and if inspection misses a field, the raw value passes through unchanged. Sensitive Data Protection reduces exposure only for the data it actually finds and transforms.

questions.prompt: A shipping firm keeps 12-digit tracking numbers in a shipments table and a labels table. Step 1: a custom infoType defined by the team flags the tracking-number column during inspection. Step 2: the legacy label printer rejects any value that is not exactly 12 digits, so the output must keep the same shape. Step 3: the warehouse team must later be able to reverse the transform to recover the original numbers, so the key has to stay outside the data. Step 4: the transform must therefore be the one that fits these needs. Which choice fills that blank?
choices: Redaction, which removes the tracking number entirely
Format-preserving encryption, with the key held outside the data
A one-way unkeyed hash of the tracking number
Masking that shows only the last four digits
questions.why: Format-preserving encryption keeps the 12-digit shape so the printer still accepts it, and because it is a key-based encryption the original numbers can be recovered by whoever holds the key.
