questions.prompt: A university research group replaces student ID numbers with stand-ins so that counts still match across two tables. They never need to recover the original IDs. Which transform fits this need?
choices: Keyed cryptographic hashing that produces a stable stand-in
Redaction that removes the ID entirely
Masking that shows only the last two characters
Format-preserving encryption with a key held outside the data
questions.why: Keyed cryptographic hashing gives the same stand-in every time the same input appears, which keeps counts working, and it cannot be reversed, which suits a case where originals are never needed.

questions.prompt: A retailer hashes customer phone numbers with an unkeyed SHA-256 function and describes the column as anonymized. What is the main weakness?
choices: The hash output is too short to store in a database column
Attackers can try every candidate number and match hashes
The original numbers are lost, so orders cannot be verified later
Inspection will no longer detect the column as sensitive
questions.why: Phone numbers have a small set of possible values, so an attacker can hash every candidate without a key and compare the results, which is why an unkeyed hash is not anonymization.

questions.prompt: A team deletes the key after pseudonymizing a customer table with a reversible transform, then wants the original values back. What is the consequence?
choices: The values reappear once the table is scanned again
The pseudonymized values cannot be restored, because the key that reverses the encryption is gone
The values can be recovered from the stand-ins using the hash function alone
Inspection automatically rebuilds the originals from its infoType patterns
questions.why: A key-based reversible transform can only be undone with its key, and since the key is held outside the data, losing it means the pseudonymized values stay unrecoverable.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between redacting a credit card number and pseudonymizing it with format-preserving encryption, and name one limit of the option you pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: Redaction is right when nobody downstream needs the value, such as a free-text log that only needs to show a card was used. Pseudonymization is right when the value must still be joined, counted or validated later. Format-preserving encryption keeps the 16-digit shape so existing checks still pass, and a key holder can reverse it. The limit is that it is only as safe as the key. Anyone who can reach the key can recover every card number, so the key needs tight access control and rotation planning. Also, very short values give little room for encryption to work with, so the shape-preserving option is weaker there than the same technique on longer values.
rubricPoints: Redaction removes the value and suits cases where nothing downstream needs it
Pseudonymization keeps joins, counts or format checks working where the value is still needed
Format-preserving encryption keeps the shape of the value but depends on key protection
Names a concrete limit, such as key exposure or weak results on short values

suggested.rationale: An exam-style scenario asking which transform fits a given data need adds the most, since the core skill is choosing the right control for the situation.

lessons.plain: Restricting access to data services means deciding who can open, read, or change the data stored in places like BigQuery (a warehouse for large tables you query), Cloud Storage (a store for files called objects), and Cloud SQL (a managed relational database). Access is set by saying which person or program (a principal) may do which action on which resource. The narrower the grant, the smaller the damage if something goes wrong. Think of a building: you can give a key to the whole campus, to one floor, or to one room, and good practice is the smallest key that does the job. Security engineers also add network boundaries so the data can be reached only from trusted places.
lessons.guessPrompt: A contractor needs to read one table in your data warehouse. Would you grant access at the whole project level, at the level of the single dataset that holds that table, or to every group in the company? Why?
lessons.teach: Access control on Google Cloud data services answers three questions: who (a principal, such as a user, a group, or a service account), what they may do (a permission, such as reading data), and on which resource. Identity and Access Management, called IAM, stores these grants as roles, which are named bundles of permissions. A grant made higher up, on a project or folder, flows down to everything inside it, so the level you choose decides how much you expose. The best practice is the narrowest level that still works: a dataset in BigQuery, a bucket in Cloud Storage, or a single Cloud SQL instance. For Cloud Storage, turn on uniform bucket-level access so IAM is the only control and old per-object lists cannot quietly grant more. Turn on public access prevention so nobody can make a bucket readable by everyone on the internet. BigQuery adds finer tools: policy tags can hide sensitive columns, and row access policies can filter which rows each viewer sees. Cloud SQL instances should prefer private network addresses, and IAM database authentication lets people log in with their Google identity instead of shared passwords. A service perimeter adds a network layer: even a valid credential is refused when the request comes from outside the allowed network, which limits copying data out. Worked example: an analyst group needs read access to one BigQuery dataset. Step 1: identify the principal, which is the group. Step 2: choose a read role that applies to datasets. Step 3: grant it on that dataset only. The group can now query that dataset and nothing else. Common mistake: granting a broad Editor or Owner role on the whole project to make an error disappear. Every dataset and bucket in that project then inherits that power, so one leaked key exposes everything. Narrow grants keep a single compromised identity from reaching the whole project.

questions.prompt: A fintech startup stores its loan records in a Cloud SQL instance named ledger-replica inside the project payments-dev. A reporting job runs as the service account reporting-job@payments-dev.iam.gserviceaccount.com and needs to read from that one instance. Step 1: the principal is the service account. Step 2: the narrowest resource is the single instance ledger-replica, not the whole project. Step 3 is missing from this plan. Which step completes it?
choices: Set the instance to use a private network address and have the job connect over that private path, so the instance is not reachable from the public internet.
Grant the Owner role on payments-dev so the job never hits a permission error.
Add a policy tag to every column so the job can read the table without any network restriction.
Turn on uniform bucket-level access on the instance so IAM is the only control.
questions.why: A private address keeps the instance off the public internet, which is the Cloud SQL control the teaching text recommends alongside narrow IAM grants, while the other three options are either broad grants or controls that apply to Cloud Storage or BigQuery rather than Cloud SQL networking.

questions.prompt: In Identity and Access Management, what is a role?
choices: A named bundle of permissions that is granted to a principal on a resource.
A network boundary that refuses requests from outside an allowed range.
A single permission, such as the ability to read one table.
The login identity of a user or service account.
questions.why: A role is a named group of permissions that IAM attaches to a principal on a resource, while a single permission, an identity, and a network boundary are each different things.

questions.prompt: A team stores internal design drawings in a Cloud Storage bucket and wants to make sure nobody can ever make that bucket readable by everyone on the internet. Which pair of settings best achieves this?
choices: Turn on policy tags for every object in the bucket.
Grant the Editor role on the whole project so admins can fix exposure faster.
Add the allUsers principal as a reader so the bucket is clearly marked internal.
Turn on public access prevention and turn on uniform bucket-level access.
questions.why: Public access prevention blocks anyone from making the bucket public and uniform bucket-level access makes IAM the only control, whereas the other options either open the bucket up or describe BigQuery features that do not apply to Cloud Storage objects.

questions.prompt: A team lead gives an analyst the Editor role on a whole project so that one query stops failing with a permission error on a single BigQuery table. What is the main risk of this choice?
choices: Editor only lets the analyst rename the project and its labels.
The analyst's queries will run slower because the account carries more roles.
Nothing extra happens, because Editor applies only to the table that failed.
Every dataset and bucket in the project inherits that power, so one leaked credential could expose all of them.
questions.why: Grants made on a project flow down to everything inside it, so a broad Editor role reaches every dataset and bucket, which is why a narrow grant on the one needed resource is the safer fix.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would give a data analyst read access to one BigQuery dataset in Google Cloud, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you chose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would grant the analyst's group a read-only data role on that one dataset, not on the project, so they can query that dataset and nothing else. The grant goes to a group rather than to one person, so when someone joins or leaves I change group membership and not the data permissions. The tradeoff is that dataset-level access is coarse: everyone with that role sees every table and every column in the dataset. If some columns are sensitive, I would add policy tags to hide them, or a row access policy to filter rows, and I would say so in the access request. Finally I would check that the same group does not already hold a broader role, such as project Editor, because inherited grants silently widen what the analyst can reach.
rubricPoints: Grant on the narrowest resource, the dataset, not the project.
Assign the role to a group so membership changes happen in one place.
Name the tradeoff: a dataset-level role exposes every table and column inside it.
Mention finer controls such as policy tags or row access policies for sensitive data.
Check for broader inherited roles that would widen the access.

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right control for a given data situation is best practised by reasoning through exam-style scenarios, which no current mission covers directly.

lessons.plain: A secret is any value that proves who you are or unlocks something, such as a database password, an API key, or a token that lets a program call another service. If you paste that value into code, a config file, or a chat message, anyone who can read those places can use it. Secret Manager is Google Cloud's managed vault for these values. You store the value there once, control exactly which identities may read it, and let your application fetch it when it runs. The value never has to live in your source code.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web app needs a database password. Where would you put it so that a developer who can read the code repository cannot see it, and so the password can be changed later without editing and redeploying the code? Write down your first instinct before reading on.
lessons.teach:
A secret is a value whose exposure lets someone act as you or reach a protected resource. Examples are database passwords, third-party API keys, and signing tokens. Secret Manager is Google Cloud's managed service for storing these values. Each stored item is called a secret. Every change to its contents creates a numbered secret version. Application code requests a specific version, or the latest enabled one, at the moment it needs the value.

Why this works: the contents are encrypted at rest, and access is controlled by IAM, which is Identity and Access Management, the system that decides which user, group, or service account may perform which action. A service account is an identity that a program runs as. If you grant that identity permission to read one specific secret, only that identity can read it. Each access can be recorded in audit logs, so you can later see who read what and when. Rotation means adding a new version and disabling the old one, with no code change.

Worked example: a payments service needs a database password. Step 1: an engineer creates a secret named orders-db-password and adds version 1 with the password. Step 2: the service runs as a service account called orders-api. Step 3: the platform grants orders-api read access on that one secret only. Step 4: at startup the service requests the latest version, holds the value in memory, and connects. Step 5: the password changes. A new version 2 is added and version 1 is disabled. The next start fetches version 2, and no repository file changed.

Common mistake: granting the read role at project level, so every service can read every secret, or copying the fetched value into an environment file in a shared bucket. Either move turns a controlled secret back into a broadly readable one.

Consequence in a running system: if the service account loses access, or the only enabled version is disabled, the service cannot open its database connection and fails at startup, instead of quietly running on an old password.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company keeps a webhook signing token in Secret Manager, a managed Google Cloud service for storing sensitive values, under the secret name ticket-hook-token. Step 1: an engineer adds version 1 containing the token. Step 2: the dispatch worker runs as the service account dispatch-worker, which is an identity a program runs as. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: at startup the worker requests the latest enabled version and holds the value in memory. Which action completes step 3 so that only dispatch-worker can read this secret?
choices: Grant the read permission at project level so every worker in the project can read it.
Grant dispatch-worker read access on the ticket-hook-token secret only.
Turn on audit logging so that the worker is blocked from reading the secret.
Copy the token into the worker's environment file and store that file in a shared bucket.
questions.why: Granting the read permission on that one secret limits access to the single identity named, while the other options either widen access or do not grant access at all.

questions.prompt: In Secret Manager, what is a numbered secret version?
choices: A project-level permission that lets a user read every secret in the project.
The name of the service account that is allowed to read the secret.
A record of one change to a secret's contents, which an application can request by its number.
A backup copy of the secret placed in a shared storage bucket.
questions.why: Each change to a secret's contents creates a new numbered version, and applications request either a specific version or the latest enabled one.

questions.prompt: A museum's booking service reads its API key from a secret called booking-api-key, which has versions 1 through 3. Version 3 is the only enabled version. During a cleanup, an engineer disables version 3, and then the service restarts. What happens?
choices: It starts normally, because Secret Manager always keeps disabled versions readable.
It falls back automatically to version 1 because it is the oldest version.
It keeps running on the key it loaded before the restart, because restarts reuse a saved copy.
It fails at startup, because no enabled version remains for it to fetch.
questions.why: The service requests the latest enabled version when it starts, and with none enabled it cannot obtain the value, so it fails rather than running on an old value.

questions.prompt: A parking-app team needs to change its database password without changing any application code. Which approach achieves this?
choices: Edit the password inside the source code repository and redeploy the application.
Add the new version but keep the old one enabled, so the app continues to use the old password.
Delete the secret and recreate it under the same name with the new password, then grant access again.
Add a new version containing the new password, then disable the old version, so the app fetches the new version on its next start.
questions.why: Rotation means adding a new version and disabling the old one, so the next startup fetches the new value with no code change.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is about to add a database password to a deployment why the password should live in Secret Manager instead of a plain environment variable, and name one limit or tradeoff of using it.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would store the password in Secret Manager as a secret and give only the service's own service account read access to that one secret. The app fetches the value at startup, so the password never sits in the repository, the container image, or a plain config file that many people or tools could open. Reads are logged, and rotating the password means adding a new version rather than redeploying. The tradeoff is that the app now depends on Secret Manager being reachable and on the service account having the right permission. If either breaks, startup fails, so we should test that path during deploys. Also, once the value is fetched it sits in the process's memory, so Secret Manager does not protect against a process that is already compromised. It narrows who can see the value and makes access visible, but it does not limit what the app does with it.
rubricPoints: Defines a secret and explains why plaintext copies in code or config are exposure risks
Explains that access is granted per secret through IAM to a specific service account, following least privilege
Mentions versioning so the value can be rotated without changing code
States a real limit, such as startup dependency on the service or the value existing in memory after fetch

suggested.rationale: That mission has the learner fix how a deploy gets its credential while keeping the secret out of the repo and logs, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: Every virtual machine in a cloud can ask its hosting platform a few questions about itself, such as its name, its zone, and which account it runs as. The platform keeps these facts in a small settings store called instance metadata, and a local metadata service hands them to the machine on request. Some of these settings are harmless, but others can hold SSH keys, startup scripts, or access tokens that let whoever reads or changes them take control of the machine. Protecting metadata means deciding who may write these settings, who may read them, and which request paths the platform still answers.
lessons.guessPrompt: If software on a virtual machine reads its settings from a store the platform manages, and a startup script stored there runs with full power on the next boot, who should be allowed to edit that store, and why might that matter more than who can log in to the machine?
lessons.teach:
Instance metadata is a set of key-value settings attached to a virtual machine, called an instance. Project-wide metadata is a set of values shared by every instance in a project unless an individual instance overrides them. The metadata server is a service reachable only from inside the machine at a fixed internal address; software on the machine queries it to learn its identity and to fetch short-lived credentials for the service account attached to it. Writing metadata requires an access-control permission on the instance or project, and that permission is separate from the permission to log in.

Why it matters: software on the machine trusts what it reads from metadata. A startup script or SSH key placed there can run or grant access without anyone logging in, so anyone who can write metadata can effectively run code as the machine. Tokens served by the metadata server let the machine call other cloud services with whatever roles its service account holds. The main controls are therefore: restrict who can write metadata; move SSH access to OS Login, which ties access to identities in the access-control system instead of raw keys sitting in metadata; block project-wide SSH keys on instances that should not accept them; require the newer request format that needs a special header, which stops simple forwarding tricks where an attacker tricks a web application into fetching the metadata address; and give each instance a service account holding only the roles it needs.

Worked example: a team stores a database password under a custom metadata key. Step 1: a developer with read access reads it, which is acceptable only if that read access was intended. Step 2: a contractor who holds permission to write project metadata adds a startup-script key that copies the password to a publicly readable bucket. Step 3: on the next boot the script runs as root and the password is exposed. The fix is to remove the password from metadata, keep it in a dedicated secrets store, and narrow who can write metadata.

Common mistake: treating metadata as harmless configuration because it is not labelled as a secret. Anything a machine reads from metadata is effectively trusted input, so a write is a change to code and access.

Consequence in a running system: one write to project-wide metadata can change how every instance in the project behaves at its next boot, so these changes need review and logging. Metadata protection is a write-control and trust-boundary problem as much as a secrecy problem.

questions.prompt: A clinic runs a booking app on an instance named booking-3 in a project called harbor-prod. The instance's service account can read one storage bucket and nothing else. Step 1: a flaw lets an outsider make the app fetch any address they choose, and they point it at the metadata address. Step 2: this is the step left for you to name. Step 3: the attacker receives an error page instead of a token, so the bucket stays private. Which control, applied in step 2, produced that result?
choices: The team copies the storage key into a project-wide metadata entry that every instance can read.
The team adds a second instance so the attacker's forged request is split between two machines.
The team requires the header-bearing request format, so a forged plain request is refused.
The team grants the instance a service account with the owner role across the whole project.
questions.why: Requiring the newer request format with a special header stops a forged plain fetch of the metadata address from returning a token, which is the trick the teaching text describes.

questions.prompt: A teammate says metadata is harmless configuration because nothing in it is labelled as a secret. Which response is correct?
choices: No labels mark it as sensitive, so unlabelled metadata needs no review at all before it is changed.
Yes, only keys named as passwords deserve review, since other settings cannot affect running software.
No: the machine trusts what it reads there, so any write changes code and access.
Yes, metadata is only read by the metadata server, so writes cannot reach running software.
questions.why: Software on the machine trusts metadata, so a write is effectively a change to code and access regardless of whether anything is labelled as a secret.

questions.prompt: A payments instance named ledger-5 in project kestrel-fin should never accept SSH keys that were added to the shared project metadata. Which setting applies to it?
choices: Block project-wide SSH keys on that instance so it ignores the shared list.
Delete the instance's service account so that it cannot read any metadata at all from the server.
Attach a larger machine type with more memory so it ignores metadata when the system is under heavy load.
Turn on project-wide SSH keys, which makes the instance check the shared list first.
questions.why: Blocking project-wide SSH keys on an individual instance stops it from accepting keys from the shared project metadata, as the teaching text recommends for instances that should not accept them.

questions.prompt: A developer has login access to build-9 in project quarry-dev but no permission to write its metadata. She tries to add a startup-script key. What happens and why?
choices: The write succeeds, since logging in already grants metadata write permission on the instance.
The write succeeds for the startup-script key only if the instance has a service account attached to it.
Refused: writing metadata needs its own permission, separate from the permission to log in.
The write succeeds but only takes effect after an administrator reboots the instance by hand.
questions.why: The teaching text says writing metadata requires its own access-control permission, which is separate from the permission to log in, so login alone does not allow the write.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a permission to edit a virtual machine's metadata can be as dangerous as a login, name one control you would put in place, and state its tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: Metadata is read by software on the machine and trusted, so a startup script or SSH key written there runs or grants access at the next boot without anyone logging in. That means whoever can edit metadata can effectively run code as the machine, which is why I treat the write permission as a security boundary. One control I would use is OS Login, which ties SSH access to identities in the access-control system and avoids raw keys in metadata. The tradeoff is that people need their accounts managed through the identity system, and if that system or its group membership is wrong, legitimate access can break until someone fixes it. I would pair this with logging of metadata changes so a bad write is visible and reviewable.
rubricPoints: Explains that metadata is trusted by software on the machine, so writes can run code or grant access
Names a concrete control such as narrowing write permission, OS Login, or blocking project-wide SSH keys
States a real tradeoff of that control, such as operational friction or dependence on the identity system
Notes that metadata should not hold secrets and that changes should be reviewed or logged

suggested.rationale: An exam-style situation asking who can change metadata and what follows from it adds the most, and no listed mission covers metadata directly.

lessons.plain: Data stored on a cloud service is scrambled so that someone who gets hold of the raw storage cannot read it. Unscrambling needs a secret key. This objective is about who holds that key and who can switch it off. There are three choices: Google handles everything by default, you hold a key inside Google's key service so you control its life, or the key stays in a system outside Google so Google never holds it. Each choice trades convenience against control, and against depending on another system being up.
lessons.guessPrompt: Imagine a cloud provider's disks were stolen. What single thing decides whether your stored data can be read: the disks, or the key that unlocks them? Who should hold that key, and why might a company not want the provider to hold it?
lessons.teach:
Encryption at rest means data sitting on disk or in a storage bucket is scrambled with a key, so the raw storage is unreadable without that key. Google Cloud encrypts stored data by default. The three options differ in who holds the key.

Google default encryption: Google generates and manages the keys. You do nothing, and you cannot see or revoke them directly. Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK): you create and control a key in Cloud KMS, Google's key management service, and supported services are told to use your key. If you disable that key, the data it protects becomes unreadable. External key manager (EKM): the key material lives in a key system outside Google. When a service needs the key, Google asks that external system over the network, so Google never stores the key itself.

Why it works: most services use envelope encryption. Data is encrypted with a data encryption key, and that key is wrapped (itself encrypted) by a key encryption key. Your choice decides where the outer key lives.

Worked example: a company stores customer records in a bucket using CMEK. On write, the service asks Cloud KMS to wrap a new data key with the company's key, and stores the wrapped data key beside the data. On read, it asks KMS to unwrap that key. If the company disables its key, unwrapping fails and the records cannot be read, even by Google staff.

Common mistake: assuming CMEK or EKM protects data from every risk. These options control who can unlock data; they do not replace access control. Losing or disabling a key can make data permanently unrecoverable.

Consequence in a running system: with EKM, if the external key manager is slow or down, every read or write that needs the key fails, so that outside system becomes part of your availability.

Choose default when no rule asks for key control, CMEK when you need control and audit over key use, and EKM when keys must never be held by the cloud provider.

questions.prompt: A regional bank must ensure that no cloud provider ever holds its encryption key material, and it accepts that its own key system must be reachable for its services to work. Trace the decision. Step 1: the requirement rules out Google default encryption, because Google generates and manages those keys. Step 2: the requirement also rules out CMEK, because the key still lives in Cloud KMS, which is Google's service. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the bank chooses EKM and records that its external key system is part of its availability.
choices: Ask Google staff to keep a backup copy of the bank's key in Cloud KMS as insurance.
Confirm that the external key system can be reached whenever the bank's services need to read or write encrypted data.
Switch to default encryption for archived records, since it has no availability dependency.
Store the external key inside each encrypted file so that no network call is ever needed.
questions.why: With EKM, every read or write that needs the key calls the external system, so confirming its reachability is the step that completes the decision.

questions.prompt: Which option means the key material is kept outside Google, so Google never stores the key itself?
choices: External key manager, where the key lives in a system outside Google
Both default encryption and customer-managed keys
Customer-managed encryption keys held in Cloud KMS
Google default encryption, because Google generates the keys
questions.why: With EKM the key material lives in an outside key system and Google asks it over the network when needed, so Google never stores the key.

questions.prompt: A startup wants to disable one key and immediately make a set of stored records unreadable, while keeping a record of who used the key. Which option fits best?
choices: Customer-managed encryption keys, where the company controls the key in Cloud KMS and can disable it
External key manager, where the key is controlled by Google's own service
No encryption option; access control alone can make the records unreadable
Google default encryption, where the company can revoke the key directly
questions.why: CMEK lets the company disable its own Cloud KMS key, which makes the protected data unreadable, and gives control and audit over key use, whereas default keys cannot be seen or revoked and access control does not replace key control.

questions.prompt: A team chose EKM for a reporting database. Its external key system goes down for an hour. What happens to the database?
choices: Only new writes fail, while existing reads continue because the key is kept in the database.
Reads and writes that need the key fail until the external system recovers, and the stored data is not lost.
Data is automatically re-encrypted with a Google default key, so reads continue without interruption.
Nothing changes, because the key is stored inside the database and not in the external system.
questions.why: EKM asks the external system over the network whenever the key is needed, so an outage blocks those operations until the system recovers, while the data itself remains intact.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between Google default encryption, CMEK and EKM for a new service that stores customer payment records. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from the requirement, not the feature. If no rule asks for key control, I would keep Google default encryption: Google manages the keys and their availability, and we cannot lose a key by mistake. If auditors want us to control and audit who can use the key, I would pick CMEK: we create the key in Cloud KMS, and we can disable it, which cuts off access to the data. If the payment records must never be held by the cloud provider, I would pick EKM. The tradeoff I would name for EKM is availability. Every read and write that needs the key calls our external key manager, so if that system is slow or down, the payment service fails. I would only choose EKM if we can run that external system with high availability and accept the extra latency of each call.
rubricPoints: Default encryption: Google holds and manages the keys, with no customer control over them.
CMEK: the customer creates the key in Cloud KMS and can disable it, controlling access to the data.
EKM: keys stay outside Google, so every use depends on the external system being available.
The choice follows the requirement: convenience, key control, or keeping keys away from the provider.

suggested.rationale: Picking the right key option for a stated requirement is a reasoning skill that a scenario exercise builds better than reading definitions alone.

lessons.plain: A key is a secret value that locks or unlocks data. Cloud services can keep those keys in two different kinds of places. A software key is held by ordinary managed software running on shared servers, a bit like a key kept in an office drawer that staff can reach under supervision. A hardware key lives inside a dedicated security device built so the key cannot be copied out in readable form, like a safe that only opens from inside. Hardware gives stronger assurance and is often required by strict rules, but it usually costs more and can be slower. This lesson is about deciding which kind a system actually needs.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team stores its encryption keys in ordinary managed software on shared servers, and a second team stores theirs in a dedicated tamper-resistant device. Both encrypt data correctly. What is one situation where the second team's choice would be required, and why might the first team's choice still be acceptable?
lessons.teach:
Start with the terms. A cryptographic key is the secret value a system uses to encrypt or decrypt data. A key management service (KMS) is the managed service that creates, stores, and uses those keys for you. In Google Cloud KMS, a key is given a protection level when it is created. A software-protected key has its key material handled by software on shared infrastructure. It is encrypted at rest and access-controlled, but the cryptographic operations run in general-purpose software. A hardware-protected key is held in a hardware security module (HSM), a tamper-resistant device that performs cryptographic operations internally and is built so the key cannot be read out in plain form.

Why does the choice matter? The protection level changes how much you can prove about who could ever see the key. Choose hardware when a regulation, contract, or internal policy requires keys in validated tamper-resistant hardware, or when you need the strongest assurance that key material is never exposed in software. Choose software when the data does not demand that level, when cost and simplicity matter most, or when very high volumes of operations would be expensive on dedicated hardware.

Worked example. A payments team must encrypt cardholder records. Step 1: the compliance requirement says keys must be held in validated hardware. Step 2: the team creates the key with a hardware protection level. Step 3: the application asks the KMS to encrypt, and the HSM performs the operation and returns ciphertext. Step 4: a low-risk internal export uses a software key, because its requirement is only encryption at rest.

Common mistake: defaulting to hardware for everything because it sounds safer. This adds cost and can add latency to each encrypt call without any compliance gain.

Consequence in a running system: a key's protection level is fixed when it is created. Choosing the wrong level later means creating a new key and re-encrypting the data under it, which is planned work, not a quick setting change. Decide from the requirement first, then weigh cost.

questions.prompt: A regional freight company, Northwind Freight, encrypts scanned driver licence images. Step 1: its government contract requires that encryption keys be held in validated tamper-resistant hardware. Step 2: the team creates a new key with a hardware protection level. Step 3: the team must handle the archive of images already encrypted under an older software key. Step 4: the image service sends encrypt requests to the KMS, and the HSM performs the operation and returns ciphertext. Which action completes Step 3?
choices: Leave the archive as it is, because the contract only applies to images uploaded after the new key exists.
Edit the old software key's protection level to hardware in the console, so the existing archive needs no changes at all.
Copy the old software key's material into the HSM so that the existing ciphertext can be used without changes.
Re-encrypt the archive under the new hardware key, since a key's protection level is fixed when the key is created.
questions.why: A key's protection level is set at creation and cannot be changed later, so the archive must be re-encrypted under a key that has the required hardware level.

questions.prompt: Brightwater Clinics needs a key for an internal analytics export. Its only requirement is encryption at rest, and the export makes millions of encrypt calls per day. Which protection level fits best?
choices: Software, because a software key can be upgraded to hardware later with one setting.
Software, because the only requirement is encryption at rest and high volume on dedicated hardware costs more.
Hardware, because a hardware key is the safer default for every encryption job.
Hardware, because the HSM removes any cost concern for high-volume calls.
questions.why: When the requirement is only encryption at rest and volume is high, software is the sensible choice, since dedicated hardware would add cost without a compliance gain.

questions.prompt: A team puts every key on hardware for a telemetry pipeline that performs millions of operations per hour. No regulation or contract requires hardware for this data. What is the most accurate consequence?
choices: The data becomes unreadable until the keys are exported to software.
The hardware keys are automatically downgraded to software after a month.
Compliance is breached, because hardware keys are not permitted to encrypt data at rest.
Extra cost and added latency on each encrypt call, with no compliance gain.
questions.why: Hardware adds cost and can add latency per call; without a requirement for hardware, that cost buys no extra assurance the team needs.

questions.prompt: A company created a software-protected key last year. Its auditor now requires hardware-protected keys for that data. Which action is correct?
choices: Edit the existing key's protection level in the console and keep the same ciphertext.
Create a new hardware-protected key and re-encrypt the data under it.
Export the key to an HSM file and keep using the old ciphertext unchanged.
Wait for the KMS to upgrade the key during its next automatic rotation.
questions.why: The protection level cannot be changed on an existing key, so the correct path is a new hardware key and re-encryption of the data under it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would choose a hardware-protected key over a software-protected key, and name one limit or tradeoff of the hardware choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd choose a hardware-protected key when a rule or contract says keys must live in validated tamper-resistant hardware, or when the data is sensitive enough that we want the strongest proof that key material cannot be read out in software. For ordinary data that only needs encryption at rest, a software key is usually enough and simpler. The main tradeoff of hardware is cost and operational weight: dedicated devices cost more per key and per operation, and very high volumes of encrypt calls can add latency or spend. Also, the protection level is fixed when the key is created, so if we pick hardware and later find we did not need it, the fix is not a settings change. We would have to create a new key and re-encrypt the data. So I'd settle the requirement first, then check the cost, before creating the key.
rubricPoints: Hardware-protected keys are held in a tamper-resistant security module, software keys in shared software
Choose hardware when a regulation, contract, or policy demands it or the strongest assurance is needed
Hardware carries higher cost and possibly latency, so it is not automatically better
The protection level is fixed at key creation, so changing it means re-encrypting data under a new key

suggested.rationale: The planned envelope encryption lab would let learners compare how key protection levels affect where encryption operations run and what changes when a key must be replaced.

lessons.plain: A key is a secret used to lock and unlock information. When a company stores data in the cloud, it can choose to hold some of those keys itself instead of letting the provider manage them all. Managing keys means handling their life over time: swapping in a fresh one on a schedule (rotation), cutting off access quickly if something goes wrong (revocation), and bringing in a key generated somewhere else (import). Think of a building. Rotation is changing the locks on a schedule while keeping old keys for doors you still need to open. Revocation is taking a key away from a lock. Import is handing the building's lock maker a key you cut yourself. Mishandle any of these and the data can become unreadable, which is why the details matter.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you rotate an encryption key used by a storage bucket, do you expect the files already stored in that bucket to become unreadable? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A customer-managed encryption key (CMEK) is a key you create and control in Google Cloud's key service, Cloud KMS, and point a service such as a storage bucket at it, so the service encrypts data with your key rather than a provider-owned default. Cloud External Key Manager (EKM) goes further: the key material stays in a key manager you run or buy outside Google, and Google asks that external system for the key each time it needs it. Envelope encryption is the pattern underneath both. Data is encrypted with a data key, and that data key is itself encrypted, or wrapped, by your key, so controlling the wrapping key controls access to everything beneath it.

Three lifecycle actions matter. Rotation creates a new key version on a schedule and makes it the one used for new writes, while older versions stay available so existing data can still be decrypted. Revocation cuts access. Disabling a key version blocks its use immediately and can be reversed, whereas destroying it starts a scheduled destruction window and then cannot be undone. Import, often called bring your own key, means generating key material outside Google and loading it into Cloud KMS wrapped under a transport key so the raw key is never sent in the clear. From that point you own the original copy and must protect it.

Worked example: a bucket encrypts its objects with version 1 of a CMEK key. On rotation day you create version 2 and make it primary. Step 1: new objects are written using version 2. Step 2: existing objects still open with version 1, because version 1 is still enabled. Step 3: during a cleanup you disable version 1 by mistake. Every older object now fails to read with a key-unavailable error, even though the bucket and its access settings have not changed. Re-enabling version 1 restores access.

The common mistake is treating rotation as permission to destroy old versions. Once the destruction window ends, every object encrypted under that version is lost for good.

In a running system the consequence is wider with EKM. If the external key manager is unreachable or the key has been revoked there, the cloud service cannot decrypt, so reads and writes that depend on that key fail across the application.

Any key version that still protects stored data has to stay available for as long as that data exists.

questions.prompt: Harbor Health, a clinic network, keeps its patient-record archive encrypted with a customer-managed key in Cloud KMS. It is rotating to a new key version using bring-your-own-key import. Step 1: it generates version 2's key material on its own secured server and wraps it under a transport key (a temporary key that protects key material while it travels into Cloud KMS), so the raw key is never sent in the clear. Step 2: it imports the wrapped material as version 2 and makes version 2 the primary version, so new writes use it. Step 3: [missing step] Step 4: after the retention period ends, it schedules version 1 for destruction. Which missing step belongs at Step 3?
choices: Schedule version 1 for destruction immediately, since version 2 now handles all new writes.
Confirm that no stored data still depends on version 1, and keep version 1 enabled until that is true.
Export version 1's raw key material to a spreadsheet so the team has a spare copy.
Disable version 1 so the older records are locked away and no longer at risk.
questions.why: Any key version that still protects stored data must stay available for as long as that data exists, so version 1 stays enabled until nothing depends on it.

questions.prompt: Ardent Freight, a shipping company, disables version 4 of a customer-managed key that encrypts its invoice archive. Which statement about this action is accurate?
choices: Disabling version 4 blocks its use right away, and enabling it again restores that use.
Disabling version 4 only stops new writes, while reads of existing data keep working untouched.
Disabling version 4 starts a destruction window, after which the archive is lost for good.
Disabling version 4 deletes its key material after a delay, so nothing can bring it back.
questions.why: Disabling a key version blocks its use immediately and is reversible, unlike destroying it, which starts a window after which it cannot be undone.

questions.prompt: Brightwater Clinics uses Cloud External Key Manager (EKM), where the key material stays in a key manager it runs on-premises. That key manager's server certificate expires and the cloud service can no longer reach it. What happens to the clinic's applications?
choices: Only new writes fail, while reads are served from a cached copy of the key.
Google copies the key from its own backup so that access continues without interruption.
Nothing changes, because EKM keys are held by Google and not by the external system.
Reads and writes that depend on that key fail across the application until the external key manager is reachable again.
questions.why: With EKM the cloud service asks the external key manager for the key each time it is needed, so if that system is unreachable, dependent reads and writes fail.

questions.prompt: Meridian Labs rotated its key to version 5 on a Monday. On Friday it destroyed version 4 to save storage costs, reasoning that new writes already use version 5. What is the consequence for older objects encrypted under version 4?
choices: Nothing is lost, because the service automatically re-encrypts version 4 objects under version 5 during rotation.
Only the bucket's access settings need updating, and the version 4 objects become readable again.
The bucket falls back to a provider-owned default key for old objects, so reads still succeed.
Objects encrypted under version 4 can no longer be decrypted once the destruction window ends, and this cannot be undone.
questions.why: Rotation only changes which version is used for new writes, so destroying version 4 makes every object still protected by it permanently unreadable after the destruction window ends.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between rotating a customer-managed key and revoking it, and name one limit or risk of importing your own key material instead of letting the key service generate it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Rotation creates a new version of the key and makes it the one used for new writes. The old version stays enabled so data already encrypted under it can still be decrypted, which means rotation is routine and does not lock anyone out. Revocation is the opposite: we disable or destroy a key version to stop its use, usually because the key may be exposed or a relationship is ending. Disabling is reversible and is the first move during an incident. Destroying starts a scheduled destruction window, and after that the data it protected is gone for good. The main limit of importing our own key is that we become responsible for the original key material. If we lose our copy, the key cannot be regenerated, and data encrypted under it becomes permanently unreadable. Keys the service generates avoid that burden, but then we have less control over where the key material originated.
rubricPoints: Rotation adds a new key version for new encryption while keeping older versions to decrypt existing data.
Revocation by disabling blocks use and can be reversed, while destroying is scheduled and permanent.
Imported key material is the customer's responsibility, and losing it makes the protected data unrecoverable.
Disabling a key version still needed for stored data can break running services immediately.

suggested.rationale: The planned envelope encryption lab would let the learner practise wrapping data keys under a key-encryption key and observe what rotation and disabling do to readable data.

lessons.plain: Encryption scrambles data so that only someone holding the right key can read it. The useful question is not whether to encrypt but which kind of protection fits where the data is: sitting in storage, moving across a network, or being worked on by a running program. Each situation needs a different protection, and a good engineer can name the right one for each. A lock on a filing cabinet does not protect papers while they are being carried across a room, and the same logic applies to data in a cloud system.
lessons.guessPrompt: A customer file sits in a storage bucket and is encrypted on the disks that hold it. Someone with a valid account that is allowed to read the bucket downloads the file. Does that disk encryption stop the download? Why or why not?
lessons.teach: Encryption at rest means data stored on disks or in buckets is encrypted before it is written, and decrypted when it is read back. Google Cloud does this by default using keys that Google manages. Encryption in transit means data moving between a client and a service, or between two services, is protected by TLS, a protocol that encrypts the connection and checks the server's certificate so you know who you are talking to. Encryption in use means protecting data while a program is actively computing on it, which needs hardware-based isolation called confidential computing; that topic is covered elsewhere, so here you only need to know it is a separate problem. Envelope encryption is a common pattern: a data encryption key (DEK) encrypts the data itself, and a key encryption key (KEK), held by a key service, wraps the DEK. Why it works: one large key handling every byte is slow and hard to manage, while small wrapped keys let you change the outer key without rewriting all the data. Worked example: a 2 GB export is written to a bucket. Step 1, the service generates a random DEK. Step 2, the DEK encrypts the file. Step 3, the KEK in the key service encrypts the DEK, and the wrapped DEK is stored beside the file. Step 4, to read the file, the service asks the key service to unwrap the DEK, then uses it to decrypt. Common mistake: treating encryption at rest as access control. Anyone the service lets read the file receives decrypted content, so at-rest encryption does not replace permissions. Consequence in a running system: if the export is sent to an endpoint over plain HTTP, the data is exposed in transit no matter how well the bucket is encrypted. Each stage of the data's life needs its own protection.

questions.prompt: A fleet-tracking company's driver app uploads a 15 MB route file from a phone to a storage bucket. Step 1: the phone opens a connection to the upload host using TLS, a protocol that encrypts a connection. Step 2 is missing and must be filled in before any file data is sent. Step 3: the phone sends the route file over that connection. Which choice correctly fills the missing Step 2?
choices: The phone encrypts the route file with a freshly generated DEK before sending it.
The phone turns on default encryption at rest for the destination bucket.
The phone checks the server's certificate against the host name and a trusted issuer before sending any file data.
The phone wraps the TLS session key with a KEK held in the key service.
questions.why: TLS only protects against an impostor if the client checks the server's certificate, so that check must happen before any data is sent.

questions.prompt: In envelope encryption, what is a key encryption key (KEK) for?
choices: It wraps each data encryption key (DEK), and the key service holds it.
It encrypts the bulk data directly, so every byte uses it.
It is the plaintext copy of the data that the client decrypts in memory.
It replaces TLS on connections between two services.
questions.why: In envelope encryption the KEK is held by the key service and is used to wrap the smaller DEKs, not the bulk data itself.

questions.prompt: A telemetry collector for a shipping firm pushes sensor readings over plain HTTP to a bucket that has default encryption at rest. Which statement is accurate?
choices: The readings are safe, because encryption at rest protects data from anyone who can read the bucket.
The readings are protected in use, because the bucket keeps them encrypted while the collector works on them.
The readings are protected at rest, and also in transit because the bucket encrypts them on arrival.
The readings are protected only once they are stored, so they are exposed while moving over the plain HTTP connection.
questions.why: Encryption at rest protects stored bytes only, so data in transit over an unencrypted connection stays exposed regardless of the bucket setting.

questions.prompt: A company gives a contractor read permission on a bucket and says the stored files are encrypted at rest, so the contractor cannot read their contents. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
choices: Encryption at rest applies only to data in transit, so the stored file is never encrypted for the contractor.
The contractor's data is safe because the bucket keeps the contents encrypted while the contractor reads them.
The service decrypts the file for any principal it lets read it, so at-rest encryption is not an access control.
Encryption at rest is switched off whenever a second account is added to the project.
questions.why: At-rest encryption is transparent to permitted readers, so permissions still decide who gets plaintext and encryption at rest does not replace them.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says the new export to Cloud Storage is safe because everything is encrypted. Explain to them, in your own words, which encryption applies at each stage of the export, and name one limit that encryption at rest does not solve.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would say it depends on the stage. While the export moves from our service to the bucket, TLS encrypts the connection, which protects it in transit and lets us confirm we are talking to the real service. Once it is stored, the bucket encrypts it at rest, usually with a data key that is itself wrapped by a key encryption key. The limit is that at-rest encryption is transparent to anyone whose identity is allowed to read the bucket, so it does not stop an over-permissioned account from downloading the file. Access control has to do that job. A second tradeoff is that envelope encryption makes the key service a dependency: if that key is disabled or unreachable, the data becomes unreadable, so key availability matters as much as the encryption itself.
rubricPoints: Names TLS or encryption in transit for the move from service to bucket
Explains that encryption at rest protects stored data but not against authorized readers
Notes that access control is still needed alongside encryption
Mentions the dependency on the key service when envelope encryption is used

suggested.rationale: The planned envelope encryption lab would let the learner trace how a data key and a wrapping key protect data, which is the core mechanism in this objective.

lessons.plain: A Cloud Storage bucket is a container for files, and each file inside it is called an object. A lifecycle policy is a set of automatic rules attached to a bucket that say what should happen to each object as it gets older, such as moving it to a cheaper, slower storage tier or deleting it after a set time. Instead of a person remembering to clean up old files, the rules do it on a schedule. This matters for security because data kept longer than needed is more data that could leak, and for cost because old data can sit in expensive storage. Lifecycle rules do not decide who can read the data. They decide how long the data lives and where it is kept.
lessons.guessPrompt: A bucket holds customer invoices that must be deleted exactly seven years after they were created. Would you rely on someone remembering to delete them, or on an automatic rule, and what would the storage service need to know about each file to apply that rule?
lessons.teach: A lifecycle rule has two parts. The condition says which objects it applies to, for example objects older than a given number of days, objects in a certain storage class, or the number of newer versions kept. The action says what to do when the condition matches, for example change the storage class to a colder, cheaper tier or delete the object. A bucket can hold several rules. Versioning is a bucket feature that keeps older copies of an object when it is overwritten or deleted; a live version is the current copy, and a noncurrent version is an older copy. Rules can treat these differently. Worked example: a rule deletes objects older than 365 days in a bucket named logs-archive. An object created on 3 January 2024 is 423 days old on 1 March 2025, so it matches the condition, and the action is delete. The rule is not applied the instant the age passes; the service evaluates rules periodically, so deletion happens on a later pass, often within about a day. Common mistake: assuming a move to a colder class saves money at once or that deletion is immediate. Colder classes have minimum storage durations, so deleting early is still billed for the full minimum, and a rule without a versioning condition can leave noncurrent versions piling up. Consequence in a running system: old copies keep storage costs and retained personal data alive long after the team believed they were gone. Lifecycle rules are only as correct as their conditions, so verify which versions each rule touches.

questions.prompt: A clinic keeps intake forms in a bucket named clinic-intake-pdfs. Its lifecycle rule says: when an object is older than 730 days, delete it. Example: an intake form uploaded on 1 May 2023 is checked on 1 May 2025. Step 1: count the days. From 1 May 2023 to 1 May 2024 is 366 days, because that span includes 29 February 2024. From 1 May 2024 to 1 May 2025 is 365 days. The total is 731 days. Step 2: 731 is more than 730, so the condition matches. Step 3 is missing: what does the service do next, and when?
choices: It records the match and deletes the object on a later periodic evaluation pass, often within about a day.
It marks the object for deletion and stops billing for it at that moment.
It deletes the object at the instant the 730-day mark passes, so the file is gone by 1 May 2025.
It first moves the object to a colder storage class and deletes it 30 days after that move.
questions.why: The service evaluates lifecycle rules periodically rather than the instant an age threshold is crossed, so the match is recorded and the deletion happens on a later pass.

questions.prompt: In a Cloud Storage lifecycle rule, what does the condition part do?
choices: It is the action the rule performs once matched, such as deleting the object.
It sets the total spend the bucket may reach before the rule fires.
It sets the fixed hourly time at which the service runs the rule.
It selects which objects the rule applies to, such as objects of a certain age or storage class.
questions.why: The condition is the selector that decides which objects match; the action is a separate part that runs only when the condition matches.

questions.prompt: A bucket has versioning turned on. The team wrote one rule: delete live objects older than 365 days. A year later, storage costs keep climbing even though the rule runs. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The rule deletes noncurrent copies as well, so storage should be falling but the reporting is wrong.
The rule was never evaluated, because enabling versioning changes the schedule the service uses.
Live objects are being moved to a colder class, which increases the stored size of the bucket.
The rule only targets live objects, so overwritten noncurrent versions keep accumulating with no rule removing them.
questions.why: A rule without a versioning condition does not touch noncurrent versions, so old overwritten copies pile up and keep costing money.

questions.prompt: A team moves audit exports into a colder storage class on Monday and deletes them the following Wednesday, expecting to pay only for those two days. Which statement explains the flaw in that expectation?
choices: The move itself is billed per object, so any savings only start on the Wednesday.
Colder classes have minimum storage durations, so deleting early is still billed for the full minimum.
Moving to a colder class deletes the data cheaply, so the two days cost nothing.
The service delays the move until the next day, so Wednesday's delete cancels the move entirely.
questions.why: Colder classes carry minimum storage durations, so deleting before that minimum still incurs charges for the full minimum period.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a Cloud Storage lifecycle rule does, and name one limit or tradeoff that someone setting one up must understand.
lessons.modelAnswer: A lifecycle rule is an automatic instruction on a bucket. It has a condition, such as an object being older than some number of days, and an action, such as moving it to a colder storage class or deleting it. We use these rules so data is not kept longer than needed, which reduces both the exposure if something leaks and the storage bill. The main limit is timing: the service evaluates rules periodically, so an object that matches is not removed at that exact moment; it may take up to around a day. The main tradeoff is with colder storage classes. They are cheaper per month, but they have minimum storage durations and retrieval costs, so moving an object and then deleting it early can cost more than leaving it alone. With versioning turned on, a rule should also say whether it applies to live or noncurrent versions, or old copies will quietly accumulate.
rubricPoints: A lifecycle policy is a set of automatic condition-and-action rules on a bucket.
Common actions are changing the storage class to a colder tier or deleting the object.
Rules are evaluated periodically, not instantly, so timing is approximate.
Colder classes have minimum storage durations and retrieval costs that affect the tradeoff.
With versioning, rules must distinguish live from noncurrent versions or old copies accumulate.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly rules, conditions and facts that a learner can absorb from a clear explanation, and no listed mission or planned engine covers Cloud Storage lifecycle.

lessons.plain: Confidential computing protects data while it is being used, the one state most protections miss. Data is normally encrypted on disk and while it travels over a network, but while a program works on it, the data sits decrypted in memory, where a compromised operating system, a rogue administrator, or the cloud provider's staff could in principle read it. Confidential computing closes that gap: the processor encrypts the memory of a protected machine with a key that stays inside the chip, and you can ask the hardware for a signed proof of which software is running. Think of a sealed room inside the building whose lock is held by the processor rather than by the people who run the building.
lessons.guessPrompt: A payroll app encrypts its database files on disk and uses TLS for every network connection. While it calculates totals, which place holds the data without either of those two protections, and why does that matter?
lessons.teach:
Data in use means data a program is actively working on, which in practice means it sits in memory and processor registers in readable form. Confidential computing is the family of Google Cloud controls that protects that state. The core mechanism is a trusted execution environment, or TEE: a hardware-isolated region where the processor encrypts memory with a key that never leaves the chip, so the hypervisor, the host operating system and cloud staff see only ciphertext. A Confidential VM is a virtual machine that runs inside such a TEE. Attestation is the second half of the idea: the hardware produces a signed report describing which software booted, and a relying party compares that report with the measurements it expects before trusting the machine or releasing a secret to it. Turning the feature on is a setting on the compute resource, and it works alongside encryption at rest and in transit rather than replacing them.

Worked example: a lender runs a credit model on a Confidential VM. Step 1: training data sits encrypted in Cloud Storage, so it is protected at rest. Step 2: it arrives over TLS, so it is protected in transit. Step 3: the VM boots inside its TEE and the processor produces a fresh attestation report. Step 4: the lender's key service verifies the signature and confirms the boot measurements match the approved image, and only then releases the decryption key. Step 5: the model runs, and the processor keeps the plaintext customer records encrypted in memory, so a compromised host reading that memory sees only ciphertext.

Common mistake: treating a Confidential VM as a substitute for encryption at rest and in transit, or enabling it and never checking attestation, which leaves the protection unverified. It also does not stop bugs in your own code from copying data somewhere it should not go.

Consequence: if key release is not tied to attestation, anyone able to start a look-alike machine could receive the data, so the verification step is what makes the memory protection meaningful.

questions.prompt: A regional insurer runs a claims-fraud model on a Confidential VM called claims-scorer-7. Its claim files are encrypted in Cloud Storage and arrive over TLS. The VM boots inside its TEE, a hardware-isolated region where the processor encrypts memory, and produces an attestation report, which is a signed statement of which software booted. The insurer's key service receives that report, and [GAP]. Only after that check does it release the key that decrypts the claim files. Which phrase correctly fills the gap?
choices: it stores the decryption key inside the VM's memory so the model can start faster
it re-encrypts the claim files with a new key so the release step is no longer needed
it verifies the report's signature and confirms the boot measurements match the approved image before releasing the key
it confirms the VM has a public IP address so the report can be sent back to the insurer
questions.why: Key release is tied to attestation: the key service checks the signed report and compares the measurements with the approved image before it trusts the machine with the key.

questions.prompt: What does a trusted execution environment mainly guarantee for data in use?
choices: Files on disk are encrypted with a customer-managed key before they are written to storage, covering data at rest.
Every application bug is blocked from copying sensitive values to other locations in the system.
Traffic between the client and the server is wrapped in TLS while it moves across the network.
Memory is encrypted with a key that stays inside the processor, so the host and hypervisor see only ciphertext.
questions.why: A TEE is a hardware-isolated region where the processor encrypts memory with a key kept on the chip, which is the protection for data in use.

questions.prompt: A team turns on Confidential VM for a payments service, but its database key is released to any machine that asks for it, without checking any attestation report. What is the main weakness?
choices: Once the feature is switched on, the processor stops encrypting memory for every workload on that machine.
Data travelling between the service and the database is no longer protected by TLS, so it is exposed in transit.
The attestation report is too large to store alongside the key, so the team must disable the feature to save space.
Any look-alike machine that can be started could receive the key and the data it unlocks, because nothing verified what booted.
questions.why: Without verifying attestation before key release, the memory protection is not verified, so a look-alike machine could obtain the key.

questions.prompt: A developer's service runs on a Confidential VM and has a bug that writes a copy of each customer record into a plain log file. Which statement is accurate?
choices: Encryption at rest on the log disk would stop the file from containing readable customer records.
The TEE does not stop your own code from copying data; the fix belongs in the code.
The Confidential VM feature prevents this, because the memory holding the records is encrypted.
Attestation would detect the bug and block the write before it happens.
questions.why: A TEE protects memory from outside parties but does not stop the application itself from copying data to places it should not go, so the bug must be fixed in the code.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what confidential computing protects that disk encryption and network encryption do not, and name one limit or tradeoff the team should weigh before enabling it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Disk encryption and TLS protect data when it is stored or moving, but once a program loads data into memory, it is normally plaintext there, visible to anything with control of the host. Confidential computing uses a hardware trusted execution environment so the processor encrypts that memory, which protects data in use. The important detail is that the protection is only trustworthy if we verify it: attestation gives a signed report of what booted, and our key release should depend on that check. The main tradeoffs are that it limits which machine types and maintenance options we can use, it adds some performance cost, and it does nothing about our own application bugs or data sent to the wrong place. So I would enable it for workloads where the in-memory exposure is a real risk, and keep the other two protections in place.
rubricPoints: Defines data in use as data being processed, sitting decrypted in memory
Explains that the processor encrypts memory inside a trusted execution environment
States that attestation must be checked before trusting the machine or releasing keys
Names a real limit, such as machine-type restrictions, cost, or no protection against application bugs

suggested.rationale: Choosing which state of data a risk sits in and which control fits it is best practised through a scenario that needs reasoning, not memorised facts.

lessons.plain: Machine learning systems learn from data, and they can accidentally expose that data. A model can memorize a customer's record and repeat it, a training file can be readable by people who should not see it, and a chat log can store every question users typed. This objective is about putting safeguards in place so that sensitive information does not leak out through the AI system by mistake. Nobody needs to attack the system for these leaks to happen. The safeguards cover who can reach the data, what goes into training, how the model is served, and what gets recorded.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team wants to train a chatbot on past customer support chats. Before reaching for any tool, what could go wrong with that data after the model is trained, and what would you change first?
lessons.teach:
Start with the risk. An AI or machine learning system holds three kinds of sensitive material: the training data used to teach the model, the model itself (its learned parameters and saved artifacts), and the inputs and outputs at serving time, such as the prompts users type and the answers the model returns. Unintentional exploitation means one of these is exposed by accident: a training table readable by too many people, a model that has memorized a customer's record and repeats it, a log that stores every prompt in plain text, or an endpoint reachable from the open internet.

The controls work in layers. Identity and access management (IAM, which decides who or what may perform which action on which resource) should grant the narrowest role that still lets the work happen. Data minimization means removing identifiers before training, so there is less sensitive content to leak. Customer-managed encryption keys (keys you control and can revoke) protect stored datasets and model artifacts. A service perimeter (a boundary such as VPC Service Controls that blocks data from being copied out of a defined set of projects) stops a credentialed user from exporting data to an outside project. Audit logging records who read what, so unexpected access is noticed.

Worked example: a team trains a support-chat model on tickets. Step 1: strip names, emails and account numbers from the tickets before they enter the training bucket. Step 2: grant the training service account read-only access to that one bucket. Step 3: place the bucket and training jobs inside a service perimeter. Step 4: deploy the endpoint with no public address and a restricted audience. Step 5: enable audit logs so every read is recorded.

Common mistake: granting a broad project-level Editor role to a data scientist 'to unblock them', which lets that person read every dataset and redeploy any model.

Consequence: a leaked training set or a memorized output becomes a privacy incident that cannot be recalled once copied. Controls must be designed before sensitive data goes into training, because removing information from a trained model is much harder than keeping it out in the first place.

questions.prompt: A retail bank is training a fraud-scoring model on card transaction records. Step 1: replace card numbers and customer names with random tokens before the records enter the training table. Step 2: grant the training service account (an identity used by automated jobs, not a person) read-only access to that one table. Step 3: store the saved model artifact encrypted with a customer-managed key the bank can revoke. Step 4 is missing: the online scoring endpoint must be made safe from outside access. Which action completes Step 4?
choices: Grant the whole project the Editor role so the model team can redeploy quickly.
Remove the endpoint's public address and restrict callers to the bank's internal network.
Store the prediction logs unencrypted so debugging is faster.
Give the endpoint a public address so fraud analysts can test it from home.
questions.why: A scoring endpoint reachable from the open internet is an exposure risk, so removing its public address and limiting callers to an internal network keeps it reachable only by intended users.

questions.prompt: A medical-scheduling startup wants its model to stop repeating patient phone numbers it saw during training. Which step, taken before training, most directly reduces the sensitive content that could leak?
choices: Make the model's endpoint publicly reachable so audits can check its outputs.
Remove identifiers such as phone numbers from the data before it enters training.
Enlarge the training set so the phone numbers are diluted among many other records.
Give every data scientist the Editor role so they can inspect the data.
questions.why: Data minimization removes identifiers before training, so there is less sensitive content for the model to memorize and repeat; enlarging the dataset does not remove the information.

questions.prompt: A team's serving logs store every user prompt in plain text, and a support engineer with a read role can browse them. Which statement best describes the risk and the right response?
choices: Prompts are sensitive serving-time inputs, so limit who can read the logs and avoid storing raw text where possible.
The logs are harmless because prompts are not model weights, so no change is needed.
Only the model artifact needs encryption; the logs are exempt from protection.
Make the logs public so anyone can audit them and catch misuse.
questions.why: Prompts are one of the three kinds of sensitive AI material, so an unintended readable log is an exposure, and the fix is narrower access plus less stored raw content.

questions.prompt: A credentialed employee at a logistics company tries to copy a training dataset from a protected set of projects into a project outside that set. Which control is designed to block this copy?
choices: A service perimeter, such as VPC Service Controls, that blocks data leaving a defined set of projects.
Data minimization, which removes identifiers from the dataset before training.
Audit logging, which records the copy so it can be reviewed afterward.
A customer-managed encryption key, which protects the dataset while it is stored.
questions.why: A service perimeter blocks export from a defined set of projects even for credentialed users, while encryption protects stored data, audit logs only record activity, and minimization reduces content but does not stop copies.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why protecting an AI system means protecting its training data, its model and its inputs and outputs, not only the servers it runs on. Name one limit or tradeoff of the controls you would use.
lessons.modelAnswer: An AI system is more than its servers.
