The training data can contain customer details, the trained model can memorize and repeat parts of that data, and the prompts and answers flowing through the endpoint can carry sensitive content. So I would protect each piece: strip identifiers from training data before it goes in, restrict who can read the dataset and deploy the model using narrow IAM roles, keep the data and training jobs inside a service perimeter so they cannot be copied out, and turn on audit logs. The main tradeoff is friction. Narrow roles and perimeters slow down data scientists, who may need exceptions, and removing identifiers can reduce the model's usefulness. Also, the perimeter does not stop someone who legitimately reads data from misusing what they see, so it has to be paired with access reviews and logging.
rubricPoints: Identifies training data, the model itself, and inputs and outputs as separate exposure points
Explains least-privilege access and data minimization as preventive controls
Names a concrete limit or tradeoff such as friction, reduced model quality, or perimeters not stopping insiders
Notes that detection through audit logging complements prevention

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a realistic exposure scenario and matching each risk to the right layer of control adds more than reading a list of control names.

lessons.plain: When a company runs its software on a cloud, someone has to be responsible for each layer of security, and the split depends on how much of the stack the provider runs for you. With IaaS (infrastructure as a service) you rent raw building blocks like virtual machines and networks, so you secure nearly everything above the hardware. With PaaS (platform as a service) the provider also runs the operating system and the runtime, so you mainly secure your code, your settings and your data. Think of an unfurnished flat versus a serviced apartment: the more the landlord provides, the fewer locks you have to change yourself. Knowing where this split falls tells you which security controls you must set up yourself.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team moves a customer database from virtual machines you manage to a managed database service. Before reading on, which security tasks do you think stop being your job, and which stay with you?
lessons.teach:
Shared responsibility means the cloud provider secures some layers of a service and the customer secures the rest. Which layers belong to whom depends on the service model, meaning how much of the stack the provider operates for you. The objective calls these training models, but the term that matters here is service model.

IaaS, infrastructure as a service, gives you raw compute, storage and networking, such as virtual machines and virtual networks. The provider secures the physical facilities, the hardware and the virtualization layer that splits one physical machine into many virtual ones. You secure the guest operating system and its patching, the firewall rules, the identities that can log in, the application code and the data itself.

PaaS, platform as a service, gives you a managed runtime or a managed database. The provider also patches the operating system and runs the database engine. You still secure your code, who is allowed to call the service, how the service is configured, and the data you store in it.

Why it works: each party controls the layers it operates, so the party holding the controls is the one that must set them. Responsibility follows control, not who pays the bill.

Worked example: a team runs a payments API on IaaS virtual machines. Step 1: list the layers from bottom to top: facility, hardware, virtualization, operating system, middleware, application, data. Step 2: the provider covers the bottom three. Step 3: the team owns OS patching, firewall rules, the application, and access control and encryption settings for the data. If the same API moves to a managed PaaS runtime, OS patching moves to the provider, but the team still owns the application code, the access policies and the data classification.

Common mistake: assuming that because a service is managed, the provider also handles data access and configuration. Managed services still need correct access policies and correct data settings.

Consequence in a running system: a storage bucket left readable by the public is a customer configuration error. The provider will not correct it, and customer data is exposed.

The customer always keeps responsibility for what it configures and what data it places in a service, whatever the service model.

questions.prompt: A regional clinic network stores appointment notes in a managed PaaS database, meaning a database service where the provider runs the database engine and patches the operating system beneath it. The worked sheet reads: Step 1: classify the service as PaaS. Step 2: the provider operates the facility, the hardware, the virtualization layer, the operating system and the database engine. Step 3 is left blank on the sheet and must say what the clinic still owns. Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Patching the database engine to the newest minor release, because the clinic installs the engine itself
Who may connect to the database, how the service is configured, and which patient data it holds
Nothing, because a managed service removes all customer security duties
Replacing failed disks in the data center, because the clinic leases the physical racks
questions.why: In PaaS the provider runs the engine and the platform, but the customer still controls access, configuration and the data it stores, so Step 3 must name those.

questions.prompt: A startup runs its own Linux virtual machines on a provider's raw compute service. Which party is responsible for applying operating system security patches to those machines?
choices: The provider, because it owns the hypervisor and therefore every layer above it
The operating system vendor, because the provider never handles software updates
The startup, because the guest operating system is a layer it operates
Shared equally, because both parties touch the machine
questions.why: In IaaS the customer operates the guest operating system, so the customer is responsible for patching it, while the provider covers the layers beneath the virtualization layer.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm moves its message queue from self-run servers to a managed PaaS messaging service. Which statement about the firm's remaining duties is correct?
choices: It no longer needs to review who can publish messages
It must patch the messaging engine itself before use
The provider now decides which of the firm's service accounts may publish
The firm still decides which identities may publish and how the service is configured
questions.why: Moving to PaaS shifts platform operations to the provider, but access policy and service configuration remain with the customer, so the firm still controls who may publish and how the queue is set up.

questions.prompt: A retailer stores order records in a managed PaaS database. An employee's account has been granted read access to every record by mistake. Who is responsible for correcting this?
choices: Nobody, because the provider's logs will prevent misuse
The database engine vendor, because it wrote the query code
The retailer, because access policies are a customer-owned control in any service model
The provider, because it runs the database engine
questions.why: Who may access data is a control the customer configures, and the customer keeps that responsibility whatever the service model, so the retailer must fix the policy.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that moving our service from virtual machines to a managed platform service means the provider now handles security. Explain to them, in your own words, what changes, what does not, and name one limit of this split.
lessons.modelAnswer: Moving from virtual machines to a managed platform does shift some work to the provider. Patching the operating system, maintaining the runtime and running the underlying hardware become the provider's job, so we no longer manage those layers ourselves. But the split is by layer, not by the whole service. We still own our application code, who is allowed to call the service, how it is configured, and what data we put in it and how that data is protected. A real limit is that we have less visibility and less control over the lower layers, so we have to trust the provider's controls and verify what we can through logs and configuration checks. If a storage bucket or database is set to be publicly readable, that is our mistake, and the provider will not catch it.
rubricPoints: The service model decides which layers the provider secures and which the customer secures.
IaaS leaves the operating system, network rules and application with the customer; PaaS moves the operating system and runtime to the provider.
The customer always owns access policies, service configuration and the protection of its own data.
A limit: less visibility and control over provider-managed layers, and misconfiguration remains the customer's risk.

suggested.rationale: Knowing where responsibility splits is best shown by explaining it to someone else, including its limits.

lessons.plain: An AI agent platform lets software, called an agent, read data, call tools and take actions for you, often driven by a language model. Securing it means deciding who or what the agent is allowed to be, which data and tools it can reach, where its data may travel, and what gets recorded. Think of onboarding a new employee: you give them a badge that opens only the doors they need, you keep a log of what they open, and sensitive files sit in a room they cannot carry anything out of. The same kinds of controls used for people and servers apply here, because the agent can act without a person approving each step.
lessons.guessPrompt: If an AI agent answers customer questions by reading a database table, what is the single most important thing to limit about the agent, and why would encrypting the table alone not be enough?
lessons.teach:
An agent is a program that takes actions, such as querying data or calling an API, often after a language model decides what to do next. On Google Cloud, an agent runs as an identity, which is a service account: a non-human account that other resources and policies can name. Least privilege means giving that identity only the permissions its job needs. Permissions are granted through IAM roles, which are bundles of allowed actions attached to a resource such as a project, dataset or bucket. A VPC Service Controls perimeter is a boundary around managed services in a project, so that data cannot be copied out to resources outside the boundary even by an identity that has access. Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) are keys you control that protect stored data, but encryption does not decide who may read the data once a legitimate identity asks for it. Audit logs record who called what, which lets you investigate after the fact.

Worked example: an agent answers questions using one BigQuery dataset. Step 1: the agent runs as a dedicated service account. Step 2: that account holds only a read-only data viewer role on that one dataset. Step 3: the project sits inside a service perimeter, so results cannot be sent to a project outside it. Step 4: audit logs record each query the agent makes.

Common mistake: granting the agent the Editor or Owner role 'so it works', or reusing a default service account that carries broad rights. The consequence is that a tricked instruction, such as text hidden in a customer message telling the agent to export every row, can do whatever that identity can do. A broad grant turns one manipulated answer into a data leak.

The controls that govern an agent are its identity, its granted permissions, its network boundary and its logs, and each one limits what a manipulated agent can reach.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm builds an agent that summarises delivery invoices stored in one Cloud Storage bucket called invoices-east. The steps are: (1) the agent runs as a dedicated service account named invoice-summariser; (2) that account holds only a read-only object viewer role on the invoices-east bucket; (3) MISSING STEP, which you must supply; (4) Cloud Audit Logs record each read the agent makes. Which step fits in position 3 to stop results being copied to a project outside the boundary?
choices: Place the project inside a VPC Service Controls perimeter so results cannot be sent to a project outside it
Attach a customer-managed encryption key to the bucket so the agent must present the key before reading
Disable audit logging on the bucket to reduce log volume and cost
Grant the invoice-summariser account the Owner role on the whole project so it can manage its own access
questions.why: A VPC Service Controls perimeter is the network boundary that stops data being copied to resources outside it, which is the missing control in step 3, while the other choices either misuse encryption, widen permissions, or remove the logs needed for investigation.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a service account in the context of an AI agent on Google Cloud?
choices: A network firewall rule that limits which IP addresses the agent can call
A billing code that groups the agent's costs under one budget
A human user login that the agent borrows from an employee
A non-human account that an agent runs as, which policies and resources can name
questions.why: The teaching text defines a service account as a non-human account that other resources and policies can name, and an agent runs as one.

questions.prompt: A team encrypts its Cloud Storage data with a customer-managed encryption key and assumes that no agent can now read the data. Where does this reasoning fail?
choices: Customer-managed keys automatically block every service account from reading any bucket
Audit logs are encrypted with the key, so they stop recording reads
Encryption does not decide who may read the data once a legitimate identity asks for it, so an authorised agent can still read it
Keys only apply to data in transit, so stored data is never encrypted
questions.why: The teaching text states that customer-managed keys protect stored data but do not decide who may read it once a legitimate identity asks, so access control must come from identity and permissions.

questions.prompt: An agent answers questions about a hotel chain's booking table. Its team gave the agent the default service account, which holds the Editor role across the project, and a customer message contains hidden text telling the agent to export every row. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The export fails because the default account cannot be used by agents
The export is blocked automatically because audit logs prevent writes
Nothing happens because the agent only reads answers and never writes files
The agent can carry out the export because its identity can do whatever the broad grant allows, turning one manipulated answer into a data leak
questions.why: The teaching text warns that a broad grant such as Editor on a reused default account lets a tricked instruction do whatever that identity can do, so the export would succeed.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that turning on encryption makes our new AI agent safe to deploy. Explain to them which controls actually limit what the agent can do, and name one limit of the controls you describe.
lessons.modelAnswer: Encryption protects data at rest and in transit, but it does not decide what the agent is allowed to do once it asks for data. What governs that is the agent's identity, which is a service account, and the roles granted to it. We give the agent a dedicated account with only a read-only role on the one dataset it needs, not an Editor role on the whole project. A service perimeter adds a second layer by blocking copies of that data to projects outside the boundary, and audit logs let us see every call afterward. The limit is that these controls cannot judge intent: if the agent is manipulated into using its legitimate read access in a harmful way, the perimeter and logs contain the damage and reveal it, but they do not stop the first misuse on their own. That is why we also keep the granted scope small.
rubricPoints: Encryption protects stored and transmitted data but does not decide who or what may read it.
The agent should run as a dedicated service account with least-privilege roles on specific resources.
A service perimeter limits where data can be copied, and audit logs record actions for investigation.
Controls limit damage from a manipulated agent but cannot fully prevent misuse by an identity that is allowed access.

suggested.rationale: Deciding what an agent may reach is best practised by reasoning through a realistic exam-style scenario that combines identity, boundaries and logs.

lessons.plain: Almost every application is built from other people's libraries and base images, and those parts sometimes contain known security flaws. A CVE is a public ID for one such flaw, a bit like a serial number for a known weakness. Scanning means checking your software against a list of known flaws and reporting the matches. Automating the scan inside your build pipeline, the chain that turns code into a deployable package, means every new build is checked before it ships. A known-bad component is stopped at the door instead of being found after customers are exposed.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team's app builds fine and passes all its tests, but it packages an old version of a popular open-source library that has a publicly known security flaw. Where in the release process would you want that flaw caught, and why not wait until after launch?
lessons.teach:
A CVE, short for Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, is a standard public identifier given to one specific known security flaw in a piece of software. A vulnerability scanner reads the components inside a container image or software package, such as library names and versions, and compares them against a database of known flaws. Each match is a finding with a severity rating. A CI/CD pipeline is the automated chain that builds, tests and ships code each time it changes. CI means continuous integration, and CD means continuous delivery or deployment.

Why automate it? A scan run by hand every quarter is out of date within days, because new flaws are published constantly and someone has to remember to run it. Making the scan a stage in the pipeline means every build is checked as it is made, and the pipeline can fail the build when a finding reaches a chosen severity. That is the prevention half: the risky artifact never reaches production. Google Cloud's Artifact Analysis service can scan container images stored in Artifact Registry, and on-demand scanning can run as a step in Cloud Build before the image is pushed.

Worked example. Step 1: a developer pushes a code change. Step 2: the pipeline builds a container image. Step 3: the scan step inspects the image's packages and finds an outdated library with a high-severity CVE. Step 4: the step compares that finding against a gate set to fail on HIGH or CRITICAL and returns a failure. Step 5: the deploy stage never runs, the previous healthy version keeps serving traffic, and the team is notified with the CVE ID so they can upgrade the library.

Common mistake: treating the scan as a one-time audit, or setting the gate to report-only so nothing ever blocks. A finding nobody is forced to act on is just a log line.

Consequence: a gate that is too strict blocks builds over unfixable low-risk findings, so teams learn to bypass it. Build-time scanning also cannot catch a flaw published after an image shipped, so scanning stored images on a schedule is the detection half that complements the pipeline gate.

questions.prompt: A payments startup called Larkspur builds a Node.js service into a container image. Its Cloud Build pipeline runs an on-demand scan before pushing the image to Artifact Registry, and its gate is set to fail only on CRITICAL findings. Step 1: a developer merges a change. Step 2: the pipeline builds the image. Step 3: the scan finds a HIGH-severity CVE in an XML parser library. Step 4: [missing step]. Step 5: the image is pushed and deployed to production.
choices: The image is deleted from Artifact Registry and the deploy stage is cancelled automatically.
The gate fails the build because any CVE, whatever its severity, is blocked by default.
The scan is skipped for the rest of the day because the team has already reviewed the finding.
The gate compares HIGH against its CRITICAL threshold, finds it below the line, and lets the build continue to the push and deploy.
questions.why: A gate only fails the build for findings at or above its threshold, so a HIGH finding under a CRITICAL gate lets the pipeline proceed to push and deploy.

questions.prompt: A team lead says the scanner flagged 'a CVE' in a library. Which statement correctly describes what a CVE is?
choices: A severity score from 0 to 10 that a scanner assigns to each container image it reads
A registry where container images are stored after the pipeline pushes them
A build tool that compiles source code and packages it into a container image for shipping
A public identifier for one known software flaw
questions.why: A CVE is a standard public identifier given to one specific known security flaw, not a score, a tool, or a storage location.

questions.prompt: A team sets its scan gate to report-only for a quarter. Which outcome best describes the problem?
choices: Artifact Registry deletes stored images once they contain a flagged finding.
Builds fail more often than the team can fix, so the gate has to be removed.
Findings are recorded but nothing forces action, so a risky image can still ship.
The scanner stops reading package versions, so future scans return no results at all.
questions.why: A report-only gate produces findings without blocking anything, so the risky artifact still reaches production.

questions.prompt: A team's pipeline blocks builds at HIGH or above. A CVE is published next week in a library already baked into an image running in production. Which approach catches it?
choices: Scheduled scans of stored images in Artifact Registry
Raising the gate to CRITICAL so the new finding is ignored automatically.
Nothing, because the build gate already checked every image the team ships.
Turning off the scan step so the pipeline runs faster without false alarms.
questions.why: Build-time gates only see an image when it is built, so flaws published later need scheduled scanning of stored images, which is the detection half.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how automated CVE scanning in a CI/CD pipeline works, and name one limit or tradeoff of putting the scan into the build.
lessons.modelAnswer: A CVE is a public ID for one known security flaw in a library or base image. Scanning compares what is inside our container image against a database of those flaws. Automating it means the pipeline runs the scan on every build. If a finding meets our severity threshold, such as HIGH, the build fails and nothing is deployed. The main limit is that the gate only sees flaws known at build time, so an image that passed yesterday can be flagged later when a new CVE is published. That's why we also scan images already stored in the registry on a schedule and alert the team. The other tradeoff is noise. If the threshold is too strict or includes flaws with no available fix, teams start bypassing the gate, so we set it based on both severity and whether a fix exists.
rubricPoints: Defines a CVE as a public identifier for a known security flaw
Explains that the pipeline scans every build and fails it when findings meet a severity threshold
Names a limit: the gate only catches flaws known at build time, so stored images need continued scanning
Names a tradeoff: an overly strict or noisy gate gets bypassed, so thresholds must consider fixability

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine builds a vulnerability scan gate, so reasoning through a build-time versus stored-image scenario is the best practice available.

lessons.plain: Binary Authorization is a checkpoint that runs right before a container image is allowed to start. Think of a venue where a guard checks each guest's wristband, which was stamped by staff the venue trusts. Here, the wristband is a signed approval that says the image passed the checks your team requires, such as a successful build or a reviewed scan. If the approval is missing or from an untrusted signer, the guard refuses entry. It stops unapproved software from running in the first place, rather than reporting on it afterwards.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team wants only container images that passed their tests to ever start on their cluster. Before any teaching, what would you check at the moment a container is about to start, and what would the image need to carry to prove it passed the tests?
lessons.teach:
Binary Authorization is a deploy-time gate. Before a container image is allowed to start on a GKE cluster (Google's managed Kubernetes) or a Cloud Run service (Google's managed platform for running containers), a policy check runs. The policy is a set of rules saying which images may run and which signed approvals must exist first. An image is identified by its digest, a fixed fingerprint computed from its contents, because a tag such as latest can be moved to point at anything. An attestation is a signed statement that a named check passed for one digest, such as this build came from our trusted pipeline. An attestor is the named identity whose signature the policy trusts, and it holds the key used to sign. A policy can require attestations from one or more attestors before admission.

Why it works: the check happens where the platform decides to start the workload, so an unapproved image is refused no matter who issues the deploy command. Worked example: CI builds an image, obtains digest sha256:4f2a..., runs the tests, and the build attestor signs that digest. The policy requires that attestor. A deploy referencing that digest is admitted. A deploy of a tag that points to an unsigned digest is rejected at admission.

Common mistake: signing or trusting a mutable tag rather than the digest, so the approval no longer matches what actually runs. A second mistake is assuming it finds problems in code already running; it only judges new admissions.

Consequence: a rejected rollout appears as a failed deployment, so the pipeline turns red and the denial shows up in logs. Break-glass exceptions should be narrow and audited.

Binary Authorization prevents unapproved images from starting; it does not detect what is already running.

questions.prompt: Northwind Freight runs a Cloud Run service called parcel-tracker. Its pipeline builds an image, and the scanner attestor signs the image's digest (the fixed fingerprint computed from its contents) after the scan passes. The team's policy requires that attestor. The worked flow goes like this: Step 1, the pipeline records digest sha256:9c1e.... Step 2, the scanner attestor signs that digest. Step 3, [missing step]. Step 4, the admission check finds the signature and starts the revision. Which completes the flow?
choices: The deploy must reference sha256:9c1e... directly, so the admission check matches the signed digest rather than a tag name.
The security team must add the tag stable to the policy's allowlist before the deploy.
The image must be rebuilt with a higher version number so the scanner signs it again.
The policy must be switched off for the rollout window so the revision starts without a check.
questions.why: The admission check can only match a signature to the digest the deploy actually references, so the deploy has to name that exact digest rather than a mutable tag.

questions.prompt: A payments startup asks what an attestation is in Binary Authorization. Which answer is correct?
choices: A signed statement that a named check passed for one specific digest.
The named identity that holds the signing key the policy trusts.
A list of which images are permitted to run on the cluster.
The digest, a fixed fingerprint computed from the image contents.
questions.why: An attestation is the signed statement that a named check passed for one digest; the digest is the fingerprint, the attestor is the signer, and the policy is the rule list.

questions.prompt: A retail company's GKE cluster has a policy requiring the build attestor's signature. An image was pushed with tag prod pointing to digest sha256:77ab..., which the build attestor signed. Later someone repoints the prod tag to a new digest sha256:e03d... that was never signed, and a deploy references prod. What happens?
choices: Admitted, because an earlier signed digest once carried the same tag name.
Allowed, because the policy only inspects images built within the last thirty days.
Rejected at admission, since the tag now points to an unattested digest.
Admitted with a warning in the log, then removed after the first health check.
questions.why: The deploy resolves the tag to the unsigned digest, which lacks the required attestation, so the admission check rejects it.

questions.prompt: A payments startup ran a GKE cluster last week with no Binary Authorization policy, and an unapproved image started then. The policy is enabled today. The security lead asks whether Binary Authorization will now find that running image. Which answer is correct?
choices: Binary Authorization only judges new admissions, so it does not evaluate the image already running; finding it needs a detection tool.
Binary Authorization removes running unapproved containers automatically once the policy is active.
Binary Authorization re-checks every running pod each hour and deletes the ones that fail.
Binary Authorization flags the running image and sends an alert to the security team.
questions.why: Binary Authorization is a prevention gate that acts only when a workload is admitted, so it does not detect or remove what is already running.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Binary Authorization does, how it differs from a vulnerability scanner that reports on images already running, and one limit or tradeoff of relying on it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Binary Authorization is a preventive control. When an image is about to be deployed to GKE or Cloud Run, the platform checks the image's digest against a policy that requires signed attestations from trusted attestors, such as the build pipeline. If the required signatures are missing, the deploy is refused. A scanner works differently: it detects and reports problems, such as known vulnerabilities, but it doesn't stop a deploy by itself. The main tradeoff is that the gate is only as good as the signing process. If attestors sign carelessly, or teams use break-glass exemptions too freely, the control gives false confidence. It also judges only new admissions, so it doesn't evaluate workloads already running unless they are redeployed.
rubricPoints: Binary Authorization is a deploy-time, preventive check that blocks unapproved images from starting.
Images are matched by digest, and approvals come from trusted attestors via signed attestations.
Detection tools such as scanners report on problems rather than blocking deployment.
A limit: it only checks new admissions, and weak signing or broad exemptions undermine it.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is telling prevention apart from detection in a realistic deploy scenario, which an exam-style situation to reason through teaches best.

lessons.plain: Hardening and patching means keeping the computers you run in a known, safe state without relying on someone remembering to do it by hand. Hardening removes or locks down features an attacker could use, such as unused services or open network ports. Patching installs the vendor's fixes for known software flaws. Automation means a tool does this on a schedule, across many machines at once, and reports what it did. A golden image is the saved template that new machines start from, so fixing the template fixes every machine built from it later. This matters because a fleet of hundreds of machines cannot be patched reliably one at a time by hand.
lessons.guessPrompt: You run 200 virtual machines, and a security advisory says one library on all of them has a serious flaw. Without any tooling, what are the steps you would need to take, and where could something go wrong?
lessons.teach: Hardening is making a system smaller and stricter: turning off services you do not need, restricting who can log in, and setting secure configuration values. A baseline is the agreed list of those settings. Patching is applying the vendor's fixes for known flaws. Patch management is the process of deciding what to patch, when, and checking that it happened. Automation here means a managed tool applies a baseline or a patch job on a schedule, to a selected group of machines, and reports which ones are compliant. A golden image is a saved disk template with the hardening and patches already applied; new machines are built from it. Image baking is the act of building that template from a repeatable script. Managed instance groups are sets of identical machines that can be replaced in a rolling update, one slice at a time, with a health check guarding each step. Worked example: a patch job targets all machines labelled env=prod, runs on Saturday 02:00 in three waves of about 10 percent, and allows a reboot. Wave one fails a health check, so the job stops before the rest are touched. The report shows which machines still lack the fix. Common mistake: patching the running machines but not rebuilding the golden image. Any new machine created by autoscaling then starts from the old, vulnerable template and the flaw comes back. Consequence: a patch that is not written into the image and not rebooted into effect protects only part of the fleet for only part of the time. Automation prevents the flaw from being present, and reporting detects the machines that drifted.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs 40 batch-worker VMs labelled tier=batch inside one managed instance group, which is a set of identical machines that can be replaced in rolling steps. The team's plan is: (1) select every machine labelled tier=batch with the patch tool, (2) patch in waves of 4 machines, (3) reboot each wave and confirm the health checks pass, (4) [missing step], (5) read the compliance report. Which step fills the gap so that machines created later by autoscaling also carry the fix?
choices: Bake a new golden image with the patch written in by a repeatable script, then point the group's template at it
Stop autoscaling for the whole patch window so no new machines appear
Turn off the health checks so the reboots cannot stop the job
Raise the wave size to 20 machines so the job finishes in one night
questions.why: A golden image is a saved disk template with the patch already applied, and only updating the template ensures that machines created later start from the fixed version rather than the old one.

questions.prompt: In this course's terms, what is a golden image?
choices: A live machine that is patched first and used as the reference for compliance checks
A list of agreed secure configuration values that every machine must match
A saved disk template with hardening and patches already applied, from which new machines are built
A group of identical machines that are replaced one slice at a time during an update
questions.why: The teaching text defines a golden image as a saved disk template with hardening and patches already applied, and new machines are built from it.

questions.prompt: A payments company patches 12 running VMs in a managed group, but the group's instance template still points at last quarter's image. Two days later, autoscaling adds 3 machines under load. What is the most likely result?
choices: The new machines start from the old template, so the flaw returns on part of the fleet
The compliance report resets every machine's patch level to the current version
The new machines are compliant because the group was patched
The new machines fail their health checks and are deleted automatically
questions.why: Patching running machines without rebuilding the golden image means new machines created by autoscaling start from the vulnerable template, so the protection covers only the machines that already existed.

questions.prompt: A security lead asks which tool answers this question: which of our 200 machines still lack this week's kernel fix? Which half of the work does that answer, and what is the tool for it?
choices: Prevention, by baking the hardened baseline into a golden image
Prevention, by turning off unused services on each machine by hand
Detection, by reading the patch tool's compliance report, which lists machines still missing the fix
Prevention, by changing the instance template to a newer image
questions.why: The question asks which machines have drifted from the desired state, which is detection, and the patch tool's report of compliant and non-compliant machines is the detection tool for this half.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate suggests patching servers every week with a home-made cron script instead of using managed patch tooling. In your own words, explain how patching and image hardening work together, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on automation alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: Patching fixes the flaws already present on running machines, while hardening and a golden image stop new machines from starting in an insecure state. A managed tool can apply a patch job in waves, check health between waves, and report which machines are still missing the fix. A home-made cron script usually runs blindly, does not know which machines failed, and does not reboot them, so the fix is not active. The main tradeoff of automation is that a bad patch can reach many machines quickly, so waves, health checks and a rollback plan matter. Automation also only covers what it is told to cover, so machines outside the target labels can quietly drift, and that needs separate detection.
rubricPoints: Explains that patching fixes known flaws on running machines while hardening and golden images control the starting state
Notes that new machines from an old image reintroduce the flaw unless the image is rebuilt
Describes staged rollout with health checks and reporting as the safety mechanism
Names a tradeoff such as a bad patch spreading fast or machines outside the scope drifting unnoticed

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises patch scheduling, golden images, or managed rollout, so this is best learned from reading and reasoning through the concepts.

lessons.plain: Think of a large building with many rooms and a rulebook for each floor. Some rules stop mistakes before they happen, like a lock that will not let a door be left open. Other checks walk the building regularly and report when a room has drifted from the agreed state, like a night guard who notices a window that was locked yesterday is now open. Across a whole company with hundreds of projects, nobody can check this by hand. This lesson covers the two cloud tools that do this work on Google Cloud: custom organization policies, which prevent a setting from being chosen, and posture checks with custom detectors, which notice when settings have drifted from what was intended. Knowing which half a task belongs to is the core skill.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company wants no storage bucket in its cloud to ever be publicly readable. Would you stop people from making one public, or find out after the fact that one is public? What would you use for each, and why might you need both?
lessons.teach:
An organization is the root node of a company's cloud hierarchy; folders and projects sit beneath it. A policy constraint is a rule set at one of those nodes that limits which settings resources below it may use. A custom constraint is a rule you write yourself, using a condition expression in Common Expression Language (CEL), a small language for testing fields of a resource. Drift is the gap between the configuration you intended and the configuration that actually exists. Cloud security posture management (CSPM) means continuously comparing real configuration against a baseline and reporting gaps. Security Health Analytics (SHA) is the built-in detector inside Security Command Center that finds common misconfigurations. A custom module is your own detector of the same kind, with a condition you write that produces a finding when a resource matches a bad state.

Why it works: prevention acts on a request before the change is made, so the bad state never exists. Detection acts on the resources that exist now, so it catches anything that slipped past, including resources created before the rule.

Worked example: the rule says no bucket may allow public access. First, a custom organization policy constraint on storage buckets has a CEL condition that is true when public access is requested. An engineer tries to set a bucket public. The request is evaluated, the condition is true, and the change is denied. Second, a custom SHA module uses the same condition against all existing buckets. A bucket made before the rule, or changed through a path the constraint does not cover, is listed as a finding for someone to fix.

Common mistake: assuming a constraint repairs existing resources, or that a finding stops a change. Neither is true. A constraint only judges new requests, and a finding only reports.

Consequence: without detection, an old exposed bucket stays exposed unnoticed. A constraint applied too broadly can block legitimate deployments in unrelated projects, so scope and testing matter.

Prevention is for stopping changes at the door; detection is for finding what is already inside.

questions.prompt: A company keeps its test virtual machines in one dev folder. Step 1: the team writes a custom organization policy constraint whose CEL condition is true when a VM requests an external IP address. Step 2: an engineer tries to create a new VM with an external IP, the condition evaluates true, and the request is denied. Step 3 is missing. Three VMs were created last year, before the constraint existed, and one of them has an external IP. Which step completes the sequence so that this older VM is handled?
choices: The constraint is edited so it deletes the external IP from the existing VM the moment the rule is saved, with no other action needed.
The organization policy is re-evaluated against the older VM at its next scheduled reboot, and that reboot is what denies its external IP.
A custom Security Health Analytics module using the same condition is run against existing VMs and lists the older VM as a finding for someone to fix.
The finding automatically stops the older VM, so its external IP is removed without anyone acting on the report.
questions.why: A custom detector using the same condition reports existing resources that match the bad state, while a constraint only judges new requests and a finding never changes the resource itself.

questions.prompt: A team's firewall rule was written to allow only HTTPS traffic on port 443. Months later, someone edited it in the console and also opened port 22 to everyone, and nothing in the rule file was updated. Which term best describes the gap between the intended rule and the rule that now exists?
choices: A policy constraint, meaning a rule set at a node that limits which settings resources below it may use
Drift, meaning the gap between the configuration you intended and the configuration that actually exists
A finding, meaning a report that stops a change from being made in the first place
A custom constraint, meaning a rule you write yourself using a CEL condition expression
questions.why: Drift is the name for the gap between what was intended and what actually exists, which is exactly the situation the firewall edit created.

questions.prompt: On a Friday, a security engineer adds a custom organization policy constraint requiring customer-managed encryption on Cloud SQL databases in a folder that already holds 12 databases created before the rule. Which statement about those 12 existing databases is correct?
choices: The constraint automatically re-encrypts all 12 databases the first time it is evaluated, so no further action is needed.
The constraint does nothing to the 12 databases, since it only judges new requests, so a custom detector is needed to list them.
The constraint blocks any future read or write to the 12 databases until each one is individually reviewed and approved.
The 12 databases are flagged as findings in Security Command Center, which will block their use until someone closes each finding.
questions.why: A constraint acts only on new requests and cannot repair existing resources, so detection with a custom module is the tool that reports the older ones.

questions.prompt: A security lead wants to stop anyone in a folder containing four projects from ever creating a service account key, because keys can be copied and leaked. Which approach fits the goal of preventing the action before it happens?
choices: A custom Security Health Analytics module that deletes any service account key it finds in the four projects during its nightly run.
A weekly CSPM baseline report that the team reviews and then repairs by hand whenever a key shows up in the folder.
A finding in Security Command Center that stops any new key from being created until someone closes it out in the console.
A custom organization policy constraint on the folder, which blocks the key-creation request before the key exists.
questions.why: Stopping a change at the door is prevention, so a constraint on the folder is the right tool, while the other options only detect or report after a key already exists.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks: we already have a rule that blocks public storage buckets, so why do we also need a detector for them? Explain in your own words what each control does, which one catches a bucket that was already public, and one limit or tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: The org policy constraint is preventive. It evaluates each new request to change a bucket and denies any that would make it public, so the bad state never gets created. Its limit is that it only judges requests going forward. A bucket that was made public before the rule, or changed through a path the constraint does not cover, stays public. The custom Security Health Analytics module is detective. It scans the buckets that exist now using the same condition and produces a finding for each match. It catches the old and the missed cases, but it only reports; someone still has to fix the bucket, and there is a delay between the change and the finding. So we use the constraint to stop new problems and the detector to find leftover or drifted ones.
rubricPoints: Org policy constraints are preventive and act on new requests before a change takes effect.
Custom SHA modules are detective and find resources already in a bad state.
A constraint does not fix existing resources, and a finding does not block a change.
Each control has a tradeoff: constraints can block legitimate work if scoped too broadly, and detection has a delay before someone acts.

suggested.rationale: A planned authorization policy evaluator would let the learner test a rule against sample resources and see which ones a preventive check would block and which would only be reported.

lessons.plain: Cloud networks carry a huge amount of traffic, and you need two different ways to handle it. One way is to stop unwanted traffic before it arrives, like a guard at a door checking a list. The other is to notice afterwards that something odd happened, like a camera that records who walked through and flags suspicious behaviour. This lesson covers the Google Cloud tools for both halves of network security: a firewall that enforces rules, flow records that describe which connections happened, a way to copy packets for deep inspection, an intrusion detection service that raises alerts, and a query tool for searching the logs. Knowing which tool belongs to prevention and which to detection is the core skill.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company's servers received a burst of connections from an unknown address last night. Before any teaching, which would you need to answer first: a rule that could have blocked those connections, or a record showing they happened? Why?
lessons.teach:
Prevention and detection are different jobs. A firewall rule is prevention: it decides, for each new connection, whether to allow or deny it before it reaches the machine. Cloud NGFW, Google Cloud's next-generation firewall policy, is the managed form of this; it evaluates rules against connections and can apply deeper inspection in some tiers. VPC flow logs are detection and visibility. A VPC (virtual private cloud) is your private software network inside the cloud, and flow logs record summaries of the connections crossing its subnets. Each record describes a connection's source, destination, port, protocol, byte count and time window. Flow logs are sampled and aggregated, so they show that a conversation happened, not what was said inside it.

Packet Mirroring copies the actual packets from selected virtual machines to a collector without changing the original traffic. That copy is what makes deep inspection possible. Cloud IDS (intrusion detection system) is a managed service that reads mirrored packets, matches them against known threat signatures, and raises alerts. It detects; it does not block. Log Analytics lets you run SQL queries over logs stored in Cloud Logging, so flow records can be searched and counted.

Worked example: an address 203.0.113.9 repeatedly tries port 22 on a web server. Step one, a firewall rule denying inbound SSH from outside blocks those attempts, which is prevention. Step two, flow logs show 400 attempts from that address over ten minutes, which is detection. Step three, a Log Analytics query groups those records by source address to confirm the pattern and size the problem.

Common mistake: treating flow logs as a firewall, or assuming Cloud IDS blocks attacks. Flow logs and IDS only observe. Consequence: without a preventive rule, the traffic still reaches the machine, and the logs tell you about it only after it has happened.

questions.prompt: A payments team runs a PostgreSQL database on port 5432 in subnet 10.40.0.0/24. Flow records show 85 connections from 192.0.2.77 within five minutes, and the team has finished two steps. Step one: a Log Analytics query groups the flow records by source address and counts them, giving 85 for that address. Step two: the same records show the connections were accepted and reached the database, so no preventive rule was in place. Missing step three: the team must stop further connections from that address, and this is done by ___. Which completion is correct?
choices: Adding a firewall rule that denies inbound port 5432 from 192.0.2.77
Running Packet Mirroring to copy the database's packets to a collector
Turning on Cloud IDS for the subnet, so that it blocks the address once a signature matches
Shortening the flow log sampling interval so that the records arrive sooner
questions.why: Only a firewall rule decides whether a new connection is allowed, while Cloud IDS, flow logs and Packet Mirroring only observe traffic.

questions.prompt: An analyst needs to know whether a payment service's traffic to an unknown address contained a particular suspicious string. Which pairing fits this need?
choices: Flow logs alone, since they record each connection's byte count
A firewall deny rule, which writes the string into its log entries
Log Analytics queries over flow records, which hold the full message text
Packet Mirroring to copy packets, then Cloud IDS to match signatures
questions.why: Packet Mirroring supplies the actual packets for inspection and Cloud IDS matches them against threat signatures, whereas flow logs only summarise connections and cannot show message content.

questions.prompt: A team wants to stop outbound connections from a batch VM to an unapproved external network. Which half of security operations applies, and which tool fits that half?
choices: Prevention: a firewall policy rule denying that outbound traffic
Prevention: Log Analytics, which filters connections as they happen
Detection: VPC flow logs, which record the outbound connection
Detection: Cloud IDS, which blocks the matching connection
questions.why: Stopping a connection before it happens is prevention, and a firewall policy rule is the managed tool that makes that decision, while flow logs, IDS and Log Analytics only observe or search.

questions.prompt: A team enabled VPC flow logs on a subnet and assumed that unauthorised connections from one address were being blocked. What actually happens?
choices: Flow logs blocked the address once its byte count passed a threshold
Connections still reach the machine, and the logs only describe them afterward
Cloud IDS dropped the packets, so the flow logs show no records for that address at all
Packet Mirroring stopped the copies from reaching the collector
questions.why: Flow logs are detection and visibility only, so without a preventive firewall rule the traffic still reaches the machine and the records appear after the fact.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to cloud security how you would split a network security task between prevention and detection. Name the tool for each half, and state one limit or tradeoff of the detection side.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking whether the task is to stop something or to notice it. For prevention, the tool is Cloud NGFW: firewall rules evaluate each new connection and allow or deny it before it reaches the workload. For detection, I would use VPC flow logs to see which connections happened, and Packet Mirroring plus Cloud IDS when I need packet-level signature matching. Log Analytics lets me query those records with SQL to find patterns. The main limit on the detection side is that flow logs are sampled and summarize connections, so they show who talked to whom but not the content, and anything already delivered before an alert fires has still reached its target. Detection therefore never replaces a deny rule; the two work together.
rubricPoints: Separates prevention (blocking before delivery) from detection (noticing after or during traffic).
Names Cloud NGFW as the prevention tool and VPC flow logs, Packet Mirroring with Cloud IDS, and Log Analytics as detection or analysis tools.
States that flow logs are sampled and summarize connections rather than capture full content.
Explains that detection tools do not block traffic and therefore complement, rather than replace, deny rules.

suggested.rationale: Choosing prevention or detection and the matching tool is best practised by reasoning through an incident-style scenario, which no listed mission covers directly.

lessons.plain: A logging strategy is a deliberate plan for which records your cloud systems keep, where those records go, how long they are kept, and who is allowed to read or change them. Think of it like a building's camera plan: you decide which doors are watched, where the footage is stored, how long it stays, and who holds the keys to the storage room. Logs are your main way to notice that something happened after the fact. A good plan records enough to answer who did what, when, and from where, without drowning you in noise or letting an attacker quietly erase their tracks.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose an engineer deletes a production database at 2 a.m. Which would be more useful afterward: a log record that only that engineer's own account can edit, or a copy stored where that account cannot change it? Why?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A log entry is a timestamped record of an event, such as an API call, a login or a network connection. Cloud Logging is Google Cloud's service that collects these entries. A log bucket is a storage container inside Cloud Logging where entries are kept for a retention period, meaning the number of days they must be kept before deletion. Cloud Audit Logs are built-in records of administrative actions. Data access logs record reads and writes of user data; they are often off by default and cost more to keep. A log sink is a rule that copies matching entries to another destination, such as a separate bucket or project. Least privilege means giving each person only the access the job needs.

A strategy answers four design questions. First, what to capture: administrative activity everywhere, data access on sensitive data, and network and system events that show possible attack paths. Second, where it lives: put security-relevant logs in a dedicated project or bucket that workload administrators cannot edit. Third, how long: match retention to compliance obligations and investigation needs, and lock retention on buckets so it cannot be shortened by accident. Fourth, who reads it: grant read access to a small security group and keep delete rights away from the people whose actions are being recorded.

Worked example. A company wants to know who changed a firewall rule last Tuesday. Step 1: the change produces an Admin Activity audit log entry, which is always on and kept by default. Step 2: a sink copies entries from the networking project into a security project's locked bucket. Step 3: the security team, who can read but not delete entries, filters the bucket on that rule and that time window. Step 4: the entry shows the principal, timestamp and source address, so the answer comes from a copy the workload team cannot alter.

Common mistake: sending everything to one bucket with default retention and broad access. This raises cost, buries real signals in noise, and leaves a trail that an account with project editor rights could erase.

Consequence: if the only copy of a log sits in a project where a compromised account can delete entries, the evidence disappears along with the incident. Logs detect; they do not prevent. A strategy matters because it keeps detection and investigation possible.

questions.prompt: Harbor Library Trust wants to prove which staff account exported its membership table from a storage bucket on 14 March. Their trace reads: (1) data access logging was switched on for that bucket a week earlier, because data access logs are off by default; (2) the export produced a data access entry in the library's storage project; (3) the step that is missing; (4) a security analyst filtered the protected copy by bucket name and date and found the account and source address. Which step belongs at (3)?
choices: A sink copies the entries to a separate locked bucket readable by security staff
Admin Activity logs are switched off so that only data access entries remain for review
The analyst deletes the original entries in the storage project to free up space and cut cost
The membership table is made public so that outside auditors can compare their own copies with it
questions.why: A sink copies matching entries to a separate destination that the people being recorded cannot alter, so the evidence survives if the storage project is compromised.

questions.prompt: Which statement best defines a log bucket?
choices: A rule that copies matching entries from one place to another destination such as a separate project
A permission that lets a user delete log entries across every project in an organisation for cleanup
A storage container inside Cloud Logging where entries are kept for a set retention period before deletion
A built-in record of administrative actions that is always switched on and kept by default in every project
questions.why: The teaching text defines a log bucket as a storage container inside Cloud Logging that holds entries for a retention period, while the other options describe audit logs, sinks and permissions.

questions.prompt: Lantern Pay must keep its transaction logs for seven years to meet an obligation, and it must be impossible for anyone to shorten that period by accident. Which setting best meets both needs?
choices: Turn on data access logs for every bucket and leave retention at the default
Rely on Admin Activity logs alone because they are always on and kept by default
Set the retention period on the log bucket to seven years and lock that retention
Route all entries to a bucket with 30-day retention so that storage costs stay low
questions.why: Matching retention to the obligation and locking it on the bucket stops accidental shortening, which is the fourth-step guidance in the strategy design, while the other choices either shorten retention or do not address retention at all.

questions.prompt: Northwind Freight keeps its security logs in the same project as its production workloads, with default retention, and a developer account with project editor rights is compromised and deletes the entries. What is the main consequence?
choices: Editor rights cannot remove log entries, so the deletion only affects the developer's own activity records
Investigators lose the only copy of the evidence, so they cannot trace what the attacker changed
Nothing is lost, because the deletion itself is recorded and the attacker's actions remain visible elsewhere
The logs would have prevented the intrusion in the first place, so the deletion has no further effect
questions.why: The teaching text warns that if the only copy of a log sits where a compromised account can delete entries, the evidence disappears with the incident, and logs detect rather than prevent.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should turn on every log type in every project and keep everything forever, because storage is cheap. In your own words, explain what a sound logging strategy would do instead, and name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Keeping everything forever sounds safe, but it creates real problems. Storage is cheap per gigabyte, yet data access logs on busy services can grow large and expensive, and a huge pile of entries makes real signals hard to find. Instead I would choose sources by risk: always keep administrative activity logs, turn on data access logs for projects holding sensitive data, and capture network and system events along the paths an attacker would use. I would route security-relevant copies with a sink into a separate project with locked retention, so people who run workloads cannot edit or delete the evidence. Retention would follow our compliance obligations, not a default of forever. The tradeoff is that we might miss something we did not choose to log, so I would review the source list each quarter as systems change.
rubricPoints: Logs are a detection tool that records events after they happen, not a prevention tool.
Sources are chosen by risk, including admin activity logs and data access logs for sensitive data.
Security-relevant copies are stored where workload administrators cannot alter them, with locked retention.
Retention and read access follow compliance needs and least privilege, and the answer names a real tradeoff such as cost or missed sources.

suggested.rationale: Designing a logging strategy is mainly about justifying choices and tradeoffs, which is best practised by explaining the reasoning back to someone else.

lessons.plain: When something goes wrong on a computer system, you need two things: a written record of what happened, and a way to notice quickly. Logging means the system writes down events as they happen, such as a login, a permission change, or a failed request. Monitoring means something watches those records and measurements continuously. When a watched pattern looks like an attack or a serious mistake, an alert goes off. Responding is what you do next: stop the damage, find out how far it went, and then fix the gap that let it happen. Think of a building with cameras, an alarm, and a written procedure for the guard on duty.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company's cloud account suddenly starts creating many new virtual machines at 3 a.m., and nobody on the team did it. Before any teaching, what are the first three things you would want to find out, and in what order would you check them?
lessons.teach:
A security incident is an event where data or a system has been harmed, or is clearly at risk, because someone or something without permission got access. This objective covers four linked activities. Logging is recording events, each with a time, an actor, an action and a result. Monitoring is watching those records, or numbers derived from them, continuously. Detection is the moment a watched pattern is flagged, usually as an alert. Response is the work after an alert: containment stops the harm from spreading, investigation works out what was touched, and remediation removes the cause and restores a safe state.

Why it works: attackers and mistakes leave traces. A rule such as 'this identity was used from a place it never uses' only fires if the event was recorded and something evaluates it. Without logs you cannot prove what happened. Without alerts, the logs sit unread.

Worked example. A service account, which is an identity used by a program rather than a person, has a key, a secret credential. The key is used at 03:00 from an unfamiliar address. Step 1: an audit record, a log entry of who did what to which resource, is written with the key identity, source address, time and action. Step 2: a monitoring rule matches the unusual location and raises an alert. Step 3: the responder contains it by disabling that key so new calls stop. Step 4: the responder searches the logs for everything that key did since it was created, which establishes the scope. Step 5: remediation deletes the key, moves the workload to short-lived credentials, and narrows who may create keys. Step 6: the timeline and findings are written up.

Common mistake: closing the alert after disabling the key without checking what the key already did, so data taken earlier is missed.

Consequence: if log retention is shorter than the gap between intrusion and discovery, the evidence is gone and the scope of the incident cannot be known.

questions.prompt: A regional logistics firm runs a cloud project where a developer's account is used to edit firewall rules. At 02:10 on a Sunday, that account changes a rule so that port 22, the standard port for remote shell access, is open to the whole internet. Step 1: an audit record is written with the identity, source address, time, the rule changed and the result. Step 2: a monitoring rule that flags any change opening port 22 to all addresses matches the record and raises an alert. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: the responder checks the rule history to confirm exactly when the rule was open, and writes the timeline.
choices: Responder deletes the developer's account so no further changes can be made, then closes the alert as contained.
Responder searches the logs for connections to port 22 during the window the rule was open, to find out what was reachable and what was touched.
Responder changes the rule to allow only the office address range and marks the incident resolved without reviewing any further records.
Responder waits for the next weekly audit before touching the rule, since one change is unlikely to matter and the audit will catch anything real.
questions.why: Investigation must establish what the exposure allowed, which requires searching the connection records from the period the rule was open, not just reverting the setting or closing the alert.

questions.prompt: A security team has a dashboard that counts failed logins per hour, and a rule that sends a message to on-call staff when that count passes 50. Which statement correctly describes these two parts?
choices: The dashboard is detection, because it shows the numbers, and the message is containment.
The dashboard is logging, because it records each failed login, and the message is remediation.
The dashboard is monitoring, because it watches the derived counts continuously, and the message is detection, because it flags a pattern as an alert.
Both are logging, because both store information about failed logins.
questions.why: Monitoring is continuous watching of records or numbers derived from them, and detection is the moment a watched pattern is flagged as an alert, so the dashboard is monitoring and the message is detection.

questions.prompt: A company keeps its audit logs for 7 days. An intruder who began touching customer files 30 days ago is discovered today. What is the most serious consequence for the investigation?
choices: The company must pay a fine automatically, because logs older than seven days are required by default to be reported.
The intruder's access is still active, so the investigation cannot begin until the logs are restored from a backup.
The records from the first 23 days of the intrusion no longer exist, so the full scope of what was touched cannot be known.
The investigation can only be finished by notifying the intruder first, so the log window does not matter.
questions.why: If retention is shorter than the gap between intrusion and discovery, the evidence for that gap is gone, and the scope of the incident cannot be fully established.

questions.prompt: An alert fires because an employee's session is used to download large files from a storage location at an unusual hour. Which action is containment rather than investigation or remediation?
choices: Revoking that session and blocking new use of the credential so no further downloads can happen.
Writing the timeline of events and sending it to the management team for review.
Deleting the uncommon files from the storage location and rewriting the access policy.
Reviewing every download the session made since it started, to list which files were taken.
questions.why: Containment means stopping the harm from spreading, and revoking the session and blocking the credential stops new downloads, while the other options are investigation, remediation and reporting.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only run servers the difference between detecting and responding to a security incident, and name one real limit of relying on alerts alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: Detection is noticing that something suspicious happened, usually because a rule over logs or metrics fired and produced an alert. Response is everything after that. First you contain the harm, for example by disabling a credential or isolating a machine. Then you investigate by searching the logs to find what was touched and when. Then you remediate, which means fixing the cause, such as a leaked secret or an over-broad permission, and returning to a known-good state. The main limit of alerts alone is that they only cover patterns someone already wrote a rule for, so new attack methods and slow, quiet changes can pass unnoticed. Alerts also produce false positives, and a team that ignores them will miss the real one. So alerts need a tested response procedure and periodic review of the rules themselves.
rubricPoints: Detection means noticing a suspicious event, usually through an alert from a rule over logs or metrics
Response has distinct steps: contain the harm, investigate its scope, then remediate the cause
Alerts only catch patterns someone anticipated and can produce false positives
Investigation depends on logs being recorded and kept long enough to reconstruct events

suggested.rationale: That mission has you read authentication logs to spot a suspicious pattern, which practises the detection and investigation half of this objective.

lessons.plain: Logs are the written record of what happened in a system: who logged in, what changed, which requests failed. Logs can also contain sensitive details, so the people and programs allowed to read or change them need to be chosen carefully. Designing secure access to logs means deciding who may view them, who may send copies somewhere else, who may change where they are kept, and who may delete them. The goal is that an attacker who gets one account cannot quietly erase the evidence of their own actions, and that a curious employee cannot read data they have no reason to see. Think of a security camera system: the footage only matters if the person being filmed cannot switch off or wipe the recording.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a developer on your team needs to read application error logs to debug a bug, should they also be able to delete those logs, and why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Start with the core rule: access to logs is itself a security control, so it gets least-privilege treatment like anything else. Least privilege means each identity gets only the permissions its job needs. In Google Cloud, permissions are granted through IAM (identity and access management), which attaches a role (a named bundle of permissions) to a principal (a user, a group, or a service account) at a level of the resource hierarchy such as a project or an organization.

Logs are stored in log buckets, which are containers with a retention period. Several separate permissions matter. Reading logs needs a viewer role. The ordinary viewer role usually excludes Data Access audit logs, which record reads of sensitive data, and those need the private log viewer role. Creating, changing or deleting buckets and sinks needs configuration roles, which should sit with a small platform or security group. A log sink exports a copy of matching entries to a destination such as another bucket, a storage bucket, or a Pub/Sub topic. The sink runs under its own writer identity, which must hold write permission on that destination.

Why this works: separating reading from configuring from deleting means one compromised account cannot both do damage and erase the record. Log views can narrow what a reader sees to a subset of a bucket, and a bucket can be locked with a retention policy so entries cannot be deleted before the period ends.

Worked example: a developer needs to debug a checkout error. Step 1: the team group receives the ordinary viewer role on the project. Step 2: they query checkout errors and can read them. Step 3: they try to open Data Access logs and are refused, because that needs the private viewer role, which only the security group holds. Step 4: a sink from the security group copies entries to an archive bucket, and that archive bucket has a retention lock, so nobody can shorten its retention period.

Common mistake: granting a broad Editor or Owner role to a debugging team. That quietly includes the power to delete sinks and buckets. Consequence in a running system: if an attacker using that account deletes the sink and the bucket, the evidence of earlier access is gone and the investigation starts blind.

Designing log access means deciding separately who reads, who configures, and who can erase, and then checking that no single identity holds all three.

questions.prompt: Harbor Lane Foods has a new project called cold-chain-prod. Its security group wants Data Access logs copied to a separate archive bucket that nobody can shorten. Step 1: the security group creates a log sink on the project, with the archive bucket as its destination. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: the archive bucket gets a retention lock of 400 days, so entries cannot be deleted before that period ends. Which choice completes Step 2 so that copies actually reach the archive?
choices: The cold-chain engineers are granted the Editor role so they can check the copies.
The sink's writer identity is granted write permission on the archive bucket.
The sink is given the Owner role on the project so it can create the bucket.
The retention lock is removed so the sink can write older entries.
questions.why: A sink runs under its own writer identity, and that identity must hold write permission on the destination before any entries can be copied there.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches a log bucket as the teaching text defines it?
choices: A permission that lets a user delete log sinks without changing a project.
A container that stores log entries and carries a retention period.
A service account that writes log entries into another project on behalf of a team.
A filter that hides selected entries from anyone with a viewer role.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a log bucket as a container for log entries that has a retention period, which matches only the last choice.

questions.prompt: A retail chain gives its support group the Owner role on the project that holds its logging buckets and sinks. What is the main risk in one sentence?
choices: The support group can no longer read ordinary application logs.
Billing for the logging buckets will be charged to the wrong project.
Log sinks will stop copying entries to their destinations automatically.
One identity could both read the record and erase the sinks and buckets that hold it.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that a broad role quietly includes the power to delete sinks and buckets, so one account could both do damage and erase the evidence of it.

questions.prompt: A dashboard team needs to read general project logs to build charts. It must not be able to read Data Access audit logs, and it must not change any buckets or sinks. Which role fits?
choices: The log bucket configuration role
The ordinary viewer role
The private log viewer role
The Owner role on the project
questions.why: The ordinary viewer role lets a reader see logs while usually excluding Data Access audit logs and giving no power to change buckets or sinks, so it matches the dashboard team's needs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why the person who reads production logs should not also be able to change or delete the log sinks and buckets, and name one tradeoff this separation creates.
lessons.modelAnswer: Reading logs and controlling where they go are different powers, and they should be held by different identities. If one account can read logs and also delete sinks or buckets, a single compromised login lets an attacker hide what they did, because the record of their own actions disappears. Keeping read access with the debugging team and configuration with a small security or platform group means an attacker needs two separate breaches to both act and cover it up. The tradeoff is friction: when a developer needs a new sink or a longer retention period, they must file a request and wait for the other group, which slows routine changes. Teams often accept that cost for the security benefit, and they reduce it by making the request path clear and fast, and by giving the security group an audit trail of every change.
rubricPoints: Reading logs and configuring sinks or buckets are separate permissions that should be held by separate identities.
A single account holding both can read and then erase its own evidence.
Least privilege limits the damage a compromised account can do.
Naming a real tradeoff, such as slower change requests, shows understanding of the limit.

suggested.rationale: The objective is about IAM roles, log buckets, sinks and access rules on a cloud console, which is reference material rather than a listed hands-on mission.

lessons.plain: Logs are the written record of what happened in a cloud project: who signed in, which settings changed, which service failed.
