The main property to state is that the tunnel provides confidentiality and integrity for traffic in transit, and the two-tunnel design provides availability. A common mistake is to think that Interconnect is automatically encrypted in every configuration; it is not, so encryption must be checked separately.

scenarios.title: Harborline Freight: protecting shipment and customer data
scenarios.scenario: Harborline Freight Co is a fictional mid-sized logistics firm that ships parcels across three countries. Its data team has just moved its analytics into Google Cloud. Three things need attention before launch. First, a BigQuery table called delivery_addresses holds customer names and home addresses, which count as personal data (information that can identify a specific person). Second, an engineer has pasted the password for the reporting database into a configuration file in a shared code repository. Third, a Cloud Storage bucket called export-staging collects nightly shipment files that are only needed for 90 days. Your manager, Priya, asks you to review the plan and answer these three questions: 1. For the delivery_addresses table, name the state the data is in when it sits stored, the state when it moves between services, and the state when a query is actively processing it. For each state, name the Google Cloud control that protects it there, and explain whether Google default encryption, a customer-managed encryption key (CMEK, a key you create and control in Cloud KMS), or an external key held outside Google (Cloud External Key Manager, EKM) is the right choice for the stored data, with one reason. 2. Explain where the reporting database password should live instead of the configuration file, what the service that stores it does in generic terms, and how you would make sure the old copy in the repository stops being usable. 3. Write the object lifecycle rule you would set on export-staging so files are removed after 90 days, and explain what happens to a file on day 91 and why this is not the same as deleting the bucket.
subParts: State of delivery_addresses data and the controls for each state, plus the key choice for stored data
Where the database password belongs, and how to neutralise the exposed copy
Lifecycle rule for export-staging and what happens on day 91
modelAnswer: Data at rest means data sitting on storage, such as the table's stored files. Data in transit means data moving across a network, such as a query result travelling from BigQuery to a dashboard, and it is protected by encryption on the connection (typically TLS, a standard that encrypts traffic between two endpoints). Data in use means data currently being processed in memory. Confidential computing, a technique that keeps data encrypted in memory using a hardware-backed trusted environment, is the control for that state; for a plain BigQuery query, the control is the platform's isolation plus access restrictions, and confidential options apply only if the workload is set up for them. For the stored data, Google default encryption is applied automatically and is sufficient for many workloads. Because the table holds personal addresses and Harborline needs to be able to disable access quickly, a CMEK in Cloud KMS is the better fit: the key lives in a key ring the company controls, and disabling or destroying it cuts off access to the table. EKM is justified only if a policy requires the key material to stay outside Google entirely, which is not stated here. The common mistake is assuming encryption at rest alone protects a table from people who already have query access; access control (who can read the table) is a separate control from encryption.

The password belongs in Secret Manager, a managed secrets store that keeps secret values encrypted, controls who can read them through access policies, and records each read in audit logs. The application fetches the password at runtime using its service identity, so the value never sits in code. To neutralise the exposed copy, treat the password as compromised: rotate it in the reporting database (set a new value), add the new value as a new version in Secret Manager, update the application to read the new version, then disable the old version. Removing the line from the repository is not enough because version history in the repository still contains it, so the password itself must change. The consequence on a running system is that the old password keeps working for anyone who copied it until it is rotated, so rotation must come before cleanup.

A lifecycle rule is an automatic instruction on a Cloud Storage bucket that changes or deletes objects (stored files) based on their age or other conditions. For export-staging, you add a Delete action with an age condition of 90 days, so each object is removed once it is 90 days old. On day 91 the object is no longer present in the bucket and the storage is no longer billed for it, but the bucket itself remains and continues to accept new files. Deleting the bucket would remove the container and everything in it, which is a different and far larger action. A common mistake is setting the age to count from when the file was last modified rather than from when it was created, which can keep files longer than intended if they are rewritten; check which timestamp the rule uses and confirm with a test file before relying on it for retention limits.

scenarios.title: Harbor Lane Logistics: prevent, detect, and route
scenarios.scenario: Harbor Lane Logistics is a fictional shipping-software company that runs its booking service on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE, a managed service that runs containers on clusters of virtual machines). The platform team has three concerns this quarter. First, a developer once deployed a container image that nobody had reviewed, and no one could say where it came from. Second, the security analyst wants to know right away when someone changes who holds project-level permissions, and wants those records copied into the company's external security information and event management system (SIEM, a central tool that collects and searches logs from many systems). Third, container images are built by a CI/CD pipeline (continuous integration and continuous delivery, an automated line that builds, tests, and ships code), and the team wants known software vulnerabilities (CVEs, publicly catalogued security flaws) caught before an image is ever stored for deployment. Answer the following. 1. For the unreviewed image problem, say whether the fix is automation (stopping a bad action before it happens) or detection (noticing it after it happened), name the Google Cloud tool for that half, and explain in one or two sentences what it checks. 2. For the permission-change concern, name the log type that records who changed permissions, explain how a log sink (a rule that continuously routes matching log entries to a destination) would send those records to the external SIEM, and name one access control the team should place on the logs themselves. 3. For the vulnerability concern, describe where in the pipeline the CVE scan should run and what the pipeline should do when a serious CVE is found.
subParts: Automation or detection, and the tool
Pipeline CVE scan placement and response
modelAnswer: This is automation, because the goal is to stop an unreviewed image from running at all. The tool is Binary Authorization, a deploy-time gate on GKE that only lets through container images carrying an approved attestation (a recorded, signed statement that a trusted process reviewed the image). Before a deployment starts, the gate checks that the image has the required attestation and blocks it if it does not. Detection of such events would be a separate job for logs and findings, not this gate.

The log type is Cloud Audit Logs, which are automatic records of administrative actions, including who changed an IAM policy (IAM, identity and access management, the system that grants roles to people and services), when, and from where. A log sink matches these entries using a filter and writes them to a destination, such as a Pub/Sub topic (a managed message queue) that the SIEM reads from, or a Cloud Storage bucket. The sink's own service identity must be granted write permission on the destination, or the export silently fails. An aggregated sink set at the organization level can collect the same records across all projects. One access control is to limit who can read or change the log sink and the log bucket, for example giving the security analyst a read-only role and restricting deletion or retention changes to a small admin group, so that logs cannot be quietly removed.

The scan should run in the CI/CD pipeline after the image is built and before it is pushed to the artifact registry (a managed store for container images), using vulnerability scanning that compares the image's packages against CVE data. The pipeline should fail the build and not push the image when a finding exceeds an agreed severity threshold, such as critical or high with a fix available, and it should notify the owning team with the CVE identifiers. Because new CVEs are published after an image was already stored, the team should also re-scan stored images on a schedule, not only at build time.

scenarios.title: Brightpath Labs: Trial Data in the EU
scenarios.scenario: Brightpath Labs is a fictional company that runs a research app. It stores de-identified clinical trial results in Cloud Storage, a managed object store for files, and in BigQuery, a managed analytics database. A regulator's letter sets three requirements. First, the data must stay physically within European Union regions, which is called data residency. Second, every human access to the data must be recorded in a way the company can review later. Third, the company must have a record of any access by Google's own support staff. The shared responsibility model is the agreement that splits security duties between the cloud provider, who secures the underlying infrastructure, and the customer, who secures its own data, identities, and configurations. An organization policy is a rule set at the top of a company's Google Cloud hierarchy that limits what teams can configure below it. Your team lead asks you to answer three questions for the audit file. 1. Explain which parts of the regulator's requirements Brightpath Labs is responsible for under the shared responsibility model, and which parts Google handles. 2. Name the organization-level control that can stop resources from being created outside EU regions, and explain why Assured Workloads alone does not prove compliance. 3. Explain what audit logs would show for a data-reading action in BigQuery, and state the logging setting the team must confirm to be sure those reads are recorded.
subParts: Shared responsibility split for the three requirements
Organization policy for EU-only residency and the limits of Assured Workloads
Audit log coverage for BigQuery data reads
modelAnswer: Google is responsible for securing the physical data centers, hardware, and the underlying platform. Brightpath Labs is responsible for who has access to the trial data, how identities are granted permissions, which regions its resources are placed in, and whether its logs are switched on and kept. So residency settings and access reviews fall to the customer, while physical protection falls to Google. The customer cannot hand off the duty to prove its own compliance just because the provider has certifications.

An organization policy that restricts resource locations, using the resource locations constraint, can limit where storage and BigQuery datasets may be created to EU regions. Assured Workloads is a managed setup that creates a folder with a chosen compliance regime and applies a bundle of controls, but it only covers what it configures and does not prove that the company's own data handling, staff training, or processes meet the regulator's rules. It supports compliance and does not replace the company's own evidence. Scope should be stated: the folder and projects inside it are in scope; anything outside that folder is out of scope unless separately controlled.

Admin activity logs record configuration changes and are on by default. Data access logs record reads and writes of user data, but for most services they are off by default, and BigQuery is an exception only in part, so the team must check the data access log setting on the project or folder and enable it for BigQuery. Without it, a data read may leave no entry, which would leave a gap in the regulator's requirement to review human access. The team should confirm the setting, test with a read, and confirm an entry appears in the logs.
